title: The Fathers on Matthew
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Christ means anointed, and Jesus was anointed by the divine Spirit rather than by oil from a horn.
comments.comment:
… Matthew says “of Christ,” though, because the old kings and priests were anointed with oil from the horn.

Our Jesus Christ was not named Christ because a horn anointed him, but because the divine Spirit did. For he truly and properly had the Holy Spirit himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the title Christ means and why Matthew uses it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abraham and David are named because each foreshadows Christ: Abraham the two peoples who believe, David the second Adam who is king.
comments.comment:
Matthew names Abraham because Abraham was the first type of the two peoples who would believe in Christ. He believed while still uncircumcised, and after circumcision he remained faithful.

Matthew names David especially because David too was a type of Christ. When Saul was cast out as rejected, David was appointed second as a king well-pleasing to God. In the same way, when the first human — Adam — was cast out through disobedience and no longer ruled the rest, a second Adam was brought in: Christ, king of all, so that what was lost in Adam might be recovered for humankind through Christ. He is king not only of earth but of heaven. He is called Son of Man by nature because he has all that Adam had, while now being God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Matthew names Abraham and David in the opening verse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Matthew opens with the genealogy to show that Christ was shown by the prophetic voices, so unbelievers have no excuse.
comments.comment: Blessed Matthew immediately, having had the purpose to teach all things from the prefaces, that Christ was shown according to the prophetic voices, providing the truth regarding the fulfilled promises and leaving not even one pretext of ignorance to the unbelieving ones, says, 'the book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham' (Mt 1:1).
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The genealogy names men because woman accompanies man.
comments.comment: [On why the genealogy lists men:] That is why the genealogy’s names run through men: “the woman is the glory of the man,” (1 Corinthians 11:7) an accompaniment, not the man’s beginning.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Zerubbabel rebuilding the temple and holding a stone in his hand points to Christ rebuilding the soul and giving faith that shows itself in works.
comments.comment:
Zerubbabel rebuilt the temple Solomon had once built and the Babylonians had burned. The Lord is the true builder of the rational temple that fell apart through transgressions and burned with an alien fire — a fire we ourselves kindled, not only making the soul’s intellect follow the fleshly mind as a slave, but also shamelessly lighting the fuel of the passions by what we do.

Zerubbabel also holds in his hand a stone adorned with seven eyes. For the Lord too the stone is faith in him; and it is “in the hand” (Zechariah 4:10) because faith in Christ shows itself in the practice of the commandments. The hand is plainly a symbol of practice. So the Lord, bearing the stone in his hand, teaches us to hold faith in him as something done, adorned with the seven energies of the Spirit (Zechariah 3:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Matthew says Jesus was born “out of” Mary, not “through” her, so he took his flesh from her.
comments.comment:
Matthew does not say “through whom” (Matthew 1:16) he was born, but “out of whom.” (Galatians 4:4) That overthrows Apollinaris, who claimed Christ passed through the virgin as through a tube and took nothing from her.

The evangelist says Jesus was born not through her but out of her — that is, from her all-holy blood. The apostle speaks the same way: “God sent his Son, born of a woman,” not through a woman.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Matthew words verse 16 as 'out of whom'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Matthew follows the natural line of Joseph's ancestors from Solomon, while Luke follows the line recorded by law from Nathan, and both reach Joseph.
comments.comment: … Matthew's genealogy is natural, having the succession of those born, but Luke's is considered to be of the sons inscribed according to the law for those who did not beget; for in this way, it happened that "Joseph is inscribed to Eli" (Luke 3:23), a descendant of Jacob, from Jeconiah. Thus, having started from different origins, Matthew comes from "Solomon" and Luke from "Nathan" to the same Joseph.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: After saying Jesus was born of Mary, not of Joseph, Matthew promises to explain how, since this birth differs from the others.
comments.comment: Because therefore it seemed to show something new in the transition, having said 'Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus who is called Christ' (Mt 1:16), he also promised to set forth the manner for us, according to which he is born, and says: 'Now the birth of Jesus Christ was thus'; instead of saying he was not similarly born to the others, but differently. And it is possible to understand the power of God; for indeed it is called 'spirit.'
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Betrothal gave Mary cover, a genealogy through Joseph, and a guardian.
comments.comment: She conceived after the betrothal so she would seem to have carried a child by Joseph, so the genealogy could run through him, and so she would have a guardian when plots rose against them (Matthew 1:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Matthew says she was betrothed before she conceived.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The angel calls Mary Joseph's wife so that no one will suspect another man.
comments.comment: The angel called her Joseph’s wife so no one would suspect another man. If she is named the wife of Joseph, who had not known her, the virgin is free of any thought of suspicion toward someone else (Matthew 1:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the angel calls Mary Joseph's wife.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Saving a people before birth shows Christ acts as God.
comments.comment: If he already has a people and saves them before he is born of Mary, it is clear he does so as God (Matthew 1:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'his people' shows about who Jesus is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus is the Savior and Emmanuel born of a virgin, and the angel gave the name Jesus because he will save his people from their sins.
comments.comment: … For who is so saving and a savior of the world as 'God with us, Emmanuel,' born from the experience of a woman not having a man, fulfilling the prophecy that says: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son' (Isa 7:14). The angel named the child Jesus, marking this mode of the virgin bearing without a man, and giving the reason for this designation thus. For this, he says, he shall be called Jesus, 'for he will save his people from their sins' (Matt 1:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the name Jesus and the title Emmanuel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Isaiah's sign only makes sense if the mother is a virgin, and “God with us” fits only a pure virgin's child.
comments.comment: … The Lord is recorded as having said to Ahaz: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth or in the height” (Isaiah 7:11), and next comes the sign that is given: “Behold, the virgin shall be with child and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14). What sort of sign, then, would it be for a young woman who was not a virgin to give birth? And to whom is it more fitting to bear “Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23)? To a woman who has had intercourse and conceived through a woman’s passion, or to one still pure and chaste and a virgin? For it is fitting for her to bring forth the offspring at whose birth it is said, “God with us.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Matthew reads Isaiah's 'virgin' as a miraculous sign.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Magi were the firstfruits of the Gentiles, guided by God and a star, and they showed up the Jews for not believing the signs.
comments.comment: … Many testify from the beginning to our salvation, but the beginning of all these seems to be the firstfruits of the Magi. This is also said to be the firstfruits of all the Gentiles. And not this alone, but being guided by God and by a star, they also revealed the things that were to come, and, having solved the perplexity of the Jews, they proved them condemned for not believing the signs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the Magi are and what their coming means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Magi, used to seeking signs, probably knew Balaam's prophecy of a star and came to worship the man it foretold.
comments.comment: … So the magi, wishing to do what they were used to doing, which they had formerly done by certain incantations and tricks, looked for the cause, judging that it must be a great one; and seeing a sign from God in the sky, they wanted to see what it signified. It seems to me, then, that they had the prophecies of Balaam, which Moses also recorded, since Balaam himself had been skilled in such arts. There they found what is said about the star, and the words, “I will show him, but not now; I call him blessed, but he will not draw near” (Numbers 24:17). From this they guessed that the man foretold together with the star had come into the world; and having concluded beforehand that he was stronger than all the demons and than the beings that usually appeared to them and worked for them, they wished “to worship” him (Matthew 2:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why pagan Magi would follow a star to Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Herod made even the unwilling Jews state the prophecy of the Christ's birthplace, while the Magi came as ambassadors for the nations.
comments.comment:
It was not the magi’s voice that disturbed Herod, but the rumor among all who knew the law and trusted the prophets’ words. The magi were seeking a king; the Jews were publishing that the Christ had been born.

So he left the magi, called the Jews, and asked where the Christ is born — “the one you are now publishing,” he says, “after hearing the magi.” Even unwilling, the enemies of the truth speak the truth and interpret the whole prophecy — yet in vain, for they did not add what follows.

He calls the magi ambassadors because in a way they came to the king of Israel to make peace between themselves and Israel, so that of the nations and the Jews there might be “one flock, one shepherd.” (John 10:16)

And what did that mean — that “his goings forth are from the beginning” (Micah 5:2)? People come from the ends of the inhabited world to see the manger.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel means a mind that sees God, and the church from the nations is called Israel by grace, not by flesh.
comments.comment:
Jacob was first called Israel when he saw the ladder and the angels going up and down on it through him (Genesis 28:12), wrestled with the one who appeared to him, and heard from him, “Your name shall no longer be Jacob, but Israel.” (Genesis 32:28)

The whole Jewish people received that name as something exceptional and divine, setting them apart from the other nations. Israel means a mind that sees God. That is why the church from the nations was also named Israel (Matthew 2:6) — not according to flesh, but according to divine grace.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the name Israel in the prophecy.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Magi probably came at the birth itself and saw Christ in swaddling clothes, since the star appeared before he was born.
comments.comment:
Did the magi arrive at the birth itself and see Christ in swaddling clothes, or find him later sitting in a house with his mother? I think the truer reading is the swaddling clothes.

That is also why, as we said above, the star appeared before the Lord’s birth. From this it is clear that the star also preceded the magi’s arrival (Matthew 2:7–11).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Matthew and Luke do not disagree, since Luke tells of the early days and Matthew of the Magi's arrival two years later.
comments.comment:
… But Matthew does not at all remember those things in Luke, but sets aside those things which were silent in the other; I say indeed those things concerning the Magi, who perhaps, having set out from their own land at the same time as Jesus was born, had not yet made such a long journey in a short time. But how much was this intervening time between the appearing of the star and the arrival of the Magi? The evangelist himself taught it, saying 'after two years' and 'according to the time which was determined by the Magi'; has not a two-year period already passed from the birth of the Lord until the arrival of the aforementioned?

So then those things in the sacred evangelists do not disagree, if Luke brings him up to Jerusalem with the parents on the eighth day of the birth and from there leads him to Nazareth, but Matthew records him again in Bethlehem after a two-year period having passed, and having departed from there to Egypt because of the king's plot. …
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The star stopped without leaving heaven or settling on the house, and it moved in a strange way unlike other stars.
comments.comment: The star stood as a single unmoved fixture so the magi would go no farther. It did not come down from heaven and stand on the earth, nor lodge itself above the house. Its custom was not to travel like the other stars, but to run a strange course, appearing at different times in different regions — and only then did it stand still. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the star stood over the child.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unlike the shepherds, the Magi found the child in a house with his mother and worshiped him two years after his birth.
comments.comment: They do not catch the child lying in a 'manger' just like the shepherds, but they see him inside in a 'house with his mother'. For because there was no 'place in the inn', he is placed in a 'manger'; here, after two years, he is found by the magi 'with his mother', … 'and having fallen down they worshiped him' (Mt 2:11).
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The gifts mean king, death and God, and an angel rewarded the Magi's worship by warning them to avoid Herod.
comments.comment: … They brought “gifts,” and these they “offered” to one who was, if I may call him so, a kind of compound of God and mortal man: gold as a symbol for a king, myrrh as for one who would die, and frankincense as for God (Matthew 2:11). … But since the Saviour of the human race, who exists above the angels who help human beings, was God, an angel repaid the magi for their reverence in worshipping Jesus: he warned them not to go to Herod but to return to their own country by another way (Matthew 2:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of the three gifts and the warning in 2:12.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Escaping to Egypt was better than a showy miracle that overrode Herod's free choice, for such help would spoil Christ's aim of showing a real man with something divine within.
comments.comment: … it was certainly better that the child Jesus should slip away from Herod’s plot and go abroad with those who were bringing him up “into Egypt” “until the death” of the one plotting against him (Matthew 2:14–15), than that the providence watching over Jesus should hinder the free choice of Herod, who wanted to kill the child; or that it should put about Jesus what the poets call the “cap of Hades” (Homer, Iliad 5.845), or something like it; or that it should strike those who came to kill him, as the men in Sodom were struck (Genesis 19:11). For help given to him in a wholly extraordinary and more conspicuous way would not have served his purpose: to teach that he, a man to whom God bore witness, had something more divine within the man who was seen. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus fled to Egypt instead of being protected by a plain miracle.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The slaughtered infants are a type of the people, who will be saved from death through faith.
comments.comment: … The infants slaughtered by Herod are taken as a type of the people. … Just as a resurrection awaits the infants, so it is shown, just as the people shall be saved from death through faith. As a type of the people of Israel, the evangelist received the prophet's word regarding the children slaughtered by Herod.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: “Go” instead of “flee” hints at relief, and Egypt repeats Israel's captivity and rescue.
comments.comment:
He no longer says “flee,” (Matthew 2:20) but “go,” hinting at relief after the trial. …

In Christ’s economic [relating to God's plan of salvation] descent into Egypt and his return from there into Judea, God recapitulates the people’s captivity and redeems them from the plot, leading them home again.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the change from 'flee' to 'go' and why Christ goes to Egypt and back.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nazareth lay at Judea's edge, showing Christ would leave the Jews for the nations.
comments.comment: It is worth noting that Nazareth lay at the edges of Judea. By settling there, Christ shows that because of the Jews’ murderousness he was about to leave Judea and go over to the nations, giving lovers of learning an occasion for faith in Christ. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the significance of Nazareth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: “Nazorean” can mean holy or flower, and both fit Christ through Daniel, Isaiah and the Song of Songs.
comments.comment: If “Nazorean” (Matthew 2:23) is interpreted “holy,” or according to some “flower,” the name shows up in many places. Daniel calls him “holy of holies.” Isaiah says, “a rod from the root of Jesse and a flower from it.” (Isaiah 11:1) And the Lord says of himself in the Song of Songs, “I am a flower of the field, a lily of the valleys.” (Song of Songs 2:1)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the name 'Nazorean'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The kingdom is justification through faith and sanctification through the Spirit.
comments.comment: The kingdom of the heavens is justification through faith and sanctification through the Spirit. That is why he also says elsewhere, “The kingdom of the heavens is within you.” (Luke 17:21)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the kingdom of heaven' means in John's call.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's presence is the kingdom, granting a share in the Father and heaven.
comments.comment: The presence of Christ is the kingdom of heaven; for this grants us the participation of the Father and the ascent into the heavens and the unshakeable good for the saints in the coming age (Mt 3:2).
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: John's baptism did not itself forgive sins.
comments.comment: John’s baptism did not give forgiveness of sins. It taught people to run to baptism because of their sins (Matthew 3:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what John's baptism did and did not do.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Like young vipers that kill their mother, they left their mother Jerusalem for dead, and the coming wrath is what the Romans inflicted for the killing of Christ.
comments.comment:
As men more learned in the law than the rest, they came to John later. He calls them offspring of vipers because of their likeness: when vipers are about to come into the light, they burst their mother’s belly and leave her dead.

In the same way these men left their own mother, Jerusalem, as if she were dead, and were being saved from the killing of Christ — the crime for which they endured incurable evils for a time under the Romans, which he calls the coming wrath (Matthew 3:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John calls them 'offspring of vipers' and what 'the coming wrath' is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Ancestry is no excuse to neglect virtue.
comments.comment: Do not neglect the virtue of the soul, even while being honored by the ancestors (Mt 3:7–9). …
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The fruits of repentance are chiefly faith in Christ and the gospel way of life, so no one should plead descent from Abraham.
comments.comment:
Someone might say the fruits of repentance are chiefly faith in Christ, and with it the gospel way of life that is “in newness of life,” (Matthew 3:8–9) freed from the thickness of the letter.

So do not, he says, put forward the usual excuses — that God can raise children for Abraham from these stones. That is what he added (Matthew 3:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God can make people from stones, as he made Adam.
comments.comment: Just as he turned Lot’s wife to stone, so he can also make humans from stones, as he earlier made Adam from earth (Matthew 3:9) (Genesis 19:26) (Genesis 2:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God can raise children from stones.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The axe is Christ, who cuts unbelieving Jews off from the patriarchs, the root onto which the nations are grafted.
comments.comment:
By “axe” (Matthew 3:10) he means Christ, “sharper than any two-edged sword,” who is about to cut away the unbelieving Jews and estrange them from the patriarchs’ honor and fellowship. He also called those patriarchs the root — the fathers of old who pleased God, those around Abraham, and as many as were holy before.

Their unbelieving descendants were cut off as fruitless branches, but the root remained, and onto it those from the nations were grafted (Romans 11:17–24). Irenaeus says the axe is the word of God, as Jeremiah also does: the word of the Lord is “like an axe cutting rock.” (Jeremiah 23:29) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the axe and the root in John's warning.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The axe is the word of God, lying at the root to make us better through fear.
comments.comment: He likens the word of God to an axe. Jeremiah says the same: the word of the Lord is “like an axe cutting rock.” (Jeremiah 23:29) So it lies against the root, that by fear it may make you better and prepare you to bear fruit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The axe cuts from the patriarchs those who boast in vain and bear no good fruit.
comments.comment: What does he mean by axe? Nothing but what is about to cut from the patriarchs those who boast in vain and have done no good. Those who come from such lines and prove fruitless must be cut out and thrown into the fire (Matthew 3:10).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Baptism in fire is a figure for the Spirit's life-giving energy, not literal fire.
comments.comment: The blessed Baptist joins the Spirit’s meaning with fire’s energy and meaning. He is not saying we will be baptized in fire itself through Christ, but marking the Spirit’s life-giving energy by the figure of fire (Matthew 3:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ baptizes the holy in the Holy Spirit, but washes in fire the believer who has sinned again.
comments.comment: … That is why Jesus baptizes (perhaps I find the meaning now) 'in the Holy Spirit and fire.' (Matthew 3:11) Not that he baptizes the same person 'in the Holy Spirit and fire,' (Matthew 3:11) but the holy one 'in the Holy Spirit,' and the one who, after believing, after being counted worthy of the Holy Spirit, has sinned again, he washes in 'fire' — so that it is not the same person being baptized by Jesus 'in the Holy Spirit and fire.' (Matthew 3:11) Blessed, then, is the one baptized in the Holy Spirit and not needing the baptism from fire. Thrice-wretched is that one who has need to be baptized with the fire. …
comments.selected_reason: A second reading of 'Spirit and fire' that a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ saves the righteous, burns sinners.
comments.comment: He [Christ] snatches the righteous into the city above, and the sinners into what is to be burned (Matthew 3:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the winnowing in verse 12.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ, being sinless, came up at once because he was baptized to cleanse, not to repent.
comments.comment: The ancients before Christ used to hold those they baptized in the water until they confessed their own sins. Christ, being sinless, came up at once. He was not baptized as one repenting, but as one who cleanses sins and sanctifies the waters (Matthew 3:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus came up out of the water immediately.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The voice was the Father's, and the Father, Son and Spirit are all shown at the baptism.
comments.comment: … some say concerning the saying of the voice: 'This is my beloved Son,' that it was an angelic substitute for the person of the Father, or something else prepared by chance. But the saying 'in whom I am well pleased' was spoken in the context of other sons, who were neither becoming beloved nor being extremely pleasing to him; for those in the law were also worthy of adoption. Yet, through the witness of the Father and the descent of the Spirit, the hypostases [the distinct persons] of the Holy Trinity are demonstrated.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's voice is heard only by those he wishes to hear it, which is why the crowds did not hear the voice at the baptism.
comments.comment: … At any rate, the voice from heaven that proclaimed him to be the Son of God and said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), is not recorded to have been within the hearing of the crowds, as Celsus’s Jew supposed. Moreover, the voice from the cloud on the very high mountain was heard only by those who had gone up with him (Matthew 17:1–5; compare Mark 9:2–7; Luke 9:28–35). For the divine voice is of such a kind that it is heard only by those whom the speaker wishes to hear it. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who heard the voice from heaven.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil needed permission.
comments.comment: He [Jesus] was led by the devil by permission (Matthew 4:1).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ was tempted only after his baptism as an example, since the unbaptized cannot bear Satan's assault.
comments.comment: … But mark this—for the force of the thought is most useful: he was not tempted before the holy baptism, nor was he led by the Spirit into the desert (Matthew 4:1) then, setting the matter as a type for us. For it is impossible for those not yet baptized either to bear manfully Satan’s hard assault or to be led spiritually; the fitting time for such bright and admirable achievements is after the holy baptism. For thus strengthened by sharing in the Holy Spirit and sealed with the grace from above unto spiritual vigor, we shall be unconsumed by Satan and shall live as in the Spirit’s power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the temptation comes right after the baptism.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Christ refused to turn stones into loaves because the devil wanted to draw him into vain glory, not to believe.
comments.comment: Christ did not obey the devil so as to turn the stones into loaves, because that request was not for the devil’s benefit. He was not asking so that he might believe and become again the angel he once was — for he is unrepentant — but so that he might drag Christ into vain glory. Knowing this, the Savior did not obey him (Matthew 4:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus did not do what the devil asked.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Satan asked for a sign to pull Christ into empty glory, and the saints should never love glory in anything useless.
comments.comment:
Wanting to drag Christ into the passion of love of glory, Satan did not say to him, “Eat,” (Matthew 4:3–4) but, “Make a sign.” He did this not to gain any help himself, but — as I said — to pull Christ into empty glory. Knowing that, Christ did not obey him.

With the same aim he also refused the Pharisees when they wanted to see a sign from him. They were not coming to him with an undoubting heart as to God; they were testing him as a man. So let this stand for the saints as an unfailing rule toward unbelievers or testers: do not love glory in anything useless.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Food from paradise served the new Adam, who restores through virtue what the first Adam lost.
comments.comment: … food from paradise served him [Christ] so that, just as Adam, who was not commanded, was losing the food there, so the new Adam, from whom nothing was commanded, might restore the original goodness through an excess of virtue in Matthew 4:11.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus' withdrawal teaches that no one should come to the school before baptism, the Spirit, fasting and victory over temptation.
comments.comment: Jesus’ withdrawal is itself a teaching. The word clearly teaches that no one should come to the school unless he is first baptized, receives the Holy Spirit, fasts completely, and conquers every kind of temptation — as the type of the truth began in Christ and happens through Christ (Matthew 4:12).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ withdrew not from cowardice but to teach us to withdraw from persecutors, and from Judea to the nations.
comments.comment: He did not withdraw through cowardice, but by what he did he teaches us to withdraw from persecutors. He withdraws from Judea to the nations, showing that he stands away from the Jews not only when they insult God himself, but also when they sin against the holy prophets. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus withdraws to Galilee.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John's work ended once he had baptized Jesus, and he was then handed over to prison and death.
comments.comment: It seemed that John, having fulfilled in Jesus the service of baptism, ended with him, to be handed over and to be shut up in prison; for after the baptizing of Jesus, we find nothing written about John … Jesus, having heard that John was handed over, withdrew into Galilee. … According to the four then evangelists, neither before baptizing Jesus did John encounter any obstacle while baptizing, nor did he baptize after these things, but it was necessary for John's things to end at the beginning of the gospel being administered by Jesus. Perhaps the guarding power left John, until he completed the administration of baptism in Jesus, to the trial in prison and to the beheading.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The names Zebulun, Naphtali and Galilee describe believers who journey well, are blessed, and once rolled down into destruction.
comments.comment:
… Note also that the inheritance of the tribe of Zebulun and Naphtali stretched as far as the gentile city Sidon, and that Jews were already living mixed with the nations. Zebulun is interpreted “good journey” (Matthew 4:15) and “blessing”; Naphtali, “a loosened stem,” that is, a plant stretched out.

Those who believed in Christ became these things. Journeying well, they were counted worthy of the divine blessing and were broadened in every good — those who were formerly in Galilee, which is interpreted “rolling down,” that is, those rolling down into the pits of destruction.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of the names in the prophecy Matthew quotes.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ and the gospel are a great light, far beyond the short gleam of the law that left the gentiles in darkness.
comments.comment: … Christ our Lord is a great light, and so is the brightness of the gospel proclamation — not the law, which had been compared to a lamp. That is why a lamp always burned in the tent: the law’s gleam was short, able to send its own light only as far as the Jewish boundaries. So the gentiles were in darkness, as those who did not even have lamp-light (Matthew 4:12–16) (Isaiah 9:1–2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'great light' of verse 16.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John prepared the people with 'repent', while Jesus, receiving what was prepared, begins the new and no longer needs to say it.
comments.comment:
In some copies “repent” (Matthew 4:17) is not present. If the Savior says the same things as John, one God sent them both. Perhaps John, as one preparing a people made ready for God, first says “repent,” while Jesus, receiving what was already prepared and no longer needing repentance, does not say “repent.”

He is not heralding against the law and the prophets. John having finished the old, he begins to herald the new, himself becoming its beginning. That is why “he began” is not written of John — for John was an end. One heralds in the desert, the other among the people.

The kingdom of the heavens is not in a place but in a disposition, for it is within us (Luke 17:21). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Jesus' preaching relates to John's.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Weakness is temporary irregularity; disease is disproportion among bodily elements.
comments.comment: If someone asks the difference between disease and weakness, we answer: weakness is the body’s temporary irregularity; disease is disproportion among the elements in the body. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two words 'disease' and 'sickness' in verse 23.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The poor in spirit are the humble, and the humble are the patient.
comments.comment: For whom has the Lord called happy except the patient, saying, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 5:3)? No one is poor in spirit unless humble. And who is humble unless patient? Because no one can subject himself without the prior patience of subjection itself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'poor in spirit' as humble.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: Only spiritual poverty is blessed.
comments.comment: … In the same way, poverty too: the spiritual kind is blessed. That is why Matthew added: Blessed are poor persons—how?—in spirit (Matthew 5:3).
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Mourning is blessed as the start of comfort, whether one mourns his own sins or the fall of others.
comments.comment:
So what, then, is the good in mourning? For it brings blessedness. For 'blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted' (Matt 5:4). Mourning is a prelude and a beginning of comfort. …

In many ways, one can mourn himself having become lost in sins, if he perceives it. And he is blessed, the one mourning himself, having made himself worthy of mourning and having fallen from the blessed life, so that he may be comforted. And he mourns others also, when he is a lover of children.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the blessed mourning is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tears of the saints come from love for God and grief for sinners, and they deepen rather than destroy joy.
comments.comment: [Against the objection that mourning conflicts with 'Rejoice always':] To these objections we will say that the laments and tears of the saints came about because of their love for God. Always gazing, then, at the Beloved and increasing the gladness that came to them from there, they managed the affairs of their fellow-servants: mourning those who sinned and correcting them through their tears. Just as people standing on the shore share the suffering of those drowning in the sea but do not surrender their own safety in their concern for those in danger, so also those who grieve over the sins of their neighbors do not destroy their own gladness. On the contrary, they make it greater, since they are counted worthy of the Lord's joy on account of their tears for a brother. For this reason, blessed are those who weep, and blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted, and they will laugh (Matthew 5:4; Luke 6:21). By laughter he does not mean the sound that bursts from the cheeks when the blood boils up, but the cheerfulness that is unmixed and unmingled with anything gloomy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how mourning and joy fit together.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Hungering for righteousness means taking in virtue by practice and Scripture's hidden meaning by thought.
comments.comment: … those partaking in His teaching by practicing virtue are said to eat, but by the intellectual examination of the hidden meaning of Scripture, they are said to drink, just as Christ says: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness" (Matt 5:6), those partaking in this by both practice and thought.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The reward is enjoying what is to come.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 5:6, another says that the reward for such a desire is promised to him: the enjoyment of those things to come.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Matthew specifies Luke's 'hungry' as those who forgo fleshly delights for the good, and their thirst for righteousness is satisfied.
comments.comment: In Matthew 5:6, the hungry are remembered simply by Luke as 'the hungry,' but now Matthew specifies those who abstain because of the desire for the good, from the delights of the flesh. Thus, we hear similarly from both. He who thirsted for the righteousness of God found the truly desired thing, whose longing he fulfilled not in any way merely by the one acting according to appetite; for he did not only desire the participation of the righteous as food, for it was incomplete. Now, he made this good thing also drinkable, so that the warmth and the clarity of desire might be the passion of thirst.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The pure heart sees God as a cleansed eye sees light, yet what is seen is God's wisdom in creation, not his essence.
comments.comment:
The heart sees God (Mt 5:8); for the incorporeal is comprehensible to the incorporeal. …

This happens through the cleansing of what hinders, just as the eye, once cleansed of obstacles, sees the light.

How then does the divine Scripture say, 'No one has ever seen God' and 'No one shall see my face and live' and 'Whom no man has seen, nor is able to see'? …

We say that He is seen and seized through the Word; or, through the divine Scripture, we see God with the eyes of knowledge, or through the wisdom manifest to all, we see through reasoning the One who made all things, just as in the case of human creations, the maker of the work in question is seen in a certain way by the intellect.

But not the nature of the artisan is seen, but only the technical skill.

Thus also, he who sees God in creation does not depict the essence, but the wisdom of the One who made all things is portrayed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the pure in heart see God without contradicting 'no one has seen God'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who want to serve God must first be purified, and then they are fit to behold him.
comments.comment: Those, then, who long for close fellowship with God, and whose aim is, as it were, to stand before him and serve him with strength and eagerness for every good thing, must first be purified. Such a person would then be quite fit even for this: that he too should already, in some way, behold God, according to the Savior’s word: ‘For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew 5:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why purity comes before seeing God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: God is invisible because he is not a body, but a pure heart can behold him with the mind.
comments.comment: Further, in our teaching God is invisible because he is not a body; but to those who can contemplate him he can be beheld with the heart, that is, with the mind; and not with just any heart, but with a pure one (Matthew 5:8). For it is not right for a defiled heart to gaze on God; what would behold the Pure One as he deserves must itself be pure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what way the pure in heart see God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The heart that sees God is one from which no evil thoughts come forth.
comments.comment: And what sees God is a pure heart, from which there no longer “come forth evil thoughts,” no “murders,” no “adulteries,” no “fornications,” no “thefts,” no “false witness,” no “blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19), no “evil eye” (Mark 7:22), nor anything else that is wrong. That is why it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A peacemaker shows scripture agrees with itself and, imitating the Son, is called a son of God.
comments.comment: A peacemaker is the one who shows that the battle others see in the scriptures is agreement: old with new, legal with prophetic, gospel with gospel. Having imitated the Son of God, he will be called a son, receiving in deed the spirit of adoption (Matthew 5:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peacemakers include those who tame anger and desire and those who bring unbelievers to faith, and they imitate the Son and reign with him.
comments.comment:
Peacemakers are not only those who reconcile enemies, but also those who tame anger and base desire, living rightly in deed and word through unfailing faith — and those who re-teach unbelievers and lead them to faith, making God’s enemies friends to him.

Blessed are such people, as those who have imitated the Son of God. They will be called sons, sharing immortality, or they will reign with Christ at his second coming (Matthew 5:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what peacemaking includes beyond reconciling enemies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peacemakers persuade unbelievers to believe and so reconcile them to God.
comments.comment: Peacemakers are also those who persuade unbelievers to believe, making God’s former enemies at peace with him. They are called peacemakers who persuade unbelievers to believe God (Matthew 5:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Children of God ought to be peacemakers, gentle and harmonious, clinging to one another in unity.
comments.comment: If we are heirs of Christ, let us remain in Christ’s peace. If we are children of God, we ought to be peacemakers. “Blessed,” he says, “are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). God’s children ought to be peacemakers, gentle in heart, simple in speech, harmonious in affection, faithfully clinging to one another by the bonds of unanimity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God's children are called peacemakers.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Peacemakers lead people divided in intention into harmony, and make peace within themselves too.
comments.comment: … the Savior says to others that 'the peacemakers are blessed,' 'because they are sons of God' (Matthew 5:9). To be peaceful is to be sons of God. And he said 'peacemakers' to mean those making peace. When they lead those who have been divided by intention into harmony and friendship, they are peacemakers. And they are peacemakers toward themselves also.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the peacemakers are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Righteousness does not wrong its own.
comments.comment: But he who is removed through righteousness, the present things and the future things, instead of these, will bear fruit, for righteousness is not unjust toward its own (Mt 5:10).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those persecuted should not be surprised but should pray to suffer unjustly rather than for sin, and rejoice if persecuted for righteousness.
comments.comment: Therefore those who are persecuted must not be surprised, but must do everything, only praying that they be persecuted unjustly and not justly — not for injustice, not for sin, not for greed. And if someone is ever persecuted for righteousness, let him also hear, 'Blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you and say every evil word against you, lying, for my sake (Matthew 5:11). Rejoice and be glad, because your reward is great in the heavens; for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.' (Matthew 5:10–12)
comments.selected_reason: Explains how to take persecution.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Reproach is blessed only when it comes because of Christ, not because of our own sins.
comments.comment: But we wretched ones have reproaches not because of the word of the Lord but because of our own sins, and we are reproached for what we stumble in, and we are reviled for our evils. And the Savior does not want us to be reproached with such reproaches, saying: 'Blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you and say every evil word against you because of me. Rejoice in that day and leap.' (Matthew 5:11)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words 'because of me'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Rejoicing in persecution is possible only for one who has practiced patience and first despised adversities.
comments.comment: And when he says, "Rejoice and be glad whenever they curse and persecute you, for your reward is great in heaven" (Matthew 5:11-12), he certainly does not promise this to the impatience of exultation, because no one will exult in adversities unless he has first despised them. No one will despise them unless he has practiced patience.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: Suffering believers are consoled by fellowship with those who suffered before them.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 5:12, from this, they will be provided the consolation from the fellowship of those who suffered badly before them, so that even from them it became possible for us to know that it is not possible to establish those who pursue virtue outside of the sorrowful ones.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Salt is apostolic understanding, without which a soul is tasteless to God.
comments.comment: He calls salt prudence, of which the apostolic word is full. Sown in our souls, it settles the word of wisdom in us, compared to salt because it is savory and graceful. Just as without salt neither bread nor relish is edible, so without apostolic understanding and teaching every soul is foolish, tasteless, and not pleasant to God (Matthew 5:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the salt of the earth stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's people are the salt that preserves the world's order, which holds together while the salt is not spoiled.
comments.comment: For the men of God are salt that preserves the order of the world on earth, and the things on earth hold together as long as the salt does not go bad. For “if the salt has lost its taste,” it “is no longer fit either for the soil or for the dunghill,” but “is thrown out” and will be trampled “by men” (Matthew 5:13; Luke 14:34–35).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the salt of the earth does.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers must not speak the word secretly.
comments.comment: “A city cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14): those established on the faith as on a high mountain ought not to speak the word secretly or with cowardice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the city on a mountain means for believers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ lives in the believer and through him lights the world.
comments.comment: Having become light by participation, when you live it is no longer you who live, but the light — Christ — lives in you, able through the word to illuminate the whole world (Matthew 5:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how believers are the light of the world.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lamp is the Word, once hidden under the basket of the Law and now set on the lampstand of the cross.
comments.comment: [On the cross:] No longer do 'they light a lamp and put it under the basket' (Matthew 5:15), and by the basket I mean the Law, 'but on the lampstand', and by the lamp I mean the Word. For the Word was under the Law and was hidden from unbelievers, as under the basket; but when he came to the cross and was set on the lampstand …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lamp, basket and lampstand.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: Homily I on the Holy Pascha

comments.capsule: The light we are given is a gift that departs if neglected, so we must not cover it through sloth.
comments.comment:
For it is necessary to strive to keep the brightness given to us in a high place and not to cover it up through sloth, of which the couch resting the body with fleshly pleasures is a symbol (Mt 5:15); for the beautiful is not to us by nature, but by a gift.

But such a thing, being neglected, departs. … A virtuous life is light (Mt 5:16).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ says 'before men,' since a lamp does not shine before the sun; our light is virtuous conduct, boldly shown.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 5:16, he does not say: 'let your light shine before God'; for even the light of lamps does not shine before the sun. Regarding Matthew 5:15–16, virtuous conduct is light. It is not necessary to speak the evangelical word in secret, but with boldness, so that the men upon the earth might be enlightened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'before men' and not before God.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The law is not abolished but completed in Christ, as added colors bring earlier outlines into clearer view.
comments.comment: Now that things have passed over into truth, and what was in types and riddles has been changed for the better, we do not say that the law has been abolished, but rather that it has been brought to completion at the time when the truth, that is, Christ, shone upon us. For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, and he would not speak falsely when he says, “I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it” (Matthew 5:17). For just as the many colours, added in due time, by no means do away with the shadowy outlines first sketched on painted panels, but rather bring them into clearer view, in the same way we say that the shadows of the law have not been overturned, but rather brought to completion, as in an advance toward the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Christ came to fulfill the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Commands endure but sacrifices were temporary, and with Christ's coming they were fulfilled, not condemned.
comments.comment: Virtues and sacrificial victims are not governed by the same principle: commands are enduring; sacrifices are temporary. Yet when Christ came, whom the ancient sacrifices foreshadowed, what had been established was fulfilled, not condemned. Those observances are not denounced as having been practiced in their proper times; they came to rest when the perfection promised through their service arrived (Matthew 5:17) (Hebrews 10:1).
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Christ fills up what the law lacked by attaching a penalty to the least commandments that had none.
comments.comment:
Whoever sets aside one commandment of the law is set aside by God as a God-fighter and as one who legislates against God. And now from the gospel law he receives the punishment that the old law had not defined. So Christ says consistently that he did not come to destroy the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17–19).

What was lacking there, he filled up here. The law said, “You shall rise before a gray head,” (Leviticus 19:32) and, “If you see your enemy’s beast fallen under its load, raise it with him.” (Exodus 23:5) If someone transgressed these, the law had defined no punishment. Filling that up, Christ says such a person will be set at nought in the kingdom of God. That is what he calls the least commandment: one on which no penalty was brought for transgression.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'least commandment' is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christians now keep the law's worship spiritually, which the Jews no longer kept in the flesh.
comments.comment:
In place of fleshly worship the Lord introduced worship “in spirit and truth.” (John 4:23) Perhaps what the Jews were not even doing fleshly, Christ’s disciples now do spiritually. That is why he says one iota or one horn will not pass from the law until all happens.

Clearly the Jews did not do all of it — or if they did, they stopped, no longer allowed to do those things, partly through fear of kings, and partly because the temple had been destroyed, the only place where the sacrifices had to be completed (John 4:23).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever sets aside the least commandment is set aside by God as an opponent.
comments.comment: Whoever sets aside the least of the commandments in the law will be called a God-fighter, he says. That is why he is also set aside by God, as one who opposes him and legislates against him (Matthew 5:19).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law's split hoof teaches us to walk by word and deed together, with deed preferred to word alone.
comments.comment:
That is also why Moses’ law accepts the split hoof: that through riddles it may teach us to journey by both — by word and by deed. I think the split hoof in the law signifies this: that we journey by word and deed, neither acting without reason nor holding a word apart from deed.

If something from such things wants to stand alone, let it be deed and not word. An unbridled word has often pushed those who have it over cliffs; deed never has (Leviticus 11:3).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The righteousness that must exceed the Pharisees' is God's righteousness, received through Jesus Christ by faith.
comments.comment: By saying the righteousness of God, he [Paul] means that which comes to all who believe through Jesus Christ, which He Himself also desired. He says all things were sent so that one might be found having the righteousness from God through faith and not his own. Wishing this to be present also for the disciples, Jesus says to them, 'If your righteousness does not exceed that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 5:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what exceeding the scribes' righteousness means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The law judged deeds of the flesh, but Christ requires blessedness through the Spirit, so the one who rages at a brother faces eternal judgment.
comments.comment:
The law judges fleshly things, those things done through the flesh, but the Lord, sanctifying spirits, requires blessedness through the Spirit (Mt 5:21-22).

Therefore, he calls the spiritual one 'brother,' the one dwelling according to the Spirit, being named brother. … he hands the murderer over to the judgment of the law, but the one raging is handed over to the eternal judgment. …

Regarding Matthew 5:22, he says that the one who called his brother 'Raca' is liable to the judgment of the saints.

For he who blasphemes against the common part sins.

Raca, indeed, calls the despised one, as another says; for so also among the Syrians the scoundrel is called.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Even the law ordered us to cast out hatred of the heart, but Christ stretches justice further, making anger liable to judgment.
comments.comment: Therefore the law says: ‘You will not walk with deceit in your nation, and you will not hate your brother in the heart; with rebuke you will rebuke your neighbor, and you will not take a sin because of him.’ (Leviticus 19:17) Therefore he has commanded not only to stand off from the deed of the hatred, but also to cast out the very disease of the mind; for the one hating in heart has already been blood-guilty, even if he should not yet stretch out the hand for murder. And Christ also, defining the Gospel justice more severely, was saying: ‘You have heard that it was said for the ancients: You will not murder; yet I say to you that everyone being angered with his brother emptily will be liable to the judgment.’ (Matthew 5:21–22) Therefore the justice in Christ has been stretched beyond the law’s boundary.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: Since Christ came, even a word of insult or Fool risks judgment and anger is forbidden.
comments.comment: But after he [Christ] came and composed grace of faith with patience, it is no longer permitted even to insult with a word, or even to say 'Fool,' without the danger of judgment (Matthew 5:22). Anger is forbidden, the spirit is restrained, wantonness of hand is checked, the tongue's poison is removed.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how far Christ's rule against anger reaches.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: God's way of escape for sinners is repentance and healing the one grieved, and he rejects worship from someone at odds with his brother.
comments.comment:
Saying, “If you offer your gift,” (Matthew 5:23–24) and what follows, makes this clear: God invented a way of salvation and an escape from punishment for sinners — a change of mind — and he says healing the one who was grieved will overturn punishment.

Since the one who does not love his brother does not love the Lord, he reasonably does not accept the one who approaches while his brother is in grief, as one not truly coming to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ sends the offerer to be reconciled first.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sinners escape punishment by repenting and asking pardon of those they wronged.
comments.comment: Here the Savior teaches us how sinners escape punishment. Afterthought over our sins, appeal to the one we grieved, and asking forgiveness of the fault heal both the brother and God (Matthew 5:23–24).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A man at odds with his brother must be reconciled before he offers his gift, for without peace with his brother he cannot have God at peace with him.
comments.comment: And he [the Lord] calls back from the altar the one who comes to sacrifice while at odds with a brother, and orders him first to be reconciled with his brother, and then to return in peace and offer his gift to God (Matthew 5:23-24). For God did not even look upon Cain’s gifts (Genesis 4:5), since no one who lacked peace with his brother through the discord of envy could have God at peace with him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why reconciliation comes before the offering.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Anger and bitterness must be destroyed before one can settle with an adversary or complete an offering at the altar.
comments.comment: When he brings his dispute with his adversary before the judge, will he settle the matter agreeably unless he has first destroyed his anger, his hardness, his bitterness—that is, cut off the very veins of impatience? How will you forgive and be forgiven if you cling to a wrong because patience is absent? No one whose spirit is torn against his brother will complete his offering at the altar unless he first turns back, reconciles with his brother, and returns to patience (Matthew 5:23-24).
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: We settle with an adversary who wants our property by giving him even more.
comments.comment: Carefully, then, the Lord here names “adversary” (Matthew 5:25) the one who tries to take something that belongs to us. We are well disposed toward him if we keep the Lord’s command: “To the one who wants to go to law with you and take your tunic, give him the cloak as well,” (Matthew 5:40) and likewise in every such matter.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'adversary' is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We must be freed from the devil and our passions on the road of this life, or conscience will condemn us and God will hand us to the exactors.
comments.comment:
So let us be freed from the enemy and avenger — that is, the devil — while we are still on this road, and from the passions of dishonor, which are our adversaries. No one else is our adversary unless we make ourselves so through these things, and unless conscience condemns us for despising its reminder.

Otherwise we will be handed over to God, the judge of all, convicted by conscience. He will hand us to the exactors — the punishing angels — and we will be charged penalties for every fault, small and great (Luke 12:59).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Be reasonable before judgment, since once held you will not be released until you pay the last obol.
comments.comment:
What he means is this: be reasonable before judgment. If you are accused and jailed, you are not released until you pay down to an obol — that is what the quadrans shows.

He exhorts us to be reasonable and not to trust the lawsuit. If something goes against hope and the judge holds you, you will not be released until you pay the last obol. That is what is called a quadrans (Matthew 5:25–26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture of the road, the judge and the last coin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We should make every effort to be freed from our accuser Satan while still on the road of life, or we will pay every debt to the punishers.
comments.comment:
Suppose someone, he says, brings charges against you before one set in authority, then points you out to those who lead to court and has you hauled off. While you are still with him on the road — that is, before you reach the judge — give diligence: do not hesitate to use every effort to be freed from him.

If that does not happen, he will hand you to the judge. When you are found liable for the debts, you will be handed to the exactor — the collectors — and after shutting you up they will demand even “the last lepton.” (Matthew 5:25–26)

So all of us on earth are liable for faults. Each person’s adversary and accuser is Satan, for he is enemy and avenger. While we are still on the road — that is, before we reach the end of this life — let us be freed from him, loose the charges against ourselves, and seize the grace through Christ that frees us from every debt and sets us outside judgment, punishment, and fear.

Otherwise, still carrying the stain unwashed, we may be carried to the judge and handed to “the exactors,” the punishers, whose harshness no one escapes. Then penalties will be demanded for every fault, small and great. Far from this will be those who prove the time of Christ’s coming and have not ignored the mystery in him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Lust sees a woman's flesh as beautiful, but love of purity sees her soul.
comments.comment: The one who looks at a woman and desires is judged when her flesh appears beautiful to him for desire, and he sees her fleshly and sinfully. The one who looks at beauty through love of purity does not count the flesh beautiful, but the soul (Matthew 5:28).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what looking to desire means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ adds to the law by forbidding sins of the will, so the lust of a look is punished like the deed.
comments.comment: Finally, how does the Lord show that he is building an addition onto the law, except by forbidding sins of the will as well? He defines as an adulterer not only the one who has actually fallen into another's marriage, but also the one who has defiled himself by the lust of a look (Matthew 5:28). So what is forbidden to be carried out, the mind dangerously enough represents to itself, and rashly works out the effect through the will. Since the will's force is so great that it satisfies itself and stands in place of the deed, it will be punished in place of the deed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a look counts as adultery.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: Christ, having strengthened human nature, commands what is beyond the law as now possible.
comments.comment: Perhaps some have received such a gift that they do not desire. But Christ, having strengthened human nature, also commands what is beyond the law as now possible. Even if this was impossible for those before Christ, for the faithful cutting out desires is easy to accomplish (Matthew 5:28–30).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ speaks of cutting off members not literally but to kill them off and make them inactive toward sin.
comments.comment:
Regarding Matthew 5:29-30, concerning the bodily things he speaks of members; and excessively, not that one must actually cut off the members, but such as to kill them and to set them aside sluggishly for sin, as the Apostle has said; and not to spare even the most necessary things, if through them someone is to experience a bad activity.

It is not necessary to cut off the members, but such as to kill these and make them inactive toward sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that cutting off the eye or hand is not meant literally.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The eye that must be cut out is the thought of desire.
comments.comment: When he says, “If your eye causes you to stumble,” (Matthew 5:29–30) and what follows, by “eye” he means the thought of desire, which he says must be cut out.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'eye' stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eye and hand mean a friend who harms your soul, from whom you should separate.
comments.comment: “Eye” (Matthew 5:29–30) and “hand” are understood as the friend. If you love someone as a right eye, and count him useful as a right hand, and he harms your soul, cut them off from you and separate far from them. When you do not save each other but rather both perish together, it is better that, once separated, at least one be saved.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Divorce papers do not end a marriage before God; only an improper deed does.
comments.comment: The one who casts out a chaste wife gives her leave to marry another — a form of adultery, as if the yoking were not loosed. For divorce papers do not loose marriage before God; improper deed does (Matthew 5:31–32).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why remarriage after a bill of divorce is adultery.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We must not swear by creation, lest we make it a god, or by Jerusalem, since only God swears by himself.
comments.comment:
For this reason he forbids us to swear by heaven and earth: that we not give creation a dignity beyond creation and make it a god. Those who swear, he says, “swear by the greater,” (Hebrews 6:16) as the apostle said.

He also forbids the oath by “Jerusalem,” (Matthew 5:35) because earthly Jerusalem is a type of the Jerusalem above, and God swears by himself alone — that is, by his own glory. Since that likeness surpasses us, we ought not swear by ourselves or by our own glory. We are not free as God is; we are under God’s authority.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ forbids oaths by heaven, earth and Jerusalem.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Instead of oaths, believers will have yes and no.
comments.comment: “You shall not swear falsely,” (Matthew 5:33–37) and what follows. If someone shamelessly lays an oath on the saints, instead of the oath they will have yes and no.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God rests among the saints yet is not contained by heaven, his throne.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 5:34, the heaven is therefore the throne of God, since God is holy and 'rests among the saints'; but He is not contained by such a throne, but pervades all things by a creative and watchful and sanctifying power.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The earth is God's footstool because it is under his authority.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 5:35, the earth is a footstool, because it is under authority, even if it is not currently receptive to his holiness because of the sins. And Jerusalem is the city of the great king. He says this regarding the perception of the Jews.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: A man whose word is never doubted needs no oath, since his yes is yes and his no is no.
comments.comment: He who possesses an unfailing word fulfills many commandments of Jesus. It is impossible for one not possessing an unfailing word to keep that: 'Let your yes be yes and your no, no' (Matt 5:37); for one who is not believing is sometimes required to swear an oath. But if one always possesses a word that is not scrutinized, no one ever doubts him, whether he previously tells the truth or not, or whether he says and does as he says, when an oath is required and his yes is yes and his no is no, such a word is indeed unfailing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how a person can keep 'Let your yes be yes'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ forbids oaths so strictly that he puts the one who swears alongside the Evil One, whoever the swearer is.
comments.comment: For the law I read about oaths is not a slave’s law but a king’s law. And when a king’s letters are read, let all the dignity of slaves be silent. If you can say that Christ commanded us to swear, or that Christ does not punish this when it happens, show me and I am persuaded. But if he forbids it with such earnestness and shows such care for the matter that he places the one who swears alongside the Evil One—for “anything more than these, than yes and no,” he says, “is from the devil” (Matthew 5:37)—why do you bring this man or that man into the discussion? God will not render his verdict to you based on the negligence of your fellow servants, but based on the command of his own laws.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how seriously Christ forbids oaths.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Patience under a blow defeats the shameless man, who is struck more by our enduring.
comments.comment: If someone tries to provoke you with his hand, the Lord's admonition is ready: "If anyone strikes you on the face," he says, "turn the other cheek also" (Matthew 5:39). Let shamelessness be wearied by your patience; whatever blow he lands, let him be bound fast by pain and disgrace. You strike that shameless man more by enduring, and he will be beaten more severely by the Lord; for he will be beaten by the one for whose sake you endure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why turning the other cheek is strength.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: Christ means that we should not flee a lawsuit that threatens our piety, but bear loss gladly.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 5:40, he did not say to the one wanting you to take the tunic, 'give also the other,' but to the one wanting you to be judged, demonstrating that it is proper not to flee from contention toward opponents when they bring this piety upon us, and undergoing both sufferings and loss gladly, so as not to neglect piety. We should look to guard this for the sake of virtue.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Giving joins us to God; receiving separates us.
comments.comment: Be ready, Christ says, not to receive but to give. Receiving separates us from God; giving joins us to him — especially when the one who asks is worthy and the request is just (Matthew 5:42).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the command to give to everyone who asks.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Love enemies as human beings, not as sinners.
comments.comment: Let us love enemies not insofar as they are adulterers or murderers, but insofar as they are human. Sinning belongs to activity, not to essence; that is why sin is not God’s work (Matthew 5:44).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how to love enemies without approving their sin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul cursed Alexander as an enemy of the gospel, not a private enemy.
comments.comment: Someone may ask how blessed Paul curses Alexander the smith. We say he cursed him not as a private enemy but as an enemy of the gospel, teaching that one must always war against God’s enemies.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God sends sun and rain on all alike and urges us to do likewise.
comments.comment: … and that God, being good, “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). He [God] urges us to do the like, so that we may become his sons (Matthew 5:44–45), and teaches us to extend our good deeds to all people as far as we can.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why we love enemies.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Perfect means imitating God.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 5:48, the man is perfect in imitation of God in his own measures.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God and blessed humans share the same virtue, so we are taught to be perfect.
comments.comment: For in our view the same virtue belongs to all the blessed, so that the virtue of a human being and of God is also the same. That is why we are taught to become “perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Do good for goodness itself, not for show.
comments.comment: The one who does the good for the good itself has a boast of virtue above the world (Matthew 6:1).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Almsgiving is to aim at God's glory, not human praise, which is the only reward of one who seeks it.
comments.comment:
Regarding Matthew 6:1-2, in other matters he speaks of righteousness, thus calling almsgiving.

But the aim of almsgiving he sets before us as the glory from God, not from men; for whoever wishes to please someone, he receives praise as a reward from them.

Not indeed he who has already been seen has done it for the sake of being seen, but he who wishes to be seen and is doing this also.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Sounding a trumpet is a figure for hypocrites staging their giving to draw a crowd.
comments.comment: [On "sound no trumpet":] This is said by a metaphor from the trumpet in the camps. When they want to gather the army together, they sound the recall. The hypocrites do not want to gather anyone; they want to put on a show for the crowd (Matthew 6:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the trumpet image in Christ's words.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Seeking human glory in giving or praying spoils even a good deed and loses God's reward.
comments.comment:
In many places, then, our Savior is seen pressing against ambition as a passion that destroys; which he has done here also, turning men away from performing a hypocrite's work at the season of prayer. For it is a hypocrite's work to want to preen oneself before men for piety or for fellowship. …

Even what was thought good and praiseworthy is polluted when deemed to be done — when we do it 'that we may be glorified by men' or 'that we may be seen by men.' That is why no recompense from God follows upon it. … He says of those who do good for show to win human glory, or who pray 'in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets' (Matthew 6:5) 'that they may be seen by men,' the same thing: 'Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward.' (Matthew 6:5)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ wants prayers brief and sober because God already knows our needs, and long repetition is what idol-worshippers do.
comments.comment:
That is why Christ urges that prayers be made briefly. He knows the mind is easily pulled aside and led astray by empty thoughts and cares, especially at the time of prayer. He commands us to ask God soberly and quickly for what we seek — not by announcing everything we happen to want. … God knows what we need even before we ask.

“Battology” (Matthew 6:7–8) means many words. It is named from a certain Greek, Battus, who made long, many-lined hymns to the idols, full of the same thing said over again. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ forbids many words in prayer and what the word means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God knows what we truly need, and those who do not know God do not even know what to ask for.
comments.comment: So our prayers must not be likened to heathen who babble or are wordy or do whatever they do 'after the likeness of the serpent.' (Psalm 58:4) For the God of the saints 'knows' 'before' what things his sons 'have need of,' since they are worthy of the Father's knowledge. But if anyone does not know God, he does not know the things of God either — and he does not know 'what need' he has: for the things he thinks he needs are wide of the mark. … But he who has contemplated what better and more divine things he lacks, known by God, shall obtain what he contemplated, known to the Father even before the asking.
