comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ says the Father knows what we need before we ask.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hallowing God's name means doing nothing profane or base, so that his name is honored.
comments.comment: We all in the Gospel are instructed in prayer to say: 'Hallowed be thy name' (Matt 6:9). And even if the voice is imperative, since we say it in prayer, it is a prayer. Therefore, in all ways of the elevation of the name and its being hallowed, we take this: do nothing profane, nothing wretched and lowly, so that the name of God may be elevated, so that it may be hallowed; turn the appellation of God away from every base thing, from every earthly matter; for then the appellation of God is hallowed. But this will exist most especially when 'God becomes all in all' (1 Cor 15:28), when eternal joy seizes one from the footsteps of pain and distress and sighing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to ask that God's name be hallowed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We keep praying for God's name to be hallowed and his kingdom to come because the perfect hallowing and kingdom come only as we advance without ceasing.
comments.comment: But someone will say, to both — both the 'Hallowed be thy name' and the 'Thy kingdom come' — that if the pray-er prays to be heard, and is heard at some point, then plainly at some point God's 'name' shall be hallowed for someone, as aforesaid, and God's 'kingdom' shall stand in him. And if these things shall be his, how will he still becomingly pray concerning things present as though not present, saying 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come' (Matthew 6:9-10)? … We must say to this that, as one who prays to obtain a 'word of knowledge' and a 'word of wisdom' becomingly prays concerning these things always — always receiving, as he is heard, more contemplations of 'wisdom' and 'knowledge,' yet knowing 'in part' whatever at present he can hold, with the perfect, which annuls 'the partial,' 'then' to be revealed, when mind without sense assails the realities 'face to face' — so the perfect, both of hallowing God's 'name' in each of us and of his kingdom standing in him, cannot be unless the perfect 'come' also concerning 'knowledge' and 'wisdom' — and perhaps concerning the other virtues too. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Praying for the kingdom is praying that unbelievers will accept Christ as their king, so that life and incorruption reign.
comments.comment:
Economically, as man, Christ is called king, though he is God by nature. So the faithful pray that this may hold also for unbelievers: that, believing in Christ, they may call him their own, and through him share the perfect goods — now having only the earnest and the partial good.

Then the passions will not be at work when passionlessness is present; death will be gone and corruption unseen, when life reigns in us and incorruption holds the power.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We pray that God's will be done in us on earth as it is by those in heaven, so that we become like them.
comments.comment: 'Thy will be done, as in heaven, also upon earth.' (Matthew 6:10) Luke, after the 'Thy kingdom come,' passed over these words in silence and goes on: 'Our daily bread give us day by day.' (Luke 11:3) So let us examine the words we set first, as lying in Matthew alone, in sequence with what went before. Still being 'on earth,' those who pray conceive that God's 'will' has come to be 'in heaven' among all the dwellers in heaven; and we pray that God's 'will' may come to be in us, who are 'still on earth,' in all things as with them. Which shall happen when we do nothing against his 'will.' And when God's 'will' — 'as in heaven' — is accomplished in us who are 'on earth,' we who are likened to those in the heavens, having borne, like them, 'the image of the heavenly,' (1 Corinthians 15:48–49) shall inherit the 'kingdom of the heavens' (Job 40:19 (LXX)) — we who pray on earth that we, having become 'in heaven,' be likened to them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "as in heaven, also upon earth" simply and clearly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The daily bread cannot be mere bodily food, since Christ told us to ask for great and heavenly things.
comments.comment: 'Give us this day our daily bread' — or as Luke has it, 'Our daily bread give us day by day.' (Matthew 6:11) … Since some suppose these words are said concerning bodily food — that we pray for it — it is worth removing their false opinion by these arguments and setting forth the truth concerning the daily bread. We must say to them: how could he who says we must ask heavenly and great things — when neither is the bread dispensed into our flesh heavenly, nor is the request concerning it a great petition — as it were forgetting what he taught, command the address of an entreaty to the Father concerning an earthly and small thing?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Epiousion' means the bread of the coming age.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 6:11, … some say that the 'epiousion' is that which is to come and to approach … bread not of the present age, but of the one to come
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: We ask for the coming bread, whose pledge is the Spirit.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 6:11, give us today the coming and destined food, the life-giving one, and in the present age, as if providing a pledge, providing the Holy Spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain meaning for the bread of the Lord's Prayer.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Our debts are what we owe others in gifts, gentle speech, works and goodwill, which we either pay or leave unpaid.
comments.comment: Concerning debts, the Apostle says: 'Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute, fear to whom fear, tax to whom tax, honor to whom honor. Owe no one anything, except to love one another.' (Romans 13:7) We owe, then — holding certain duties — not only in giving, but in gentle speech too, and in certain works; and we owe a certain disposition toward them. These debts we either pay, by performing what the divine law commands, or, by despising the wholesome word, not paying, we remain in owing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "debts" means in the prayer.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since all earthly life is a trial, praying not to be led into temptation needs explaining.
comments.comment: 'And bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.' (Matthew 6:13) … If the Savior does not command us to pray impossibilities, it seems to me worth inquiring how we are commanded to pray not to enter 'into temptation' — when the whole life of men on earth is a trial. For as long as we are on earth, girt with the flesh that wars 'against the spirit' — whose 'mind' is 'enmity' 'toward God,' wholly unable to submit 'to God's law' — we are in temptation.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God delivers us from evil not by keeping trials away but by helping us stand firm in them.
comments.comment: And God 'delivers us' 'from evil' — not when the enemy in no way approaches us, wrestling, with whatever methods of his, and serving his own will — but when we conquer, standing manfully toward what befalls. So too we took the 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and from them all he shall deliver them.' (Psalms 34:19) For God delivers from afflictions — not when afflictions no longer occur (if even Paul says 'afflicted in all things,' as though never 'not afflicted') — but when, 'afflicted,' we 'are not straitened' by God's help. Of being afflicted — after a certain Hebrew idiom — the involuntary circumstantial is signified; of being straitened, the voluntary: overcome by affliction, yielding to it. Whence Paul well says: 'Afflicted in all things, yet not straitened.' (Psalm 33:20 (LXX)) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what deliverance from evil means for a believer in trouble.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The saints pray not to be overcome by trouble, not for their tormentors to be struck down.
comments.comment: And indeed, when the saints are in tribulation, they pray, praying only this: 'Let us not be taken by the tribulation' (Matthew 6:13), not rather against those surrounding them with tribulation; for they receive it as a contest, not as a punishment. And he who receives it as a contest is not so against the opponents, as to wish them no longer to exist. 'Bring us not into temptation'; for he has not said, 'Strike those who tempt us.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fasting must be free of gloom and love of glory.
comments.comment: So one must not look gloomy, nor carry any charge of love of glory, but wash off what is dirt of the soul (Matthew 6:16).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: People work hardest at what they treasure.
comments.comment: What a person has set before himself, that he also thinks and works at most readily, and strives to set it right. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Burying wealth buries the heart with it, as Christ said: where your treasure is, there your heart will be.
comments.comment: But when wealth is split into a thousand uses and still remains over, it is pushed down into the earth and kept in hidden places. For the future is uncertain, they say, in case some unforeseen need should overtake us. It is uncertain whether you will ever come to need that buried gold, but the loss of your humanity is not uncertain. When you could not spend your wealth completely even with a thousand devices, then you hid it in the ground. A terrible madness: while the gold was still in the mines, you searched the earth for it; once it was brought to light, you made it disappear into the earth again. And then, I think, when you bury your wealth, you bury your heart along with it. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21). …
comments.selected_reason: Illustrates "where your treasure is, there your heart will be".
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Scripture's "heart" means the mind, so your mind is wherever your treasure is.
comments.comment: The heart and the mind mean the same thing; for when it is said: 'Where your treasure is, there also your heart will be' (Matt 6:21), there also is your mind. 'Blessed are the pure in heart' (Matt 5:8). Therefore, to say mind and heart is the same. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "heart" means in this verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: By "body" Christ means the spirited and desiring part of the soul, and by "lamp" the mind.
comments.comment: And Christ in the Gospels calls the soul 'body', saying, 'the eye is the lamp of the body' (Matt 6:22). Having said lamp, he means the intellect—for it is the receiver of knowledge—but 'body' refers to the spirited and desiring part of the soul, which some call the irrational part and others the passionate part.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words "lamp" and "body" in the verse.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The sound eye is sincere love and the evil eye is pretended love, or hypocrisy, which darkens the whole person.
comments.comment: The eye is the lamp of the body (Matthew 6:22). So if your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. And if the light in you is darkness, how great is that darkness (Matthew 6:23)? The sound eye is sincere love, through which, when the whole body is enlightened, love brings forth through the outward parts the same things as the things thought within. The evil eye, on the other hand, is pretended love, which is also called hypocrisy, and through it the whole body of a person is darkened.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the sound and the evil eye stand for.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Christ's question about the darkness exposes the hypocrites.
comments.comment: Therefore the Savior clearly convicts these people [the hypocrites] when he says: If the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness (Matthew 6:23)?
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: If the mind, which should be the lamp, loses its light, the rest of the soul is darker still.
comments.comment: And this is what the Savior says: 'If the light in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!' (Matthew 6:23). For if the eye of the body, that is, the mind, which ought to be a lamp, is deprived of light, then the other is much more so; in this way, the body of the soul becomes darkness, but it is not a human body, rather it is that which happens according to its irrational composition.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not loving money and loving it are opposite masters, so no one can serve both.
comments.comment: The un-money-loving manner is a good master; the one who loves money is a base one. So one must cling to the one. It is not possible to please both, for they are different and opposite habits (Matthew 6:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why no one can serve both God and money.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's aim was to turn his hearers away from worldly cares.
comments.comment: He brought forward: 'You cannot serve God and mammon,' (Mt 6:24) showing throughout that his aim was to turn those listening away from the care regarding present things. …
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Loving money is slavery to mammon, and no one can serve both evil and virtue, since loving God means hating evil.
comments.comment: … 'No one is able to serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other; you cannot serve God and mammon' (Matt 6:24). And it is clear that the love of money is the slavery of mammon, and it is upon every evil. For it is in no way possible to serve both evil and virtue; for the one doing sin is a slave of sin, and everyone who does sin hates the evil things. For those who love God hate the evil things. … 'For either he will hate the one and love the other'—for the virtuous one loves God and hates evil—'or he will hold to the one and despise the other,' which is precisely said; for he said 'to hold against' the evil, not 'to love' it. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Soul and body outrank food and clothing, so care for them first.
comments.comment: Since soul and body are more honorable than foods and garments, one must also despise the lesser things and care for the more honorable — I mean soul and body (Matthew 6:25).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul is more honorable than the body, so we should care for the body only as far as it does not hinder the soul.
comments.comment:
The soul is more honorable than the body’s essence, as God’s image and inbreathing. The body is its instrument and co-worker toward what is finest. So we must take thought for both body and soul together — for the body only so far as is enough for it and does not hinder the soul.

To the soul one must always give what is its own, care for it in every way, and draw it up through the virtues toward its creative cause (Matthew 6:25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the order of care Christ sets between soul, body, food and clothing.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God gives bodily needs to those who seek spiritual things first.
comments.comment: To those who seek the things of the soul God also gives what suits the bodies, so that we, not caring about such things more than we must, will not be hindered toward what is finest (Matthew 6:33).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the promise that these things will be added.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We should ask for great heavenly things and trust that small earthly needs will be supplied.
comments.comment: With these benefits to holy men through prayers expounded as we could, let us examine, from the Gospel record 'Ask for the great things, and the small shall be added to you; and ask for the heavenly things, and the earthly shall be added to you,' (Matthew 6:33) what asking great heavenly things is, and small earthly things. … that whoever wants to be spiritual, asking through prayers for heavenly great things, may inherit heaven's kingdom as heavenly and enjoy great goods as great — with earthly small things supplied to him by need's measure for bodily needs, since the Father knows what we need before we ask him.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One day's care is already heavy.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 6:34, if caring for one day is heavy and wretched, how is the excess not unmanageable?
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Do not condemn others; look at your own sins and weep over them, since only God is free from all fault.
comments.comment:
Those being trained toward piety put the bridle of good thought on the tongue, allowing it to speak only what does no harm. …

So let us not speak against one another or condemn the brothers (Matthew 7:1–2). The one steered by understanding does not look at others’ sins, but gazing at his own evils drops a good tear over them, that he may receive forgiveness from God.

It is impossible for humans, weak as we are, not to fall into a few absurdities at all. Not falling at all belongs by nature to God alone. We who are in sins must not delight in others’ evils, but take thought how we ourselves may get outside what is base.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what "do not judge" asks of us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Do not judge who deserves help, since giving to everyone in need will surely reach some whom God loves.
comments.comment: Do not judge who is worthy and who is unworthy, for you may miss the mark in your judgment. Since the matter is uncertain through ignorance, it is better to do good even to the unworthy for the sake of the worthy than to be on guard and, by avoiding the less good, fail to encounter the excellent. For from sparing and pretending to test who will rightly receive or not, you may neglect some who are loved by God, and the penalty for that is fiery eternal punishment. But from giving to all in turn who are in need, you must certainly find some who are able to be saved with God.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Remove your own great sins before correcting another's small ones, because condemning others only paints your own character.
comments.comment:
“First cast the beam out of your eye” (Matthew 7:3–5) — that is, show yourself clean of the great sins, and then you will be a counselor to the one who errs a little. If you do not cast out the beam, yet condemn the one who has the speck, you will reasonably hear the apostolic word: “You who say not to commit adultery, commit adultery” (Romans 2:21–22); “you who say not to steal, steal.”

So the wise will be a teacher for himself and will not condemn another. The law through Moses also commands this: “Attend to yourself.” “To yourself,” he says, not to another. “Attend” means look carefully at what concerns you. The understanding person will thus train himself, not looking at others’ faults but examining his own and repenting over them.

But some do not see their own slips, and laugh broadly at others’ stumbles — lying on the ground while mocking those who stand, smeared with mire from feet to head while condemning those who have little dirt. They sometimes say of someone, “So-and-so is hard, inhuman, greedy for shameful gain, money-loving, raw, senseless,” (Luke 18:9–14) and while hanging these titles on others they do not notice they are painting their own manner. How much damage it is to condemn others we have learned through the Pharisee who despised the tax collector. Having removed all this through this good legislation, he added another command again.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the beam and the speck, and why we must examine ourselves first.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Holy things must not be carelessly shown to unbelievers, because what is sanctified is what baptism has already cleansed.
comments.comment: [Christ says:] ‘Do not give what is holy to the dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine’ (Matthew 7:6). For to bring the hidden things, the things fit only for the holy, carelessly before those who are still unbelievers is full of danger. For what is sanctified is not what is still profane and grievously sick with uncleanness, but what has already been cleansed through holy baptism.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the "dogs" and "swine" are and why holy things are held back.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The pearls are the divine words, and those who would only trample them should not be given them.
comments.comment: For they were about to be more impious, 'trampling' the divine words which are the 'pearls', and decorating the 'inner man' with worldly things; not even observing the beauty or the preciousness of them, they were about to 'trample' them instead of regarding them highly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In Christ's allegory, dogs and swine stand for flatterers and lovers of pleasure.
comments.comment: And the Savior, protecting his own disciples, says allegorically, 'not to give the holy thing to dogs nor to cast pearls before swine' (Matthew 7:6). For dogs and swine are flatterers and lovers of pleasure, rejoicing with the lawless …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pearl is the word.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 7:6, the word is holy and a pearl, the heretics are dogs and pigs.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Asking, seeking and knocking are three stages of virtue, and knocking means keep trying if we are not answered at once.
comments.comment:
The beginning of virtue is to pray that the way of truth be made known to someone. The second step is to seek how one must travel that way. The third is, having taken hold of virtue, to knock to Christ, that he may open the door, free him from the narrow and compressed way, and lead him into the spacious work of knowledge. All this one receives through petition from God and toward God.

Perhaps he also hinted at asking with practice when he said “knock.” (Matthew 7:7) One knocks with the right hand, and the right hand is a symbol of good practice. And if you do not receive at once, do not despair even so — that is why he said “knock.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the three verbs of the verse and the point of "knock".
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Everyone who asks receives only if he asks as he should and truly attends to the one he asks.
comments.comment: [Christ's promise:] 'everyone who asks receives' (Matthew 7:8). For even when a teacher says: 'everyone who approaches me for the sake of lessons will have their knowledge,' we understand grammatically 'to approach the teacher,' that is, to attend closely to what is from the teacher along with practicing and studying them; but he who does not do so, it must be said to him: you did not approach him as I instructed
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The good gifts are spiritual gifts, the Holy Spirit himself, who is good by nature.
comments.comment:
He calls “good gifts” (Matthew 7:11) the spiritual gifts. Luke said “Holy Spirit” (Luke 11:13) instead of “goods,” and there is no difference: the Holy Spirit is what is good by nature. That is why he also gives goods to those who share in him.

But for those who are very wicked, because they sin without yielding, badness becomes in a way a nature for them — as with Satan and the demons. One may even call these bad by nature, though they were not created bad by nature, but hardened from self-chosen badness.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the "good gifts" are, by comparing Luke's wording.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Luke shows that the good things Matthew mentions are the Holy Spirit, who is one but brings many gifts.
comments.comment: And the other Evangelist, the Holy Spirit, interpreted the good things; for writing in the same place, Matthew says: 'He will give good things to those asking Him' (Matthew 7:11), while Luke says: 'He will give the Holy Spirit' (Luke 11:13). The Spirit, being one, is a multitude of good things according to His various gifts; for he who has the Holy Spirit has the gifts of the Spirit, which are many good things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ turns the law of loving your neighbor into a rule anyone can apply: do for others what you would want done for you.
comments.comment: Cyril: Therefore the law says, ‘You will love your neighbor as yourself’ (Leviticus 19:18); yet our Lord Jesus Christ introduces for us the law of mutual-loving through as many words as parts, and setting as it were the inborn knowledge and the wish in each as advocate for the law, ‘As many things then as you wish that the humans do for you, these things you also likewise do for them.’ (Matthew 7:12) For if of as many things as someone would pray to obtain, these he should also choose to do for others himself, he will not run off from the aim; yet he will rather walk straight of the love, and will bind on the crown of the mutual-loving.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: Christ's rule appeals to the natural love every person has for his neighbor.
comments.comment: Therefore, is the commandment, existing from the beginning and heard by all men, a friendly disposition according to natural concepts? For all, being by nature diurnal and social animals, love their neighbors; whence the Savior, stirring up this natural disposition, says: 'Therefore, all that you wish that men would do to you, do likewise to them' (Matt 7:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The road is narrow because virtue takes labor.
comments.comment: For labor follows virtue, while pleasure follows ease. The Savior teaches this, saying, 'Narrow is the gate and compressed is the road leading to life' (Matt 7:14), …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the way to life is called narrow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: False friends are hard to guard against because their wickedness hides under friendship, so pursue sincerity and simplicity.
comments.comment: It is not easy to avoid such people [the double-faced], nor to guard against the harm they do, because their wickedness is deeply hidden under the guise of friendship. The Lord calls such characters ravenous wolves, appearing in garments of sheep (Matthew 7:15). Flee the varied and many-sided character; pursue truth, sincerity, simplicity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why wolves in sheep's clothing are hard to spot and what to do.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: False teachers show light in their words but plan darkness within, like wolves in sheep's clothing.
comments.comment: [Of the false prophets:] They devise deeds worthy of darkness within, yet through their outward parts they bring forth words that seem to be full of light. For they are truly wolves who have put on sheep's clothing (Matthew 7:15). They wash only the outside of the cup and dish (Matthew 23:25), not knowing that unless the inside is cleansed, the outside cannot become clean.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sheep's clothing as outward words hiding inward deeds.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Whoever teaches and does what Christ handed over enjoys the kingdom of the heavens.
comments.comment: … For this one enjoys the kingdom of the heavens, whoever shows the belonging of the works, teaching and doing these things, which he himself also handed over to men while present (Mt 7:21). …
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Knowing God's will does not sanctify or bless; only doing it does.
comments.comment: 'Teach me,' he says, 'not only to know but also to do your will' Ps 142:10; for it is not the knowing of it that is sanctifying and making blessed, but it being worked and being done. Therefore also the Savior says, 'Not everyone saying to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father' Matt 7:21.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ requires doing the will, not just saying "Lord".
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The warning is for those who began well, even working signs, but later chose evil and are treated as never known.
comments.comment:
The word is against those who at the beginning believed rightly and carefully worked virtue — so as even to do signs, cast out demons, and prophesy — but later turned to baseness by willing choice and wicked eagerness.

When he says, “I never knew you,” (Matthew 7:22–23) he places the one who lived virtuously at the start but was condemned at the end on a level with those never known at all. God says he knows those he loves, and he loves those who believe in him wholly and do what is pleasing to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who "I never knew you" is aimed at.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Calling Jesus Lord counts only when said in the Holy Spirit, with diligent work and true disposition.
comments.comment: For the Savior himself says: 'Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord' (Matt 7:22); and I, he says, will confess to them, 'Depart from me, workers of iniquity, I never knew you' (Matt 7:23). And again: 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?' (Luke 6:46). Therefore, the one saying 'Lord Jesus' in the Holy Spirit, not in mere utterance but in diligent work and true disposition, is truly a servant, …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even prophecy and miracles do not bring anyone into the kingdom unless he also walks the right and just way.
comments.comment: To prophesy, to cast out demons, and to do great works of power on earth is certainly a lofty and wonderful thing, but no one who is found in all these things attains the kingdom of heaven unless he walks by the observance of the right and just way. The Lord declares and says: “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do great works of power in your name? And then I will say to them: I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matthew 7:22-23). Righteousness is needed so that anyone may merit God as judge; his commands and warnings must be obeyed, so that our merits may receive their reward.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why signs and wonders are not enough.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Christ's "I never knew you" shows his greatness, since he knows the things that matter and the sinner is not known by God.
comments.comment: He says to those who tell him, 'Did we not eat in your name, and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works?' (Matthew 7:22) 'Depart from me; I never knew you.' (Matthew 7:23) Does that 'I never knew you' present his power as lesser, or as greater and more wonderful, because he did not know the worse and those who are perishing? For he knew the things that matter, the better things, and 'the Lord knew those who are his,' (2 Timothy 2:19) and 'if anyone is ignorant, he is not known.' (1 Corinthians 14:38) So the sinner is not known by God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To know in Scripture can mean to be united with someone, not just to have information about him.
comments.comment: To know in the Scripture does not always signify merely to have certain knowledge, but also to have experienced something and to be united to it, as in: 'not knowing sin' (2 Corinthians 5:21), and: 'I never knew you, workers of lawlessness' (Matthew 7:23); for he did not know sin as in not having certain knowledge of what sin is, but as in not having practiced it. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "I never knew you" means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The "house" in Christ's parable is the doer's conduct and way of life.
comments.comment: For when he says that the one who “heard” the “words” of Jesus and changed them into deeds “builds his own house upon the rock” (Matt 7:24), he calls the conduct and the practical and contemplative life the “house” of the doer.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the "house" stands for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who hear and do Christ's words are the firm ones founded on the rock, and belief without doing is empty.
comments.comment: These are the ones he calls strong and steadfast, founded upon the rock with a solid mass, made firm with unmovable and unshaken stability against every storm and whirlwind of the world. “Whoever hears my words and does them,” he says, “I will compare to a wise man who built his house upon the rock. The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew and beat against that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon the rock” (Matthew 7:24-25). We must therefore press on in his words, learning and doing whatever he both taught and did. Otherwise, how can someone say he believes in Christ if he does not do what Christ commanded him to do?
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: A hearer who does not act is like a house on sand that falls in trial, while the doer is strong in Christ.
comments.comment:
The hearer of the law understood spiritually, who is not also a doer, is compared to a house built on sand. In a time of trial it falls and is buried when the spirits of wickedness blow, when troubled waters enter as far as the soul, and when the muddy torrent of their lawlessness disturbs it and shakes the danger concerning the last things.

He well said “I will liken him” (Matthew 7:24–27) of the prudent man, but “he will be likened” of the foolish. The worker of virtue is altogether “strong in the Christ who empowers him,” (Philippians 4:13) from whom comes every setting-right for humans, from whom come wisdom and understanding and likeness toward the good. The base person does not have God as cause of his badness and folly; he likens himself to the senseless, having stood away from what is according to nature and come to be in what is against nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two houses and the wording "I will liken him" and "he will be likened".
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The house on the rock is the person who turns the Lord's words into works, with Christ as the rock, and the house on sand belongs to the one who hears without doing.
comments.comment: Furthermore, the Gospel clarifies such a house; for it says: 'whoever hears my words and does them is like a prudent man, who built his house upon the rock, and the rain descended, the winds blew, the rivers came, and the house was not shaken' (Matt 7:24-25), which is the state of the virtuous person of having turned the words of the Lord into works, who remains without want, not being harmed by any of the opposing energies. For upon 'the rock' he has 'Christ,' the one of such a kind has established his state and his choice. For to the one confessing him, it was said by him: 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church' (Matt 16:18); but to the one hearing the words as they happen and not connecting deeds to the words, he is 'a foolish man resembling one who built his house upon the sand' (Matt 7:26), which is the state upon the fluid things of life, things not receiving firm foundations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever denies Christ the foundation builds on sand and is easily shaken.
comments.comment: If anyone, then, denies the foundation and refuses the rock, he does not build on it but on the sand (Matthew 7:24–27), and so he will very easily be shaken down. For what Christ does not hold up will surely be moved, since it has no firm footing.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The authority of Jesus' words lay in the substance of what he said, not in fine phrasing.
comments.comment: And in the Gospel according to John are set out the things he taught, which show the grandeur of Jesus’ speech, a grandeur not of phrasing but of substance. And it is clear from the Gospels that “his word was with authority” (Luke 4:32; compare Matthew 7:28–29), at which they marveled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the crowd meant by "authority".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's touch cleansed the leper and showed that his holy flesh also sanctifies.
comments.comment: By the touch he accomplished the cleansing, making clear that his holy flesh is also needed for sanctification. The Spirit cleanses; communion with the body produces sanctification. Touching the leper, the Savior healed him, showing that the Spirit in him heals diseases, while the body, by contact, grants sanctification (Matthew 8:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus touched the leper.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus touched the leper with a touch of the mind and freed him from two kinds of leprosy.
comments.comment: In a like way, Jesus “touched” the leper (Matthew 8:3) with a touch of the mind rather than of the senses, to cleanse him, as I think, in two ways: he freed him not only, as most people take it, from bodily leprosy by a bodily touch, but also from the other leprosy by his truly divine touch.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the deeper meaning of Jesus touching the leper.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gift the law required of a cleansed leper, two birds, is a picture of Christ and his work.
comments.comment:
What was the gift the leper had to bring under the law? “Two little birds.” The priest slaughtered one “over living water,” took “cedar wood, twisted scarlet, and hyssop,” (Leviticus 14:4–7) dipped the living bird “in the blood of the slaughtered bird over living water,” and anointed the right ear, hand, and foot of the leper being cleansed. The living bird he sent away outside the city “into the open country.”

Watch how through these things Christ is painted for us in full: living bird — the living and heavenly Word; slaughtered blood — the Lord’s precious blood in his own body; incorruptible cedar — incorruptible flesh that “did not see corruption” (Acts 2:31); hyssop — the Spirit’s fervor; scarlet — confession of the blood-covenant; living water — baptism’s life-giving grace; sending outside the city — departure from the world and ascent into the heavens; right anointings — that we must become people of contemplation, practice, and journey in the things of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the offering Jesus tells the leper to bring.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Now the saved are many compared with the few who perish.
comments.comment: Just as then, for a comparison with the perishing ones, the few were the ones being saved, so understand for me that the being-saved ones are many in comparison with the perishing few now (Mt 8:11–12).
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The sick were brought at evening perhaps from caution, shame, or lack of helpers.
comments.comment: Why did they not bring them by day? Was it caution toward the scribes and Pharisees, or shame again at their weaknesses, as with Nicodemus — or because the sick had no one to bring them to Jesus (Matthew 8:16)?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Matthew turns Isaiah's word about the cross into healings because Christ's passion healed men.
comments.comment: How does the evangelist lift up the word brought to the cross according to Isaiah (Isaiah 53:4) into healings (Mt 8:17)? Because even his passion was a healing for men, and the Lord suffered no more than he worked through those dishonoring him and through his own death, preparing and fighting against the life of men by setting himself apart for them. Isaiah brought the word to the cross, but Matthew to the healings of diseases; and he did this because even that passion of the Savior was a healing for men, and it is evident that his death also granted life to us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Matthew applies Isaiah's words about suffering to Jesus' healings.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ took our passions on himself, and distress, grief and fear are ailments of the soul.
comments.comment: Rather, the Word was displaying in himself the passions of our nature, taking up the part that was given over to suffering. As it is written, “He himself took up our weaknesses and bore our ailments” (Isaiah 53:4; Matthew 8:17). For distress, grief and fear are ailments of the soul; but weariness, sleep and the wounding of the body are weaknesses of the flesh.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Christ crossed the lake to avoid seeming to seek praise, to spare the Pharisees, and to reach nearby cities.
comments.comment: Christ withdrew from the crowds so that no one would think him applause-loving, glad of praise from the many; so that the Pharisees would not be angered at him (for it distressed them greatly that many followed him); and so that he might shine his own saving light on the nearby cities (Matthew 8:18).
comments.selected_reason: Gives three reasons Jesus left the crowds.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus took only the disciples across so they could learn what suited them, and so cross from earthly things to heavenly.
comments.comment:
Jesus commands only the disciples to go across, so that he may not seem hindered by the crowds pressing him from letting the disciples hear the lessons that fit them, and so that God’s mysteries — spoken “in parables to the crowds” (Matthew 8:18–22) — may be revealed to them more genuinely.

Since they left everything in hand and followed him alone for love of learning, he commands them to cross from the temporary to the eternal, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the fleshly to the spiritual.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Parents are to be honored, but when honor to them blocks pleasing God, God must come first.
comments.comment:
Where honor toward God is not at stake, it is right to honor parents. But when both stand in the middle, one must cling to the one and despise the other — especially if honor to parents hinders pleasing God. God must be given the first place, lest we be found like Cain assigning God the second place.

Likewise the old law forbade priests to approach the dead and to hold to their own ministry without being dragged down into fleshly sympathies — that through shadows; but Christ teaches unveiledly that whoever wants to attend on God must make no account of kinship so as to be distracted from being with Christ. He himself, for the benefit of those with him, overlooked mother and brothers, saying, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” (Matthew 12:48) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus refuses the request to bury a father first.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dead are those who set their minds on worldly things and do not keep from deeds of death.
comments.comment: ‘Lord, let me first go and bury my father.’ But he said, ‘Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead’ (Matthew 8:21–22). By ‘the dead’, I think, he means those who have chosen to set their minds on the things of the world and have not kept away from the deeds of death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'dead' are in 'leave the dead to bury their own dead'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Asking to be saved shows faith, but saying 'we are perishing' shows little faith with Christ aboard.
comments.comment: To say “save” (Matthew 8:25) carries praise of faith; to say “we are perishing” charges little faith in those who expect danger while Christ sails with them. They are not wholly unbelieving, but little-faith — those who did not take courage in dangers while Christ was with them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the mixed faith in the disciples' cry.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The disciples show faith and little faith together, since none could perish with Christ aboard.
comments.comment: See little faith together with faith. They believe he can save, yet as little-faith people they say, “Save — we are perishing.” (Matthew 8:25–26) It was never possible to perish while the One who can do all things was with them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The demons knew Christ would come and judge them, and speak as if wronged though they are justly punished.
comments.comment:
“You have come before the time,” (Matthew 8:29) they say. They knew in the Word that Christ was also going to come and that he himself has them to judge. If they also said “before the time” as a slander on the timing of the incarnation, as if it had happened out of season, it is no wonder that, being wicked, they dare to say even this.

And yet, knowing they will be punished, they speak as if overlooking him: “What to us and to you?” For the Judge has an account with us from the time we transgressed his commandments.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the demons mean by 'before the time'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The demons say this because Christ will come in the flesh and will judge them at the end.
comments.comment: “You have come,” they say, “before the time of the prophetic words” (Mt 8:29), the demons hearing, because Christ is about to come into the world through the flesh of your flesh and because he is about to judge them in the consummation. “You have come to torment us before the time,” that is, before the consummation.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The demons wanted the swine because they could not harm men, and the Gergesenes asked Jesus to leave from lack of desire for the good.
comments.comment: Why then are they worthy to enter into the swine (Mt 8:31)? When they are not able according to men, they desire according to the irrational, of those things which are through man, just as the misanthropes harm him or his own things. Seeing such a small sign, the Gergesenes entreat Jesus to depart from their borders (Mt 8:34), because they had no desire for the good. For they did not say this judging themselves unworthy, but as being unfeeling and exceedingly unfaithful.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ healed the man because of the faith of those who carried him, and called him child.
comments.comment:
The Lord did not look at the faith of the paralyzed man, but at the faith of those who brought him. There are times when one person is healed through another’s faith, and the holy writing of the Gospels is full of such cases. Seeing their faith, he does not show their labor vain, but says “child” (Matthew 9:2) — either to him as one who also believed, or according to the word of creation.

He called the paralytic “child” by the word of creation, or as one who had believed in him and known him as Lord and Creator.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus responds to the friends' faith and says 'child'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus said 'Son of Man' to show that divine authority to forgive had come down into human nature without loss.
comments.comment:
The word went out and the wonder followed. Why then did he also say that the Son of Man forgives sins while a God-sign was being done? To show that he brought the authority of divinity down into human nature through the indivisible union with it.

“For if I also became man,” he says, “being God the Word, and through the economy [God's plan of salvation] I live and move about on earth, still I accomplish wonders beyond speech and grant forgiveness of sins. I did not take away any property of divinity or lessen it by becoming, unchangeably and truly, Son of Man according to flesh on earth.” (Matthew 9:3–7)

And a little later: he says “on earth” economically, to show that even having become man and appeared on earth he was God by nature. He commanded the paralytic to carry the bed and go home, so that through him he might also confirm to those absent what had happened to him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Matthew was turned to virtue by a word alone, though the Father draws all through Christ.
comments.comment: This too is full of a God-sign: that by word alone such a man was turned toward so great a virtue. Calling Matthew, he shows that even if no one comes to him “unless the Father draws him,” (John 6:44) still the drawing happens through Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the power of Jesus' call to Matthew.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Savior was not offended by the tax collectors' feast and ate and drank with them as master of nature.
comments.comment: So the Savior, unashamed, called a tax collector into discipleship and came into his house, where nothing else was good except the householder’s change. A large crowd of tax collectors were reclining with Jesus. The Savior is not indignant and does not take what happens as an insult to him; as master of nature he arrives at the feast, eats and drinks, showing the truth of the body and blessing the timely use of foods.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisees objected because the law kept holy and profane apart, but Christ came as physician to heal.
comments.comment:
Pharisees and scribes were also present — not to learn, but to meddle in what was happening. They see the tax collectors reclining with him, call the disciples, and blame what is going on. Jesus hears and says to them: “You also need a physician. If you were not ill, you would not blame the physician’s love of humankind. I know they are tax collectors; I know their soul’s diseases; I know they are in a bad way. That is why I have come to them: to heal their sick souls.” (Matthew 9:9–13)

The reason the Pharisees seize on the Savior for eating with sinners is that there was a law “to distinguish between holy and profane.” (Leviticus 10:10) They did not know that Christ was giving philanthropic grace above the legal use: the one cast out the evil; the other changed it. So he showed that he is present not as judge but as physician, and does what belongs to the art by being with those who also need healing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the Pharisees' objection and Jesus' answer about the physician.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The old law kept the holy from the profane but did not turn away one who came.
comments.comment: Yet the old law forbade the holy to glue themselves to the profane, lest their mind slip — not the opposite: if a profane person runs toward a holy one, one must not turn him away, according to “You shall not abhor an Edomite or an Egyptian.” (Deuteronomy 23:7)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ came for souls in a bad state, as a physician comes for the sick, since pity outweighs sacrifice.
comments.comment: For if we do not defile ourselves regarding the bodies of the suffering, it was indeed fitting to do all things for the sake of those whose souls are badly disposed, so that he might be able to have these in the best state (Mt 9:12–13). And it was necessary for you, he says, to learn from the divine scripture, how pity for the neighbor is preferable to every sacrifice. Is it just to pity some of these, who, not having the souls most beautifully, need correction so that they might have them better? So for me too, he says, the aim of the presence is not that I might benefit men being righteous (for they would not even have needed such a thing, being righteous in manner), but that those lying badly in many sins might be transferred by a proper grace toward the better; for those who are strong, he says, have no need of a physician, but those who are doing badly.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Christ wants faith and mercy rather than the sacrifices of the law, and calls those who stood far off.
comments.comment: He [Christ] wants faith that justifies the human being, not the law in letters that commands sacrifices through bloods — which he makes clear by adding also “knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings,” for “mercy” (Hosea 6:6) is the gospel word. So we are justified from faith freely, without works of law. And he calls not those who are near, but those who have stood far off.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ came to save the perishing, because the great thing is to support what is falling.
comments.comment: And another scripture says, "I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners" (Matthew 9:13). This means that he must save those who are perishing. For the great and wonderful thing is not to support what is standing, but what is falling. So also Christ willed to save the things that were perishing, and he saved many, coming and calling us when we were already perishing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ calls sinners rather than the righteous.
comments.author: Anonymous (2 Clement)

comments.capsule: The Pharisees cannot take the new teaching like a torn garment or old wineskin, and are punished more for hearing and refusing.
comments.comment:
The Pharisees, resembling a torn garment or an old wineskin, cannot receive the youthful teaching that annuls the bodily things of the law. He says the tear is worse because those who hear the gospel and do not accept it are punished more than those who never heard.

And since John’s disciples asked the Lord two things — why we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not — to them he spoke the parable of the bridegroom, and to the Pharisees the one about the wineskins (Matthew 9:14–17).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The old garment is the old man and the new cloth the new Word, and these cannot be joined.
comments.comment: “An old garment,” he said, speaks the old man; “but a coarse cloth” the new Word (Mt 9:16-17), and a joining of these does not happen; … for spiritual susceptibility in a bodily man is not. For having been accustomed to seeking the things of the flesh, he will never find joy in these, but the matter will appear harsh and unendurable to him and will be separated from him more, because the thing being dragged along burns him. And the fasts are old and the old men; but new wine is the new Word, which they cannot contain; for their soft material is torn, not bearing the strength of the spiritual life. And the Word was not given to such people for what is necessary.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ healed the woman and called her daughter, so no one with an involuntary disease is unclean.
comments.comment: Perceiving the woman with the hemorrhage, Christ did not deem her unworthy, but healed her and called her daughter as one faithful — and at the same time showing that with God no one who has an involuntary disease is unclean (Matthew 9:20–22).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus welcomed the woman whom the law counted unclean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By calling the woman near, the Lord leads the law's types over into spiritual understanding.
comments.comment: He shows that with God no one who has an involuntary disease is unclean. That is why the Lord also calls the woman with the hemorrhage near: to lead the typological law over into spiritual contemplation (Matthew 9:20–22).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only the woman touched Jesus by faith, while the pressing crowds touched only his body.
comments.comment: The outer man has perceptible touch, and the inner man has touch — that touch by which the woman with the flow of blood touched the hem of Jesus. She touched. For the one who said, Who touched me? bore witness. … So those pressing Jesus were not touching him; for they were not touching him by faith. But she alone, having a certain divine touch, touched Jesus and for this reason was healed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between the woman's touch and the crowd's.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Flute-players were present because people mourned unmarried girls with symbolic wedding rites.
comments.comment: It is a custom among people to mourn unmarried girls who die when they are at the age for marriage, with symbolic wedding rites. That is why flute-players were inside — even if the Jews were then doing this against the Jewish command (Matthew 9:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why flute-players were at the girl's house.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus took the girl's hand to show that his body gives life.
comments.comment: About the synagogue ruler’s daughter it is written that “when the crowd was put out, Jesus went in, took her hand, and the girl was raised.” (Matthew 9:25) Why did he not rather, as with Lazarus, content himself with a word for the girl’s rising, but also took her hand? To show that his body gives life — for it is a body of life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus took the girl by the hand.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ could say he was able without boasting, since his power was his by nature, and the healed men's telling of it showed gratitude, not boasting.
comments.comment: [On the blind men:] No one boasts if the power speaks about itself that it is able; but it would be boasting for one who does not have the power by nature, but receives it by grace to say 'I am able.' And the Savior commanded the blind not to say anything about what happened, teaching us not to show that it is necessary; for it was not boasting toward God to speak the truth about it. And the confession of those who were healed concerning the healing did not bring a charge, but testified to gratitude.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Calling them reapers shows that the prophets' work was also his, since all people are his own seed.
comments.comment: Calling them [the disciples] therefore reapers, showing that even the things having happened through the prophets happened through his own power and provision, and that before prophets and apostles he himself is Lord and Creator of all men, and upon his own seed, not upon another's, he sends and dispatches the disciples.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The workers are the few disciples sent.
comments.comment: He calls the disciples workers — few though they were — whom he sent into all the world under heaven (Matthew 9:38).
comments.selected_reason: Says who the 'workers' are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By telling them to pray to the Lord of the harvest and then sending workers himself, Christ showed he is that Lord.
comments.comment: He knows that the Lord of the harvest is the God of all: the intelligible threshing floor — that is, humanity — is his, and the harvest is his. Yet see: having ordered them to pray the Lord of the harvest, he immediately showed that he himself is that Lord, sending out the laborers — the holy apostles — and giving them authority over unclean spirits as God (Matthew 9:38–10:1). For it is not within the measures of humanity to give anyone the working of the Holy Spirit; yet Christ has given it.
comments.selected_reason: Shows that Christ is himself the Lord of the harvest.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The law and the prophets foreshadowed the twelve disciples, as twelve loaves with frankincense and salt.
comments.comment:
The law also prefigured these twelve disciples (Matthew 10:2), and the prophets proclaimed them beforehand. It is written in the Mosaic book: “Take fine flour and make it into twelve loaves, and set them on the pure table before the Lord, and set frankincense and salt on them.” (Leviticus 24:5–7) For the bread that came down from heaven “and gives life to the world” (John 6:33–35) is Christ himself; and by imitation of him the blessed disciples too are called breads. Having become sharers in the one who nourishes us unto eternal life, they also nourish, through their own writings, those who “hunger and thirst for righteousness.” (Matthew 5:6)

Just as the Savior, being “the true light,” named them light (“You are the light of the world”), (Matthew 5:13–14) so he himself, being “the bread of life,” also granted the disciples to be understood in the rank of the breads. See the skill of the law: “You shall set frankincense and salt on the breads.” Frankincense is a symbol of fragrance; salt, of mind and understanding. Both were present in the highest degree in the holy apostles. Their life was fragrant — they even said, “We are the fragrance of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:15) to Christ — and they were also all-understanding. That is why they also heard, “You are the salt of the earth.”

I hear the prophet David singing about them: “There Benjamin the younger in ecstasy, rulers of Judah their leaders, rulers of Zebulun, rulers of Naphtali.” (Psalm 68:27) For the divine disciples were chosen from almost every tribe of Israel and became worldwide luminaries holding a word of life — men who had been craftsmen, seafarers, and fishers, without a stock of polished words, “unlearned in speech” yet rich “in knowledge.” …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Jews had the promises and Christ came from them, so they heard first; the Samaritans count with the nations.
comments.comment: First one must preach to the Jews. The promises had been made to them, that from them Christ was going to appear according to the flesh; and when they disobeyed, then one must go to the nations. He joins the Samaritans to those from the nations, since they too were from the nations by race — Babylonians who settled Judea.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the apostles are sent first to Israel and not to the Gentiles or Samaritans.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ did not cut off the Gentiles, but Israel had to be sought first, as God promised through Ezekiel.
comments.comment: He [Christ] did not completely cut off those from the Gentiles about to believe, nor the Samaritans, desiring 'all people' (1 Timothy 2:4) to be 'saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,' but it was necessary first to go to 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' just as he himself says toward the Canaanite: 'I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' which God promised to seek through the prophet Ezekiel. But they lost the law having been given to them, not having guarded it.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The kingdom of heaven means grace received through faith.
comments.comment: By “kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 10:7) he means the grace that comes through faith — the adoption through the Spirit that unites the human being to God.
comments.selected_reason: Says what 'kingdom of heaven' means here.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The kingdom has come near in the incarnate Lord, though unbelievers think him far.
comments.comment: And he says 'has come' (Mt 10:7) not as if it were approaching; for it had approached of the incarnate Lord, but as far as those who have not yet believed, it seems Christ is far from them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: They must give freely as they received, even carrying no purse, to show they have turned from wealth.
comments.comment: You received free, give free (Mt 10:8). … just as those who received gifts from him for free, he commands to give for free. Therefore, do not be anxious to take neither gold nor silver nor bronze because of the way, he says, for need, but I want you to not even have a purse, so as to show to all by the form how much you have turned away from the desire of wealth.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The command forbids every possession to excess as a hindrance to virtue, but not necessary food.
comments.comment: The saying forbids every possession to excess — from gold down to a staff — as the greatest hindrance to virtue and piety. It does not forbid necessary food. If it were possible for us to live without food, he would have forbidden that too (Matthew 10:9–10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how far the ban on carrying things goes.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles are to be free of care for the body, though the Gospels differ on the staff and sandals.
comments.comment: For I want to show the deacons of the Gospel to be entirely free and prudent, not being humbled by care for any single thing of the body (Mt 10:9-10). And Matthew says both he and Luke say 'neither sandals' 'nor' a garment 'nor a staff,' which seems to be the most modest thing to take, 'on the way.' But Mark seems to permit them to take a 'staff' and 'to have put on sandals' in some of the copies. For he says in others that 'he commanded them so that they might carry nothing on the way,' neither a 'staff' nor a 'bag' nor 'bread' nor 'copper into the belt' nor 'having put on sandals.'
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: An apostle should not carry a dead skin, and with the Savior guarding his way he needs no sandals.
comments.comment:
[On 'nor sandals':] It is not fitting for an apostle in journeys to carry a dead skin, but to walk with life following the one saying, 'I am the way,' and to step out of a holy land wearing nothing; for they are not 'paths of serpent upon rock,' Mt 10:10 and perhaps not of any other beast.

For as much as you have the Savior lighting your darkness and guarding 'your entrance and your exit,' Psalm 121:8 you have no need of sandals.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A gentle apostle has no need of a rod, since sheep turn to the shepherd's voice alone.
comments.comment: [On 'nor staff':] Where there is no disorder, but gentleness, there is no need for a rod, so as not to frighten in the beginning by means of the rod; for beautiful sheep turn to the shepherd by voice alone, so if you have gentleness, do not fear the rod, which Paul holds up against the Corinthians.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The single tunic is Christ, put on in baptism, and the old man must be stripped off.
comments.comment: [The apostles take] Not two tunics, but the 'seamless' and 'woven from above' Christ Jesus; 'for as many as were baptized into Christ, you have clothed yourselves with Christ' (Gal 3:27); for it is necessary 'to strip off' the old man (Eph 4:22) along with his 'deeds' and his 'desires.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'not two tunics' as putting on Christ.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The apostles must not move from house to house, and those who dishonor them are punished like Sodom.
comments.comment: He does not want them to change from place to place and house to house, lest grief come to the first host, and lest they take on a suspicion of gluttony and easiness. The dust shaken from their feet is proof of a journey toward them that gained nothing, and of the toils they endured for them. They will be punished equally with the people of Sodom (Genesis 19): those dishonored the angels; these, the apostles (Matthew 10:11–15).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who refuse the apostles are punished like Sodom.
comments.comment: [Of those who refuse the apostles:] But the punishment is equal to the Sodomites for those not receiving them, since those who seemed to have received the angels as hospitality rebuked them, but those who called them to the kingdom were refused.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Be prudent like serpents, quick to flee, and gentle like doves, returning later to admonish.
comments.comment:
He wants them to be prudent: to teach the doctrines of piety openly, and, knowing the malice of the base, not to resist if some come against them, but to leave and not rush thoughtlessly toward suffering.

He likens them to serpents, teaching that they must be quick to flee if some come wanting to kill them; and to doves, since that bird does not remember evil, loves to stay in the places it is used to, and turns back to the same spot when the one driving it out stops.

So the word teaches that one must not leave the persecutors altogether, but yield for a little and return again to admonish them when the anger ceases. Christ himself did this with them: being persecuted, withdrawing from Judea, and returning again (Matthew 10:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the serpent and the dove.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Innocence is more precious to God, but shrewdness is fitting for the apostolic mission.
comments.comment: And to the holy apostles the Savior himself said: ‘Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves’ (Matthew 10:16). Yet innocence is precious with God, and compared with the other is in every way the better. But shrewd and wily conduct is fitting for the management of the apostolic mission; the blessed Paul too made use of it at times, everywhere escaping an untimely death at the hands of his enemies. So shrewdness, in godly pursuits, might well be acceptable, but it would by no means be counted as the fragrance of virtue if it were tested by its own nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how 'wise as serpents' and 'innocent as doves' fit together.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Flee pursuers as the serpent does, not cutting short the Gospel's time.
comments.comment: Just as the serpent withdraws from those pursuing and hides himself, Mt 10:16 so also you, withdrawing from those pursuing, will endure the time of the Gospel without pre-empting it.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A word is given when useful, so confession helps others.
comments.comment: “It is given,” (Matthew 10:19) he says — a word is given to some when it is useful to make a defense, so that through the confession some may be helped and the church strengthened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains when the words 'it is given' apply.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The grace to speak came only in the hour of trial, so it could not be mistaken for human skill.
comments.comment: In that very hour he promised to give the grace of debate, so that the Spirit’s gift might be shown. If he had given it before the time of trial, the matter would have been thought a thing of human nature and skill. They were not going to be hated by absolutely everyone, but by many — especially at that time. So from the greater part he said “by all,” (Matthew 10:19–22) since those who received the word loved them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ prepares the apostles for what will happen, and they are hated by many though many also receive them.
comments.comment:
He prepares the apostles so as to become ready for the things that will happen and not to be disturbed, Mt 10:19-22 and at the same time shows the power of God helping them and his own proclamation, and neither the madness nor the unbelief of the Jews being spared, nor even of their own. 'And you will be hated,' he says, 'by many'; Mt 10:22 …

for many were there receiving them in their houses and loving them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Only enduring to the end counts, since the end shows the worth of everything.
comments.comment: 'And he who endures until the end, this shall be saved,' he says; Mt 10:22 for he who only having been bold and believing in the beginning, but not until the end, this one is not a partaker of the promised good things; for in every matter, both good and bad, the end is indicative.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why endurance to the end is required.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Whatever comes before the end is only a step on the way up, so even a confessor must keep standing.
comments.comment: Confession is the beginning of glory, not already the merit of the crown; it does not complete the praise but initiates the dignity. And since it is written, “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22; 24:13; Mark 13:13), whatever comes before the end is a step by which one ascends to the summit of salvation, not the endpoint where the height of the summit is already held. He is a confessor, but after confession the danger is greater, because the adversary has been provoked more.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: The disciples are to flee persecution so as not to throw their lives away and harm those the preaching would help.
comments.comment:
He does not want them to be cowardly — rather the opposite: not, out of longing for the things hoped for, to hand themselves over ready to death and so harm those who are about to be helped by the preaching.

He urges the disciples to flee from this city to another, and from that to another. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus tells the disciples to flee.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus taught the disciples not to meet danger rashly, and set the example himself.
comments.comment: Jesus taught his disciples not to be rash, and said to them: “If they persecute you in this city, flee to the other; and if they persecute you in the other, flee again to another” (Matthew 10:23). And as he taught them, he became for them an example of a steady life, one that takes care not to go out to meet dangers at random, or at the wrong time, or without good reason.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cities of Israel also mean the assemblies of the faithful, which last until the Lord's second appearing.
comments.comment: By “cities of Israel” (Matthew 10:23) he also means the assemblies of the faithful, which last until the consummation of the age. Teachers and learners do not cease until the Lord’s second appearing. And the disciples and evangelists seem to live until then, since from their writings all teach.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bear all abuse; do not outrank the Master.
comments.comment: He teaches them to bear every kind of abuse patiently, and not to think themselves above the Master (Matthew 10:25).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the practical point of the verse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: At the judgment God looks to the heart.
comments.comment: In the time of judgment everything is made plain. He does not attend to abuses, but to the hearts (Matthew 10:26).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Habakkuk foretold the apostles' boldness: once scarcely speaking in secret, they would fill the world with their voice.
comments.comment: About the apostles’ boldness in preaching, marvelous Habakkuk also foretold: “They will open their bridles like a poor man eating in secret” (Habakkuk 3:14) — that is, the apostles who at first scarcely spoke to a few, and in secret, fed by the faith of believers, later broke the bridle of fear set on them and will fill the world under heaven with their own voice. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ will confess the one who confesses him.
comments.comment: The one who confesses that Christ is God, having humbled himself, will have Christ confessing about him to the Father that he is a genuine servant (Matthew 10:32).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Confessing Christ unites a person with him, and denying him cuts the person off.
comments.comment: I suppose that, as 'he who is joined to a harlot is one body,' (1 Corinthians 6:16) so he who confesses someone — especially in the season of torture and examination of faith — is mingled and united with the confessed; while he who denies, by denial itself, as by a dividing sword, suffers division from him whom he denies, severed from him whom he denied.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how confessing Christ joins us to him and denying cuts us off.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord's teaching divides, setting the believer against the world and in union with God.
comments.comment: He who loves the world through sinning is shown to be an enemy of God; likewise also he who, confirming friendship toward God through piety, is immediately found to be an enemy of the world; whence it is impossible, just as one cannot serve God and Mammon (Matt 6:24), so one cannot be a friend to God and the world. For the Lord, having come, made those who are friends of God and obey Him a sword and a division upon the earth (Matt 10:34); for the word of His teaching divides and separates, preparing through this to have enmity toward the world and union toward God, which is friendship toward Him; …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'sword' as the division his word brings.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ does not want physical kinship put before his preaching, which will divide families.
comments.comment: Having armed them sufficiently against insults, but also having trained them bravely to bear the three sufferings, because the disposition of kinship was extremely prone to undermining the calculation, being sufficient (for who could easily avoid having enmity toward those most intimate?), he says well, 'do not think so' (Mt 10:34); for I want you to be so turned away from regarding physical kinship, that they might know even more that my preaching will cause much division among the kin; for those who having seen once that which is toward piety, I want to place all and the nearest as kinship in the second place.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Keep no friendship with God's enemies.
comments.comment: One must not keep friendship with the enemies of God and friends of Satan (Matthew 10:34–35).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ, like the law, puts what pleases God above reverence for parents.
