comments.comment: The law bars him from such things entirely, setting what pleases God above reverence for parents. ‘For he shall not go near,’ it says, ‘his father or his mother’ (Numbers 6:6–7). For when virtue is being achieved, away with love of the flesh; let God hold the first and higher place over kinship by blood. This is what Christ himself also said: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10:37–38).
comments.selected_reason: Shows that putting God above parents was already the law's rule.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Preferring this life to Christ is unworthy; putting him first finds eternal life.
comments.comment: “The one who loves this temporary life here,” (Matthew 10:37–39) he says, “and prefers it to me ‘is not worthy of me.’ But the one who neglects this temporary life here and counts me and my commandments as much will find eternal life.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Loss of soul' here means separation from the body, while the one who finds his soul suffers undying punishment.
comments.comment: Here he calls “loss of soul,” (Matthew 10:39) by a stretched use of the word, separation from the body. The one who “finds” his soul — that is, who prefers this temporary life here and seems to gain it — endures something worse than death: he is sent into undying punishment and death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the paradox of finding and losing one's soul.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Receiving the apostles means receiving the Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: “The one who receives you,” he says, “who preach the truth, receives that divinity itself — that is, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For this is what he means: the one who receives you receives me, and the one who receives me receives the Father himself.” (Matthew 10:40)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what receiving the apostles amounts to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ rewards any welcome, so poverty is no excuse.
comments.comment: He said this so that no one would plead poverty as an excuse, wanting to give a reward to those who receive them (Matthew 10:40–42).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John asks so that his disciples will be persuaded while he is alive and not follow another teacher after his death.
comments.comment: John does not ask because he does not know him to be the Christ, or because he was about to go down into Hades, as some say — for he knew his passion. That is why he also named him Lamb. He asks so that, while he himself is still alive, he may persuade them, and they may not attach themselves to another teacher after his death (Matthew 11:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John sent to ask whether Jesus was the Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John made people ready to receive God's law.
comments.comment: He [John] prepared the Lord’s way — that is, he made people ready to receive God’s legislation. He also showed this from here — from himself he then brings a verdict, saying (Matthew 11:10)…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John is called the greatest because of his lofty worth, and Christ confirms it with an oath.
comments.comment: … And see how he confirms what concerns John with an oath: “Amen,” he says, making it known to all. “I say that no one greater than he has been raised.” (Matthew 11:11) He said “has been raised” as about some conspicuous king, or as about a plant grown very tall and run up into height by the virtues.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ says John 'has been raised'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those reborn through faith are better than all who are merely born of a woman.
comments.comment:
Together with the others who came before him, he is born of a woman (Matthew 11:11). But those who have accepted the faith are no longer called born of women. As the most wise evangelist says, “As many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.” (John 1:12–13) For we were reborn into God’s adoption not from corruptible seed, but through a living and abiding word. So those born not from corruptible seed but rather from God are better than everyone born of a woman.

John was born of a woman; but those who accepted the faith are no longer called born of women — “but they were born of God.” When Christ rose again after spoiling Hades, then the Spirit of adoption is given. Blessed John departed before the Spirit was given. So even if we are lesser than those who accomplished righteousness under the law, we have still come into greater things through Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The believer reborn through baptism is greater than John because he has entered the kingdom.
comments.comment: He calls greater than John the believer reborn through the washing — a state he names “kingdom of heaven,” (Matthew 11:11) since the kingdom of heaven is given to the faithful, which the Baptist had not yet attained. Even the one only baptized, if he does not yet have a virtuous life, is above John. So the saying is praise of holy baptism.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is 'least in the kingdom' yet greater than John.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The kingdom comes by force because one must die to the world and live to God.
comments.comment: He [Christ] says that the kingdom of the heavens comes by force to those to whom it comes, because it is necessary by force to grasp bodily nature and to be held together by spirit, having died to the world but living to God, which thing law and prophets did not yet have (Matthew 11:12).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The kingdom is faith in Christ, and those who force their way in renounce idolatry and resist their own passions.
comments.comment:
Since the kingdom of heaven is faith in Christ, it began from John’s preaching, who was pointing out the one being preached as leading through baptism into the kingdom. Those who force their way into the kingdom of heaven are the ones who renounce the old, empty custom of idolatry, and those who do not cling to the letter but are drawn over, as by a kind of force, through faith in Christ.

By saying the kingdom is seized by forcers he also hints at the malice of the Jews, who not only did not believe in Christ but also hindered others by threats and blows. Those who want to share the kingdom of heaven through faith in Christ had to prove firm in mind, despising the Jews’ threats. And the believer too, whenever he resists bodily and soul passions vigorously in order to enter the kingdom of heaven, is a God-loving forcer. “Until now” (Matthew 11:12) means until the ongoing time.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'violent' who take the kingdom by force.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The kingdom belongs to those who seize it with eager, steadfast effort, and God gladly yields to them.
comments.comment: For a person who practices and labors at freedom from passions on his own accomplishes nothing; but if he becomes clearly one who desires this exceedingly and has set his whole heart on it, he prevails through the addition of power from God. For God breathes together with willing souls—but if they abandon their eagerness, the Spirit given by God is also withdrawn. To save the unwilling is the act of one using force; to give grace to those who choose it is the act of one who gives freely. Nor does the kingdom of God belong to those who sleep and are idle, but “the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12). For this alone is a noble violence: to force God, and to seize life from God. And God, knowing those who cling violently—or rather, steadfastly—yields to them. For God rejoices to be defeated in such contests.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: John is Elijah in power and spirit, not in person.
comments.comment: And he [Christ] says that Elijah is John according to the power and the spirit of Elijah. And since what was being said was unclear, it was left to those capable of understanding the knowledge. This also the angel Gabriel said concerning him: 'and he will go out before him in the spirit and power of Elijah,' showing this one to be so, even if the one seen was a different person (Luke 1:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense John is Elijah.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Jews were pleased by neither John's gloom nor Christ's ease.
comments.comment: Just as when some children dance and others mourn, their will does not settle into one thing (for both blame companions who do not agree with them), something like that happened to the Jews: they accepted neither John’s gloom nor Christ’s ease, and were helped by neither manner (Matthew 11:16–17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture of the children in the marketplace.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John modeled mourning for sin, while Christ showed the joy of the kingdom.
comments.comment: It was fitting for John, as a household servant, to put the flesh’s passions to death through extreme austerity; but for Christ, as free, to put to death the flesh’s movements and its innate law by the power of divinity with authority — not to be helped into this by ascetic toils. Still, John, “preaching a baptism of repentance,” (Matthew 11:18–19) offered himself as a type to those who ought to mourn; the Lord, “preaching the kingdom of heaven,” reasonably showed ease and brightness in himself, through which he was sketching for the faithful inexpressible joy and toilless life. For the flute is the sweetness of the kingdom of heaven; the dirge is the pains of Gehenna.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why John came fasting and Christ came eating and drinking.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God knew the hidden state of hearts, so the powers were not done where repentance would have been false.
comments.comment: For God brings punishments with measure and timing, being long-suffering until the time of retribution arrives. Similar and constructive to this is what is said in the Gospel: 'Then Jesus began to upbraid the cities in which most of his powers had come to pass, because they did not repent: Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida, for if in Tyre and Sidon the powers that happened in you had happened, long ago they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes' (Matt 11:20-22). … And we say that the Son of God is wisdom, who also did these things; for knowing the hidden things, he knew that those repenting were not making a true repentance, and because of this the powers did not occur there.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why mighty works were done where people did not repent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'I confess' means 'I give thanks,' and it does not make the Son lesser than the Father.
comments.comment:
“I confess,” he says, in the human custom, for “I give thanks” or “I glorify you.” God-inspired scripture is accustomed to take the name “confession” in such a sense. It is written, “Let them confess, Lord, your great name, for it is fearful and holy,” (Psalm 99:3) and again, “I will confess you, Lord, with my whole heart.”

But those with a twisted mind say, “Look, he gives thanks to the Father — then how is he not lesser than him?” To this someone who knows how to champion the dogmas of truth would say: And what prevents you, my good people, from accepting that the consubstantial Son receives and praises his own Father, who saves the world under heaven through him?

If you think the confession puts him in a lesser place than the Father, look also at what follows. He confesses and calls the Father Lord of heaven and earth. And the Son of the God who rules all things surely masters all things with him — not as lesser or of another essence, but as God from God, crowned with equal glories and having equality with him in every respect essentially.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'I confess' means and why it does not make the Son lesser.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ gives thanks not that things are hidden from the wise but that infants are enabled to see them revealed.
comments.comment: It [the word “confess”] also signifies thanksgiving, as if the Savior says: 'I will confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden the divine things from the wise and understanding, and have revealed them to infants' (Matthew 11:25). He does not give thanks for the fact that 'the divine things are hidden from the wise and understanding,' but for the fact that those who are infants have been enabled to see them revealed. These are the ones from the Gentiles who have believed, whereas the wise and the understanding, from whom the divine things are hidden, are those of the circumcision.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ thanks the Father that the mystery is hidden from Israel and revealed first to the nations, as God planned.
comments.comment: Foreseeing the transition of the Word to the nations because of the disobedience of Israel, he [Christ] praises and glorifies the Father on our behalf, the ones who shall be benefited. … And he says, according to the pleasure of the Father, that the mystery concerning him should be hidden from Israel, the wise nation, but be revealed to the foolish nations first. Through which it is shown both that the coming did not fail to encounter God, nor did the presence of Christ fail the intended purpose, but these things happened because God had forewarned and having pre-ordained the plan of grace…
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the mystery is hidden from the wise and shown to others.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who become sons through Jesus come to know the Father as brothers of the Son when he reveals him.
comments.comment: Knowledge of God comes under different aspects: as Creator, by which he created; as Judge, by which he judged — and the rest. All these become clear to anyone to whom the Son reveals them, and only if that person is God’s Son in no other sense. So the one who has received authority to become a child, when he has it and has not yet come to know, does not yet have the Father; but when he becomes such, once Jesus has revealed it, he will know as a brother (Matthew 11:27).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father hands all things to the Son while still ruling through him, and as man the Son receives authority.
comments.comment: Just as the Father is said to have made all things, though he makes all things through the Son, so he is also said to hand all things over to the Son while himself having power, ruling the universe through him, and being with him. And even if, as man, he is said economically [as part of God's plan of salvation] to receive authority — since human nature is not of itself master — that too is not unreasonable (Matthew 11:27).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ adds that only the Father knows the Son, to show that his nature is as beyond comprehension as the Father's.
comments.comment: Since he [Christ] said, “All things have been handed over to me,” (Matthew 11:27) so that he would not seem to be of another kind and lesser beside the Father, he added this to show that his own nature is ineffable and incomprehensible, like the Father’s. For only the divine nature of the Trinity knows itself. The Father alone knows the Son, his own fruit of his nature; the divine Offspring alone knows the One from whom he was born; the Holy Spirit alone knows “the depths of God,” (1 Corinthians 2:10) that is, the thoughts of the Father and of the Son.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ adds that only the Father knows the Son.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only the Father knows the Son fully and only the Son the Father, and others know the Father by sharing in the Word.
comments.comment: Our Saviour and Lord too, the Word of God, shows the greatness of the knowledge of the Father: that the Father is grasped and known as he deserves first of all by the Saviour alone, and secondarily by those whose ruling faculty is enlightened by the Word and God himself. He says: “No one has known the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son reveals him” (Matthew 11:27). For no one can know the uncreated one, the firstborn of all created nature (Colossians 1:15), as he deserves, as the Father who begot him knows him; nor can anyone know the Father as his living Word, his Wisdom and Truth, knows him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who can know the Father and how.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ calls everyone, the Jews weighed down by the law and the idolaters by sin, to rest in him.
comments.comment:
So the one who has heard the call, drawn near, and clung to the One who commanded rests. “Stand away,” he says, “from a sin-loving mind and love of the flesh, turn to deeds worthy of praise, and draw near to me, so that you may become ‘sharers in the divine nature’ and partakers of the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:4) He calls all, not only those from Israel, as Creator and Lord of all.

By “those who labor” he means the Jews, who cannot bear the yoke of the law; by “those who are burdened,” the idolaters, weighed down by the devil and heavy with a mass of sins. “So you, Jews,” he says, “lean toward the truth, recognize me as your guardian and master, and take the gain of approaching near. For I release you from slavery under the law, in which you endure much toil — unable to finish it easily, and preparing for yourselves the greatest ‘burden’ of sins, the more you must keep when living in line with the law.” (Matthew 11:28)
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'weary and burdened' are and what rest Christ offers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: True humility is humbling oneself willingly under God's hand, as Jesus taught and did.
comments.comment: For more truly “humble and well-ordered” than Plato’s humble and well-ordered man is the one who is well-ordered because he walks “among great” and “wonderful things” above him, and humble because, even while among these, he humbles himself of his own will, not under just anyone but “under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6), through Jesus, the teacher of such lessons, who “did not count being equal with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave,” and “being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8). So great is the teaching on humility that its teacher is no ordinary one, but our Saviour himself, great as he is, says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By calling himself gentle and humble, the Savior teaches us not to exalt ourselves.
comments.comment: Then when we have heard and given ear, he commands us: 'And do not exalt yourselves.' (Jeremiah 13:15) For 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.' (Luke 14:11) And the Savior too, in saying, 'Learn from me that I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls,' (Matthew 11:29) teaches us not to exalt ourselves. For among the other human evils this sin also is much in us—sometimes exalting ourselves quite irrationally and over what one ought not exalt oneself even in the least, and sometimes with a semblance of reason, that what we exalt ourselves over is reasonable, yet even over that exaltation is not sound.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that Christ's 'gentle and humble' teaches us not to exalt ourselves.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's yoke is light because he does not punish as the law does.
comments.comment: Christ’s yoke is light, because he does not punish us as the law does, demanding what is sinless and free of passion. In simple words he holds out the promise and the pattern of virtue (Matthew 11:30).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ's yoke is light.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The way is narrow only for the reckless, for the earnest find the Lord's commands light.
comments.comment: If the yoke is kind and the burden light (Mt 11:30), how did he call it a 'narrow' 'way'? It is narrow for the reckless, for the earnest find the commands of the Lord to be light; for even if there is a little bodily toil, the God-fearing man, now being nourished by good hopes, bears these things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how a 'light' yoke can lie on a 'narrow' way.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The path of virtue looks hard, but training makes Christ's yoke and burden feel light.
comments.comment: The paths bearing one toward virtue seem to be hard, having much roughness; for how is the path not hard, which commands the one being struck to a place beyond the jaws, and the rest of the hand to receive insult? In addition to this, a rough path seems to be one through which someone struggles toward death for the sake of the truth. And it is, through injuries, the most bitter of threats, of fire and iron and the assault of wild beasts, the completion of this; except even if these paths and those related to them are hard, they are guarded because of the words of the lips of the protecting God, and they are made smooth as if they were no longer something hard or heavy. For John indeed writes, 'And his commandments are not heavy' (1 John 5:3), and Jesus says to those hearing his words, 'My yoke is good and my burden is light' (Matt 11:30). For from much habituation and training, approaching without interruption, the heavy things appear most light, and the bitter and joyless things are made upright with much ease.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Pharisees resent those being saved, though the new covenant replaces the old laws and they themselves break bread on the Sabbath.
comments.comment:
Where nothing great or noble is happening, they keep quiet; but where they see some being saved, they are more burdensome than anyone. So they are enemies of human salvation and ignorant of the sacred writings. For if the new covenant proclaimed through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31) is other than the first, one must certainly use not the old laws but the new.

But the Pharisees, unwilling to see this, lie in wait for the holy apostles and say about them to Christ: “Look, we see those you train opposing the legal commands. The law orders rest on the Sabbath and touching no labor at all, yet the disciples rub ears of grain with their hands.” (Matthew 12:1–2) But tell me yourself, Pharisee: when you set your own Sabbath table, do you not break the bread? Why then blame others? And how does the Savior defend them?
comments.selected_reason: Gives Cyril's answer to the Sabbath complaint.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The priests were blameless in profaning the Sabbath, as we rest from earthly pursuits yet still offer spiritual sacrifices.
comments.comment: Now God did indeed lay down long ago that all must rest from work on the Sabbath. Yet those crowned with the divine ministry and appointed to wait on the holy tent still performed the sacred rites; and though they profaned the Sabbath, as the Savior says, they were blameless (Matthew 12:5), and did not face the charge of having broken the law. So we too, in Christ, shall cease from earthly pursuits, fulfilling the inward Sabbath rest; but we shall not hold back from the sacred works — I mean, from our duty to bring God spiritual sacrifices and inward gifts (1 Peter 2:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the priests could work on the Sabbath and be blameless.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: If serving in the temple excuses the priests, serving Christ is greater than the temple, which shows who he is.
comments.comment: “Or have you not read in the law that on the sabbaths the priests in the temple profane the sabbath and are guiltless? But I say to you that something greater than the temple is here.” (Matthew 12:5–6) If priests who profane the sabbath are guiltless because they offer services to God, how is service of Christ understood as greater than what is done in the temple? Clearly those under the law served in shadow and copy of the heavenly things (Hebrews 8:5), while the inspired disciples who attended and ministered to Christ had the greater glory. And if ministering to Christ stands in better things than the worship under the law, how would he not be understood as truly God?
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'something greater than the temple is here'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ cites the prophet's preference for mercy over sacrifice against the harsh.
comments.comment: Having examined the bitter ones, they demonstrate them to be not philanthropists against those who do no wrong (Mt 12:7). Therefore also he remembers the prophetic word, which prefers showing mercy over sacrifice.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Pharisees feigned piety to destroy the pious.
comments.comment: Being impious, the Pharisees were pretending piety in order to destroy the pious. That is why they also tried to slander Christ and his disciples when they saw them shining with wonders (Matthew 12:9–14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever obeys Jesus' command to stretch out a withered hand will be restored.
comments.comment: And you, man, if you have a withered hand, having heard from the Savior: stretch out your hand while Jesus is working at good deeds, and it shall be restored to health like the other (Mt 12:13).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Since he does not cast out demons by their ruler, he does it by the Spirit, and God's kingdom has come near.
comments.comment: “Since,” he says, “I do not cast out the demons by the ruler of the demons — as he showed by saying that every kingdom divided against itself is dissolved and destroyed — then I cast them out by the power of the Spirit, and for that reason the kingdom of God has drawn near.” (Matthew 12:24–28)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since the disciples cast out demons in Christ's name, he must be truly God, for no mere human could overpower Satan.
comments.comment: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.” (Matthew 12:27) If the disciples have healed the demonized in Christ’s name — for they cried out, “In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene” (Acts 3:6) — how would he not be understood as true God? A mere human’s glory and power would not have been enough to overpower Satan.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'by whom do your sons cast them out'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: If the Spirit's energy is God's kingdom, the Spirit is no creature added to the divinity.
comments.comment: Again, the power to cast out demons by the Spirit (Mt 12:28) is as much possible for a man to have without being turned aside, according to the economy. If the energy of the Spirit is the kingdom of God, I do not by any means think the Spirit to be an addition to the divinity, being brought in from the servile creation into the construction of the divine kingdom.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The devil is called strong because of the tyranny he gained from our slackness, not by nature.
comments.comment: He calls the devil “strong” (Matthew 12:29) not as if he were this by nature, but to show the tyranny he gained from our slackness. “I plunder him,” not letting him keep humans as worshipers, but persuading them to come to the knowledge of God. How then will he become my ally against himself?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the devil is called 'strong'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever breaks Christ's peace and gathers outside the Church works against him and scatters.
comments.comment: The Lord warns and says, "Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters" (Matthew 12:30). Whoever breaks the peace and harmony of Christ acts against Christ; whoever gathers elsewhere, outside the Church, scatters the Church of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'whoever does not gather with me scatters'.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Christ cannot be allied with demons, since he works to lift everyone to God while they work the opposite.
comments.comment: How is it possible? (Mt 12:30), he says, for me to be joined with the demons thus clearly, while I am doing the opposite to them and they are all doing the opposite with skill? For I and all mine strive to lift up everyone to God, and you would want the assembly of the kin to do this, but they have strived to take away everyone.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Sin against the Son, done in ignorance of his divinity, can be forgiven, but sin against the Spirit cannot.
comments.comment: When someone sinned against a human being, it was possible to beseech God for him; but when humans blasphemed against God, it was not allowed to beseech for them. Yet since the Son of God was seen as man — even though he was God by nature — and was not very clearly recognized by the senseless, he sometimes grants forgiveness to those who sin against him from ignorance; but to those who sin against the Spirit he says perpetual punishment is brought (Matthew 12:31–32).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why speaking against the Son can be forgiven.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ spoke so strongly to show how great the sin is, though God forgives those who repent.
comments.comment: By “Spirit” he means the whole divinity of the Trinity. Still, forgiveness is given through the Spirit’s grace to those who repent and are baptized. Wanting to show the greatness of the sin, Christ said this. For though God often either exacts accounts from sinners only here and not also there — according to “the Lord will not avenge twice for the same” (Nahum 1:9) — or forbears in the present age without also granting forgiveness from there, of such people he says the punishment is indelible and without pardon both here and there.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Blasphemy against Christ as man seems lesser than against the Spirit, but is not forgiven without sincere repentance.
comments.comment: Does not the doing of wonders and the loosening of demons, which only the Spirit does, leaving these things to the demon, leave you no forgiveness for the blasphemy? He [Christ] says this, not refusing that the blasphemy against himself be forgiven, nor refusing a place of repentance for those blaspheming against the Spirit, if they wished, but claiming that the blasphemy against him, as against a man, would then only seem to be a lesser thing when compared to the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, but after the resurrection from the dead and the ascent to heaven and it being clearly shown that he is truly the Son of God and God. Even if he has become unchangeably a man, the blasphemy against him will not be forgiven, unless through a sincere repentance of his fault.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: As trees bear fruit like themselves, the evil one cannot do good nor the good one evil.
comments.comment: Because Beelzebub is evil, and the things happening from me have immeasurable goodness, the things from you are discordant (Mt 12:33); for neither can the evil one do anything good, nor the good one evil, just as even the trees do not bear fruits unlike themselves.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the tree-and-fruit saying by the nature of the one who acts.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The treasure is what fills the soul, and the same person can be good or wicked, so wickedness is not by nature.
comments.comment: When he says “treasure,” he points to the mass of what lies in the soul. And so that some may not say humans are wicked by nature, he showed this in the Pharisees’ case: that the same one person can sometimes become good and sometimes wicked, saying, “The good person speaks from the overflow of his heart,” (Matthew 12:34–35) and likewise the wicked.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'treasure' and why the Pharisees are not wicked by nature.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisees speak wickedly from their own choice and senselessness, not from a wicked nature.
comments.comment: Even if the Lord said that being wicked they cannot help speaking wicked things, he did not say this as if they were wicked by nature, but as overcome by evil from much senselessness. And even if he said that being wicked they cannot speak good things, he did not say this as if they were wicked by nature, but from their own voluntary movement (Matthew 12:34).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The tongue can serve salvation or destruction, depending on how its master uses it.
comments.comment: And why, someone says, if this instrument [the tongue] brings us so much destruction, did God put it in us in the beginning? Because it also has great usefulness. And if we are diligent, it has only usefulness and no destruction at all. Listen, then, to what the one who said those earlier things says: "In the hand of the tongue are life and death" (Proverbs 18:21). And Christ shows the same thing when he says: "By your words you will be condemned, and by your words you will be justified" (Matthew 12:37). For the tongue stands in the middle, able to be used for either purpose. You are its master. So too a sword lies in the middle: if you use it against enemies, the instrument has become your salvation; but if you thrust the blow against yourself, it is not the nature of the iron but your own lawlessness that causes the slaughter.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how words can both condemn and justify.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: They asked for a sign from heaven as if he could do nothing divine, though his works already were such.
comments.comment: “Since the signs that have happened,” (Matthew 12:38) they say, “were of demons, who produce appearances only on earth, you too make a sign from heaven by your own power.” (Mark 8:11) Another evangelist said clearly that they were asking him to make a sign “from heaven,” which it was fitting for divine power to do. They said this as if he could not do anything God-befitting, blind in mind — for opening blind eyes, raising the dead, and rebuking sea and winds belong to God-befitting authority alone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They are wicked and adulterous because they turned from God and Christ to Satan, and only Jonah's sign will be given.
comments.comment: They are “wicked” (Matthew 12:39) as spending the excellence of the mind not on love of God, but on doing and saying something against God. He called them an “adulteress,” showing both the earlier and the present unbelief. For they neither believed the Father nor stood with Christ himself, who wedded humanity and betrothed it according to humanity through what was said: “And I will betroth you to myself forever.” (Hosea 2:19) They glued themselves to Satan, naming the manner of intelligible fornication. He shows himself again to the Father — the sign of Jonah the prophet.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus calls them an 'adulteress' generation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sign of Jonah is Christ's rising, which proves he is God by nature.
comments.comment: [Christ] said to those who were asking for a sign: ‘This generation is evil; it asks for a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights’ (Matthew 12:39–40). So the sign that the Son is God by nature and was begotten of God the Father, a sign truly renowned and plain to all and enough to bring the truly fair-minded to faith, is this: he abolished death and corruption and blossomed again into life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'sign of Jonah' is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Jonah is a type of Christ only in part: Jonah hesitated and grieved, while Christ went willingly and rejoiced.
comments.comment:
So if Jonah is taken as a type of Christ, he is not taken in every respect. For example, he was sent to preach to the Ninevites, but sought to flee from God’s face and is seen hesitating toward the mission. The Son too was sent from God the Father preaching to the nations, but he was not unwilling for the service.

The prophet urged those sailing with him to throw him into the sea; he was also swallowed by a whale, then given up after three days, and after that went to Nineveh and fulfilled the service (Jonah 1–3) — yet he was not moderately grieved when God pitied the Ninevites. Christ also endured death willingly, remained in the heart of the earth, rose again, and after that went into Galilee and commanded that the preaching to the nations begin — yet he was not grieved when he saw those called into knowledge being saved. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows how Jonah is, and is not, a type of Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those freed from evil who do not grow prudent suffer worse, and Israel, once rid of the spirit, let it return by unbelief.
comments.comment:
And it is quite fitting. Once someone has been freed from evils and is not made prudent, he will suffer things much harder than before. That is why he said the spirit “finds no rest” (Matthew 12:43–45): to show that the demons’ plot will certainly and of necessity seize such a person. Two things ought to have made them prudent — having suffered earlier, and having been released. There is even a third: the threat of suffering worse. Yet by none of these did they become better.

The wicked spirit lived in them even when they were slaves in Egypt and, living by Egyptian customs and laws, were full of every uncleanness. When they were ransomed through Moses and received the law as a guide calling them toward the light of true knowledge of God, the profane and unclean spirit was driven out. But because they have not believed in Christ, the demon settled in them again. It found their heart bare and idle of every piety, as if swept clean, and dwelt in them. Just as the Holy Spirit, when it sees a human heart idle of every uncleanness, lodges and dwells and rests in it, so the unclean spirit loves to inhabit the souls of the lawless.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the parable of the returning unclean spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A man of good disposition blocks the demon, while the evil man gives it a place.
comments.comment: From this we learn (Mt 12:43-45) that a demon will not overpower a man of better disposition, but such a one will be an impassable barrier to him, having virtue preceding, and leaving no place for him, as the Preacher advises. On the contrary, the evil and reckless man is a rider for the evil spirit regarding the good. And we learn that the demons also possess a certain consolation for those who are suitable to themselves; for when they are not able to do this, they do not rest, just as it is said from the opposites that the rest of the Divine Spirit is the suitability toward men; for 'the Holy One rests in the holy ones' (Ps 99:2).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The spirit left Israel when God called it and returns with many, because Israel has rejected Christ.
comments.comment: [On the return with seven spirits:] But the entering in with many after the one-time departure has a cause in the unchangeable wickedness of man. And the seven spirits are to be considered much; for among the multitudes, many times the seven are mentioned according to the divine Scripture. In the beginning, indeed, the evil spirit dwelt among the Jews, when in Egypt they were idolaters; but it departed when they were called by God. After these things, when it had failed against the one who was called, then the grace passed over to the Gentiles, and they were being given out. And the one among the Gentiles became a dwelling of the evil ones, both harsh and inaccessible, having received God, the Gentiles. But the return to Israel is easier than before, and with a great multitude of the exodus. Therefore, it is bad that they now pass through, being constantly arranged toward the blasphemy against Christ as in Egypt, not having the covenant toward Abraham, and not expecting according to justice even as then, but being cut off from hope, because they have rejected the fulfiller of this. Thus the Lord has made manifest in the words toward them both their remaining rejection and the judgment of the coming shame, and the already-established rule by the evil one.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: His brothers did not yet believe in him, so the Lord named as relatives those who obey him.
comments.comment: That his brothers did not believe in him (Mt 12:46), we learn from John, and from Mark we have heard somewhat more: as if they were attempting to hold him having gone astray. With such a mind, the Lord did not remember them as his own, but he demonstrates the subjects; to these he foretells all the names of the relatives, who, according to the intimacy of obedience to him, were joined together. And even if Mary's opposition was only for a time, just as Simeon also foretold saying, 'and your own soul' and the following, it is fitting that the Lord also returned to these things favorably, remembering her passion and having joined her to the beloved disciple.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Parables show that Christ is the one David prophesied.
comments.comment: Christ speaks in parables (Matthew 13:3) also to show through them that he himself is the one prophesied, of whom David said, “I will open my mouth in parables,” (Psalm 78:2) and again, “And the man will be one who hides his words and will be hidden as from rushing water.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ speaks in parables.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold are different measures of the fruit that people bear.
comments.comment: The difference in size among the animals neatly points to the measure of piety and approval among those who are used to bearing fruit. For one person, we should think, bears fruit richly and above the rest, as in the calf; another moderately, as in the sheep; and another more modestly still, for a goat is smaller than a sheep. And this, I think, is the fruitful earth yielding a hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold, as in the parable in the Gospels (Matthew 13:8).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Deafness here is by choice: Christ calls for the hearing of the soul, not just of the ear.
comments.comment: The soul is deaf when it does not obey the Law, ignoring the Lord's voice; this deafness is not by nature, but by choice. For this reason the Savior said: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear' (Matt 13:9); not because those present lacked ears (for how could they have occupied themselves with teaching without the organ of hearing?), but he clearly shows that while the ear is fashioned for hearing, the perception of the soul is not joined to the hearing of the divine Law. Therefore, there is no profit in external hearing if the inner intellect is blinded.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'he who has ears to hear' means.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: Those who value the light they have receive more, and those who waste it lose even that, as the Jews lost the light of the law.
comments.comment:
In the gentle and eager to learn who already have knowledge, the divine light will settle even more richly than before. But in those who had a spark of intelligible light and turned it into senseless “knowledge,” even the small brightness they have will be quenched — which is what the Jews suffered by not believing in Christ. They had a small leading light from the law guiding them toward knowledge of God; but because they acted impiously toward Christ, they were deprived of that too.

The Lord makes clearer what he meant by “to the one who has it will be given, and from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken,” (Matthew 13:12–13) by adding: “For this reason I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor understand.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'to the one who has, more will be given' and why Christ speaks in parables.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Lest they turn and I heal them' is a stirring call showing that if they turn, he heals them.
comments.comment: Saying “lest they turn and I heal them” (Matthew 13:15) shows intensified stubbornness — yet it is also the speech of one drawing and stirring them. He shows that if they turn, he heals them. He speaks this way for their salvation. He could have said nothing at all and kept silent; yet he does everything not for his own glory, but for their salvation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words 'lest they turn and I heal them'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The disciples are blessed for hearing and seeing the Son, through whom they saw the Father.
comments.comment: So he calls them blessed as ones who have heard the Son’s voice and been counted worthy of his sight — through whom and in whom they were seeing the Father and God’s nature intelligibly — the very things the saints of old were counted worthy of, and in which they had the fullest joy in goods (Matthew 13:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the disciples are called blessed.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The seed is identified with the hearers themselves, even those in whom the word is choked and unfruitful.
comments.comment: In these things it is sought how he did not say that the word had been sown in the beginning, nor did he say the seed beside the road was sown, but this is the one sown beside the road (Mt 13:18-23); even though after a little while he showed the seed to be existing in those in whom he says the word is being compressed and becomes unfruitful. … And in the parable of the weeds he also says that the 'good seed' is 'the sons of the kingdom,'
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The road is a hard, packed mind that cannot receive the seed, which unclean spirits snatch away.
comments.comment: Let us see, in concrete terms, what it is to be “on the road.” (Matthew 13:19–22) Every road is somehow hard and useless, because it lies under everyone’s feet; none of the seed is heaped into it, but lies on the surface, ready for any birds that want to snatch it. So those who have a hard, packed mind in themselves do not receive the divine seed, but have become a road trampled by unclean spirits — for these are “the birds of the heaven.” By heaven here we mean the air, in which the spirits of wickedness move, by whom the good seed is also snatched and destroyed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the seed 'on the road' is and who snatches it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hearers range from those who do not understand to those who do, and understanding stored in memory keeps the seed from being snatched.
comments.comment:
Matthew wrote “the evil one,” Mark “Satan,” Luke “the devil.” “Beside the road” is not the same as “in the road,” and we need the difference because of “I am the road” (John 14:6); yet all three wrote “beside the road.” Most aptly Matthew and Mark say the word was sown “on the rocky places,” not on rock. Of all that is beside the road it is said that they do not understand; but of the good soil, “this is the one who hears the word and understands.” (Matthew 13:19–23) Perhaps, then, those on the rocky places and those among the thorns stand between the non-understanding and the understanding.

And it urges care for understanding. If the seed of the one who understands is not snatched, one must take up understanding and cover the seed in the earth — memory — so that it may take root and, not being found bare, may not be snatched by the spirits of wickedness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those on the rock hold a shallow faith that lasts in easy times but gives way under persecution.
comments.comment: And who are those on the rock? Some hold the faith in themselves without investigation and do not let the mind down into testing the mystery. These have a light, rootless piety toward God. If Christian affairs are carried with a fair wind and no trial storms them, they scarcely keep the faith in themselves then; but when persecution disturbs them, they have a soul unwilling to fight.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the seed on rocky ground.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Heresies will appear once Christianity has spread.
comments.comment: After the spreading of Christianity and when it already begins to appear throughout the inhabited world (Mt 13:24–30), heresies will be revealed, turning away.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Evil thoughts in the soul are tares sown by the devil, while God sows his seeds where we give him place.
comments.comment: There are some things inside in the souls which 'the heavenly Father did not plant.' For all 'the evil reasonings, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witnesses, blasphemies' (Matthew 15:19) are plants planted not by the heavenly Father. And if you want to see whose plants such reasonings are, hear that 'an enemy man did this,' the one who sowed 'the tares in the midst of the wheat.' (Matthew 13:25) So God stands by, having the seeds, and the devil. If we give 'place to the devil,' 'the enemy' sows a plant 'which the Father did not plant,' which will certainly be uprooted. If we do not give 'place to the devil,' but give place to God, God rejoices and sows his seeds on our governing mind.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Leaven here stands for the beneficial power of gospel training, not for anything blameworthy.
comments.comment: So one must conceive, according to the word fitting for these contemplations, another kind of leaven that has nothing in itself that must be blamed — rather even admired by the God-breathed Scripture. The Savior likens to leaven the renowned and beneficial power of the divine and evangelical training, saying: ‘The kingdom of the heavens is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.’ (Mt 13:33; 1 Cor 5:7)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the leaven stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 17

comments.capsule: The Son of Man's sending 'his angels' shows he is God, since angels belong to God.
comments.comment: “…all causes of sin and those who do lawlessness, and they will throw them into the furnace of fire.” (Matthew 13:41–42) Of God it is written: “Bless the Lord, all his angels.” (Psalm 103:20) For an angel is not a human’s servant; rather, all things belong to God. How, then, does he say of the Son of Man that he will send his angels? So he is God, as one who has the angels as his own and is served through the spirits above.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The wicked gnash their teeth against themselves, knowing they are punished for their own sin.
comments.comment: One gnashes his teeth sometimes against another, and sometimes against himself when he changes his mind, having fallen into the cruelties of what he has done; 'there will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth' (Matt 13:42), because knowing that they are punished because of their own impiety and sin, they weep and gnash their teeth in repentance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the gnashing of teeth means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The gospel net draws people from every kind of human character.
comments.comment: For the net of the divine discipline and of the evangelical teaching is 'a snare cast into the sea and draws from every kind' (Matt 13:47). And since the snare is not perceptible, neither are the things being fished for perceptible. If, therefore, it says, 'from every kind,' it says this: 'from every kind of human character that has fallen into the watery life.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The world is like a sea of trouble, and the Word's net gathers people of every kind from it.
comments.comment:
He [Christ] likens the world to a sea because of the bitterness and the billows of trouble within it (Mt 13:47), but the power of the Word, casting a net upon the world, gathers from various thoughts of the old and new Scripture, from Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, men and women, free and slaves, righteous and wicked.

The net is filled when the master who casts it knows; for this is not for a man to recognize.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sea and the net in the parable.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: When the net is full the wicked are separated from the good and punished in fire.
comments.comment: When the Word of instruction already has the measure of the fullness, then not all who have undertaken the learning of the Word will be found worthy to the master of the net, but a distinction then will occur between the wicked and the good; and to the useless, the end will appear as destruction… But the wicked, who for the time being are counted with the righteous, will then no longer share with them the indiscriminate sojourn, leaving behind the sweet life they enjoyed—like fish the life in the sea—and will undergo the most grievous punishment in fire, where nothing remains to console their evil.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The preaching of the gospel gathers people from every race until the end, when angels will separate the wicked from the righteous.
comments.comment:
That the call through Christ has become worldwide, he himself will confirm by saying clearly that the net of the gospel preachings gathers from every race. Just as those skilled in fishing, whose craft is the sea’s work, let down the net without distinguishing, and whatever is caught in the meshes they wholly and altogether draw to land, so also the power of the preaching and the marvelous, intricate teaching of the sacred lessons — which the good fishermen, the apostles, wove — draws from every race and gathers toward God.

It gathers until a time that will be fulfilled at the consummation, when the angels of God appointed for this, having drawn those netted out of this life, will make the distinction of all, separating the wicked from the midst of the righteous (Matthew 13:49–50).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the net gathers and when the separation comes.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A scribe is one who has stored up knowledge of both the old and new scriptures, and Christ does not cast out the old.
comments.comment: A “scribe” (Matthew 13:52) is the one who, through persistent reading of the scriptures of both the old and the new, has stored up a treasure of knowledge for himself. That is why he blesses those who have brought together in themselves both legal and gospel training, so as to bring out from the treasure things new and old. He also likens these to a scribe, just as elsewhere he says, “I send you wise men and scribes.” See how he does not cast out the old — through which the soul is adorned.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'scribe' is and what the new and old things are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The old treasure is the law and the new is Christ, and Christ admires the scribe who rises from one to the other.
comments.comment: And the Savior Himself regarded with no small admiration the one who rises from knowledge of the law to spiritual knowledge, that is, the knowledge of the gospel. For He said, “Therefore I tell you that every scribe who has been made a disciple for the kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who brings out of his treasure things new and old” (Matthew 13:52). The old are the things in the law; the new are the things in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The disciples say 'dismiss them' out of love for the crowds, knowing Christ can grant the sufferers' wishes with a nod.
comments.comment: Let us examine carefully what “dismiss them” (Matthew 14:15) means. Some of those following Christ were asking to be released from the wicked spirits holding them; others were seeking the putting away of other illnesses. So the disciples, knowing that with a mere nod he accomplishes what the suffering desire, say “dismiss them” — not themselves growing weary as if the time had passed, but holding to love for the crowds, already practicing pastoral skill, as it were, and beginning to care for peoples.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the disciples say 'dismiss them'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The barley loaves stand for Moses' writings (five) given to the more irrational, and the two fish for the apostolic and evangelical writings.
comments.comment: Since another evangelist also calls the loaves “of barley,” (John 6:9) the aim of contemplation looks to this: barley is beastlike food, which is the contemplation through Moses brought to the more irrational. That is also why we say five loaves, because of the fivefold writing of Moses, and two fish, through which is shown the double writing of the fishermen — both apostolic and evangelical (John 6:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Savior feeds some with wheat loaves and others with barley loaves, for those not yet able to receive him as purer bread.
comments.comment: …when the Savior feeds those who follow him not from like loaves but from different ones. For some of them he breaks five of wheat, and for others seven of barley — so that those who cannot partake of Christ as of a purer wheat loaf, because they still live in a beastlike way and not yet rationally, may partake as of barley (Matthew 14:17–19) (Matthew 15:34–36) (John 6:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Giving food through the disciples' hands hints at the holy ones' nearness to God.
comments.comment: Fulfilling the mystery of the economy [God's plan of salvation], the Savior looks up to heaven. For though God by nature, he took a slave’s form (Philippians 2:7), and through the disciples’ hands he gives the foods to the crowds (Matthew 14:19), hinting at the holy ones’ nearness to God. That is why those who are not such stand outside him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ looks to heaven to teach us to ask a blessing from above on our food.
comments.comment: So that by every manner he may be recognized as God by nature, he multiplies the little, and looks into heaven as if asking the blessing from above. He was also doing this economically [as part of God's plan of salvation] for our sake. For he himself is the one who fills all things — the blessing from above and from the Father. But so that we may learn, when beginning a table and about to break bread, that we ought to set them in upturned hands, as it were, and bring down the blessing from above upon them, he has become for us economically the beginning and type and way of the deed (Matthew 14:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ looks up to heaven and blesses before breaking bread.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each disciple's basket signifies the wage of those who serve.
comments.comment: And now he also filled baskets, and that rather each of the disciples was given one as the wage of service — which signifies that those who serve will have a great wage.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The leftover fragments show that hospitality is richly repaid, and the multiplication matches the manna in the desert.
comments.comment: That fragments of the loaves abounded after a not small multitude of men had been satisfied would be clear assurance that hospitality’s work has rich repayment from God. One can see the new wonders agreeing with the more ancient, workings of one and the same power. He rained the manna in the desert for those from Israel (Exodus 16); and look — again in the desert he has supplied abundantly to those in need of food, as if sending it down from heaven. For multiplying the little and, as from nothing, feeding so great a multitude would not be unlike the first sign (Matthew 14:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the leftover fragments show.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Males stand for those spiritually fit to teach others and grow to the fullness of Christ.
comments.comment: What is male is always chosen by God as most ready for combat, able to come into youth — that is, into spiritual fitness — to sow seed, to teach others, and strong enough to measure “to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” (Matthew 14:21) (Ephesians 4:13)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture often counts only the men, as with the five thousand.
comments.comment: For such a thing is customary in the Scripture; for when the Savior broke the five loaves, from which he satisfied five thousand men, the evangelist remembers, saying: 'apart from women and children' (Matthew 14:21), mentioning only the preceding numbers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ prays as high priest on our behalf, and prays until evening to teach endurance.
comments.comment: He prays not as one in need, but as high priest making petitions on our behalf. And a little later: until evening, to show that one must not be fickle about this, but have endurance and eagerness. He also teaches this: that when there is need, we ought to speak what benefits the common good to those we meet, and after such conversation and teaching proceed to prayer.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ prays and why until evening.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Take courage' asks for faith, and 'I am' removes fear because he can do all things.
comments.comment: Having said “Take courage,” (Matthew 14:27) he requires the faith through which each of those who believe sincerely in Christ is saved. And by adding “I am,” he dissolves every fear; for “I,” he says, “am the one who can do all things.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'Take courage, it is I' asks and gives.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Pharisees pressed people to dedicate themselves to God and to call their goods a gift, yet God's command to honor parents must stand beside love for God.
comments.comment:
Some of the Jews were coming forward and were eager to consecrate their own souls to God — still in type and shadow, yet according to the law — confessing as their own the honors owed to those allotted to priestly service and attending the divine altar. But some longed for that sort of glory (I mean being sanctified, holy, and a divine offering) while lack of money cut short the desire.

When Pharisees and scribes urged them that they must pursue this — for those men are exceedingly fond of money — the people put forward reverence toward parents and, speaking truthfully, said they could scarcely provide the means of life for themselves and for their parents. The Pharisees dared to persuade them to count the matter as nothing for God’s sake: even if those who begot them approached seeking the customary help from them, they taught that one must say to father or mother, “It is a gift — whatever you would be helped with from me,” (Matthew 15:1–6) that is, “Whatever you would take from me, know that you are harming the divine offering and laying hands on sacred funds; for I have dedicated myself and promised myself to God as a gift.”

But the parents, fearing the harm that comes from temple-robbery and shuddering at the laws about it, kept enduring while they wailed, and insisted that piety toward God had become a pretext of famine for them — crying out, perhaps, that the divine command itself was wronging them in what mattered most. “Why then,” he says, “did you make void the command of God through your tradition?” For it was necessary — necessary — to honor those who begot them, not to destroy the law concerning them for the sake of piety toward God. Therefore one must neither neglect what befits God because of human affairs, nor wholly neglect humans because of God; rather, assigning love’s exceptional share to the beginning of all — that is, to God — one should next, as in a second and neighboring rank, also convey to the helpers of one’s birth the honors most fitting to them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisees let children call their goods a gift to God to avoid helping parents, but God is not served by wronging them.
comments.comment: [Christ to the Pharisees:] Though God commands that parents be honored and has hung danger over those who transgress, you command the children not to honor their parents — unless perhaps the children should wish to do this from ambition — but if they ask you for something, to say to them: “Whatever you take from me, know that you are stripping this from God; for I promised to give it as a sacrifice.” (Matthew 15:4–6) God must indeed be preferred to parents; yet I say one must also require that honor toward parents be kept. For they ought not, by seeming to pretext gift-bringing to God, to wrong their own parents.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'gift' tradition that Christ condemns.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisees, loving money, taught people to call what they owed their parents a gift to God, so that neglecting parents seemed blameless.
comments.comment: For the Pharisees, being greatly in love with money and greedy for gain, wanted to see as many people as possible coming to the enrollment the law prescribed, so that their purses might grow fat as they gathered with insatiable hand what came from each one who approached. But it was likely that some would hold back from the enrollment, having their poverty as an honorable excuse for hesitating, and above all the duty of caring in old age for their fathers or mothers out of what they themselves earned, and that with no little sweat. No sooner had the wicked Pharisees learned this than they urged them to go readily to the dedication. They no longer thought as was right, and they set aside what the law had laid down, I mean, that reverence toward parents be shown in full and that they be treated with tender care; instead they urged them, so to speak, to bid a quick farewell to fulfilling what custom required. For since under the laws it was a crime and an indictable offense to take for oneself anything that had been offered for the glory of God, and ‘gift’ was the name given to dedicated offerings, they taught people to say to their own parents, when they asked for support: ‘Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift’ (Matthew 15:5). That is: whatever I might give you is a dedicated offering, and be sure that you would be wronging the law, stealing what belongs to the glory of God and taking it impiously. And the men who brought in these most shameful inventions of theirs affirmed that inhumanity toward parents was blameless in those who had chosen instead to dedicate their goods to God according to the law. This, I think, is the meaning of the words: ‘Whoever says to his father or his mother, “Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift,” need not honor his father or his mother’ (Matthew 15:5–6). For the point is this: let those be allowed not to honor a father, nor to show reverence to a mother, who say, ‘Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift’; that is, whatever I might perhaps help you with by giving it to you, that is a gift to God, and you would be a thief of sacred offerings.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: Christ reverses the Pharisees' order, since they prized bodily rules and despised the spiritual, so the prophet's word fits.
comments.comment:
The Lord turns the evil state of the Pharisees into opposites; for those caring for the bodily things despised the spiritual, but the Savior, introducing the spiritual, renounces the bodily.

Indeed, following the preceding demonstration, the voice of the prophet was applied at the right time, possessing much concord with it (Mt 15:8).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The plants the Father did not plant are the evil thoughts in the soul, sown by the enemy and sure to be uprooted.
comments.comment: To uproot what? The Savior taught, saying, 'Every plant which my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.' (Matthew 15:13) There are some things inside in the souls which 'the heavenly Father did not plant.' For all 'the evil reasonings, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witnesses, blasphemies' (Matthew 15:19) are plants planted not by the heavenly Father. And if you want to see whose plants such reasonings are, hear that 'an enemy man did this,' the one who sowed 'the tares in the midst of the wheat.' (Matthew 13:25) So God stands by, having the seeds, and the devil. If we give 'place to the devil,' 'the enemy' sows a plant 'which the Father did not plant,' which will certainly be uprooted. If we do not give 'place to the devil,' but give place to God, God rejoices and sows his seeds on our governing mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the unplanted plant is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What is not from God will be uprooted.
comments.comment: Every planting that is not from God — everything outside God — will also be uprooted. The one conformed to that planting is blind (Matthew 15:13–14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Food fills the body but does not reach the heart, so it cannot make a person unclean.
comments.comment: The Lord also calls them senseless for turning about the body, like the Pharisees, and not yet crossing over to the inner human. Foods, then, he says, fill the body; they do not touch the heart. And what does not touch the heart cannot make the true human common or render him unclean (Matthew 15:17–18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why food does not defile.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus called all to pure worship, teaching that food passes through the body while what defiles comes from the mouth.
comments.comment: It should be understood, however, that while the Jews think they understand the law of Moses, and in the matter of foods keep the rule of eating what they hold to be clean and abstaining from what is unclean, and also of not using an animal’s blood for food, nor what has been torn by wild beasts, and other such things … the teaching of Jesus wished to call all men to the pure worship of God, and not, on the pretext of a heavier law about foods, to hinder many of those whose character could be helped by Christianity. So it declared: “It is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a man, but what comes out of the mouth” (Matthew 15:11). For what “goes into the mouth,” he says, “passes into the stomach and is cast out into the drain” (Matthew 15:17); but what comes out of the mouth are “evil thoughts” put into words, and “murders,” “adulteries,” “fornications,” “thefts,” “false witness,” and “blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Canaanite woman is a type of the Church from the Gentiles, calling him Lord by his divinity and Son of David by his flesh.
comments.comment:
Where did the Canaanite woman come from?

(Mt 15:21-22) From the idolatry of Tyre and Sidon, from her own people, and from 'the house of her father.'

Where did she come from?

She came forth as a fragrance of myrrh for the Savior; for she holds a type of the Church from among the Gentiles.

But also the Savior came out from the 'kinship' of Israel and from 'his own house,' which is Jerusalem.

And the Canaanite woman receives him, she who also received Elijah, the widow; and what did she cry out, shouting: 'Lord, Son of David!'?

How did she know to call thus, having studied neither the law nor the prophets?

She called him 'Lord' according to his divinity, but 'Son of David' according to the flesh.

Consider for me the widow's son who was dead, that is, the body which had been made dead, and the soul having been purified from the demon; he restored both the body and the soul.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ spoke with the authority of God, not by prayer.
comments.comment: When he said, “Let it be for you as you wish,” (Matthew 15:28) he spoke royally — not accomplishing the matter through prayer, but through the authority that befits God in him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the royal wording of Christ's answer.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When God speaks, the deed follows at once.
comments.comment: Once the word is spoken, the deed does not delay. For God is the one speaking, the word is at work, and the power is everywhere (Matthew 15:28).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Thinking him a mere human, the crowds glorified Israel's God.
comments.comment: They had not yet learned the Lord’s dignity — that he is God — but were thinking him a mere human. That is why they were also sending up the glory to the God of Israel (Matthew 15:31).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the crowd glorified the God of Israel.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Feeding the crowd in the desert is one of many signs that Christ is God.
comments.comment: From many things Christ shows that he is God. Not least, he also presents this by feeding the crowd in the desert (Matthew 15:34–39) — doing the sign of the loaves, as if somehow unwillingly, because of necessity and how hard food was to get — which he would not have done in a city, where market goods are abundant. Yet though he could have strengthened them by a word through what is unseen, he does not do that; he did the sign of the loaves as clearly showing his God-befitting glory.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter's wording, with the article, means Christ is the one Son of God by nature, not a Christ or son by grace.
comments.comment: Peter did not say, “You are Christ,” or “a son of God,” (Matthew 16:16) but “the Christ, the Son of God.” For there are many christs by grace and who hold the dignity of adoption, but only one is Son of God by nature. That is why, with the article, he said “the Christ, the Son of God.” And by calling him Son of the living God he shows that he himself was life, and death does not lord it over him. For even if for a little the flesh weakened in dying, it rose, since the Word in it could not be held under death’s bonds.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Peter says 'the Christ, the Son of the living God'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter is blessed for confessing Christ as God's Son, which a bare human would not need to be taught from above.
comments.comment: And Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:13–17) Jesus answered him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father in heaven.” If Christ were a bare human, why is Peter marvelled at for confessing him? How is he God-taught, or what illumination from above did he need to learn the mystery about him? But he knew him to be God, and confessed him Son of the living God — and for that he is marvelled at. Yet he says one Son, not two sons; so it is impious to divide him into two.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Peter is called blessed for his confession.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The rock is Peter's unshakable firmness in confessing the faith, and the apostles are the foundations laid for those who follow.
comments.comment: For somewhere He said to the godly Peter, when Peter was wisely and blamelessly confessing his faith in Him and saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16): “You are Peter, and on this rock I will found My Church” (Matthew 16:18). By the rock, I think, He means the disciple’s unshakable firmness in faith. It is also said somewhere through the voice of the Psalmist: “His foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 87:1). The holy apostles and evangelists may very fitly be compared to holy mountains; their knowledge has been laid like a foundation for those who came after them, and it does not let those whom they gathered in their net fall away into what is counterfeit in faith.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'this rock' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter confessed the Son as of one nature with the Father, and the churches were built on that confession so the arguments of heretics did not prevail.
comments.comment: Peter did not hesitate seeing God indwelling on earth in flesh and blood; for this is that 'flesh and blood did not reveal to you' (Matt 16:17). He recognized the consubstantial and participating branch of God; in this he honored the root which was revealed to him, being self-begotten and unoriginated; he believed in his unity with the Father regarding divinity. He was made blessed by the only blessed Master.
