The churches were built upon this rock, whose 'gates of Hades' (Matt 16:18)—that is, the arguments of heretics—did not prevail; the keys of the heavens were handed to him, so that for those believing—as Peter himself seems to answer perfectly and as he heard from Christ along with the other apostles: 'baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matt 28:19)—they might be opened in the kingdom of God; but for those not thus glorifying the tri-blessed and most desirable entrance, he shall shut it. … Having truthfully confessed him as the Son of God, that is, genuine and consubstantial, he heard something nearby: 'Bar Jonah', which is interpreted: 'Son of Jonah' (Matthew 16:17). Peter was by no means of a different substance to the one who begot him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Persecutors who tried to destroy the church only raised it to greater glory.
comments.comment: Just as those who, by adding fuel to what is already burning, raise the flame higher, so also those who hastened to destroy Christ’s church, through the persecution, led it forward into greater glory and power. And if, he says, they do not prevail over the church — then he also names another honor (Matthew 16:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the gates of Hades cannot prevail.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ built the Church on one man to show its unity, though the other apostles shared equal power.
comments.comment: The Lord says to Peter: "I tell you, you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of the underworld will not overcome it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven: whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven" (Matthew 16:18-19). He builds the Church upon one man. And although after his resurrection he grants equal power to all the apostles and says: "As the Father sent me, I also send you. Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone's sins, they are retained" (John 20:21-23), yet to make unity manifest, he arranged by his own authority that the origin of this same unity should begin from one. Certainly the other apostles were what Peter was, endowed with equal sharing both of honor and of power, but the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ addresses the keys to Peter alone.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: By calling the church his own and giving the keys, Christ shows himself to be God, with authority over heaven and earth.
comments.comment:
See how he shows himself Lord of heaven and earth in summary. For he promises what is beyond our nature — rather, even beyond the angelic order — and whatever it befits to grant only to the nature and glory highest of all. First he says the church is his own, although the sacred writings dedicate it rather to God and to none of the others — “having no spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27) — and he also promises to found it, assigning it what cannot be shaken, as himself Lord of the powers, and he sets Peter over it as shepherd.

Then he said, “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of the heavens.” (Matthew 16:18–19) This voice no angel, nor any other rational power, can utter; it befits rather the God who rules all and has authority over earth and heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Christ's promise of church and keys shows about him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gift of the faith suits all the apostles, not Peter alone.
comments.comment: The time of the gift looks to the resurrection, when he said, “Receive the Holy Spirit; if you forgive the sins of any, they have been forgiven; if you retain those of any, they have been retained.” (John 20:22–23) But the gift of the faith given fits all; that is why we understand the faith as common to all the apostles, and not Peter’s alone (Matthew 16:19).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ goes to Jerusalem because a prophet is not to perish outside it.
comments.comment: But since it was not accepted that a “prophet perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13:33) — a destruction that has an analogy to “the one who has lost his soul will find it” — for that reason he [Christ] goes away into Jerusalem (Matthew 16:20–21).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What the Jews did out of impiety was God's wise plan and a saving benefit to mankind.
comments.comment: Yet he does not provide an apology to those who work the passion through these things; for the mindset and the conspiracy of the Jews did not harmonize with the counsel of God, nor did they hasten then, which God managed; so that for them, what was being done was impiety according to their opinion, but to God it was a wise dispensation and, to mankind, a saving benefit (Mt 16:23).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ invites and awakens the will but does not compel, and to take up the cross means to be crucified to the world.
comments.comment: For this reason also the Savior says in the Gospel: 'If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself and let him take up his cross and follow me' (Matt 16:24). 'If anyone wants': as far as it concerns the Savior, He wills him to do this, but He does not compel; He moves the choice, He awakens the desire. 'If anyone' therefore 'wants to come after me', 'if anyone wants to follow me'—for this is what 'to come after me' means—, 'let him take up his own cross': let him be crucified to the world, let him put to death 'his members which are upon the earth', let him become inactive toward the world. He who is crucified has his feet hindered from walking as he wants, and his hands from doing what he wants. Therefore, when someone is crucified toward the world, he neither walks according to it anymore, nor does he do its things; and by this, the world is also crucified to the one crucified, so that the world may also be inactive toward him, neither walking according to him, nor doing those things that harm him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'if anyone wants' and 'take up his cross'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ spoke to encourage the disciples, who might doubt that denying themselves was worth it, with the glory soon to be theirs.
comments.comment:
Since the disciples did not yet have “power from on high,” (Luke 24:49) it was likely they might somehow also fall into human weaknesses and, having thought something of the sort, say: How will someone deny himself? Or how, having lost his own soul, will he find it? And what equal-honoring prize is there for those who have suffered this?

Therefore, so that he might stand them away from such reasonings and, as it were, reforge them toward courage by instilling desire for the fair fame about to be theirs, he says, “There are some of those standing here,” (Matthew 16:24–28) and what follows
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son of Man has angels of his own.
comments.comment: “For the Son of Man is about to come in the glory of his Father with his angels.” (Matthew 16:27) See again: he calls the spirits above his angels, though he is called Son of Man.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The glory is God's glory, since he is the Son of God.
comments.comment: And that which is in the glory of his Father: he says 'the glory,' meaning the glory of God, because having become man, he is the Son of God (Mt 16:27).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The glory means our nature's transformation into an incomparable glory.
comments.comment: By “glory” (Matthew 16:27–28) he means the transformation and change of our nature from the form now seen into a glorious and incomparable glory. And of those who also have one glory, much more is the substance one.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The kingdom some will see is the transfiguration, a preview of Christ's second coming in the glory of God.
comments.comment: [In saying “There are some of those standing here,” Christ was] hinting at Peter and the sons of Zebedee. For these were taken along at the transfiguration, which he calls a kingdom as having shown the ineffable of his authority and the unvarying genuineness of his relation to the Father. In it he also indicated the dignity of the second coming and a frightful prelude — showing this as confirmation, as it were, of that. For he will come in the glory of God the Father, not in the smallness that is ours.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is standing here and what kingdom they see.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ climbs the mountain because contemplation needs a mind raised above life's cares.
comments.comment: He goes up onto the mountain to show that a lowly mind would not become fit for contemplation, but the one who has become his own, outside life’s cares, in quiet (Matthew 17:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ goes up the mountain.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ was transfigured into a better form that only those who could follow him to the height were able to see.
comments.comment: …our God “was transfigured” and, going up “onto the high mountain” (Matthew 17:1-2; Mark 9:2), showed another form of himself, far better than the one seen by those who stayed below and could not follow him to the height. For those below did not have eyes able to see the transfiguration of the Word into what is glorious and more divine. They could barely receive him as he was, so that those who could not see his better form might say of him: “We saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honour, falling short of the sons of men” (Isaiah 53:2-3).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: On the mountain Christ showed his glorious form together with the spiritual law (Moses) and prophecy (Elijah).
comments.comment: He [Christ] led us up onto the “high mountain” (Matthew 17:1) of the Word and showed us his glorious form and the brightness of his garments (Matthew 17:2), and not his own only, but also that of the spiritual law, which is “Moses,” seen “in glory” with Jesus (Luke 9:30–31). He showed us also the whole of prophecy, which did not die even after he became man, but was taken up into heaven; Elijah was its symbol (2 Kings 2:11).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ appeared to each person according to what he could receive, so only Peter, James and John saw his glory on the mountain.
comments.comment: Jesus, though one, was many in aspect; and he was not seen alike by all who saw him. … That even when seen he did not appear the same to all who saw him, but according to what each beholder could receive, will be clear to those who consider why, when he was about to be transfigured on the high mountain, he did not take even all the apostles, but only Peter and James and John (Matthew 17:1–2). For they alone could take in the sight of his glory at that time, and were able also to perceive Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory (Luke 9:30–31), and to hear them talking together, and the voice from heaven out of the cloud (Matthew 17:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why only three disciples were taken up the mountain.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The transfiguration was a light-like glory around the body, not a change of its form.
comments.comment: We say the transfiguration took place not by the body’s human form being changed, but by a light-like glory wrapping it around. The body remained in its form, while the features were colored more gloriously by a light-like hue (Matthew 17:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the transfiguration changed and what it did not.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Word's garments are the words of Scripture, which look dull below and bright to those who go up the mountain.
comments.comment: And “his garments” are different below: they are not “white,” they are not “as the light” (Matthew 17:2). If you go up “onto the high mountain,” you will see his light and “his garments.” The “garments” of the Word are the wording of Scripture; these words are the clothing of the divine thoughts. So as he himself appears different below, and when he has gone up is transfigured and “his face” becomes “like the sun” (Matthew 17:2), so too his clothing, so too “his garments.” When you are below, they are not bright, they are not “white”; but if you go up, you will see the beauty and “the light” of the garments, and you will marvel at “the face” of Jesus transfigured.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The body changes as the Creator wills, unlovely at one time and so glorious at another that the apostles fell down.
comments.comment: And it is not surprising that matter, which by nature is mutable and alterable, can be changed into whatever the Creator wills, and can receive every quality the Craftsman wills, should at one time have the quality of which it is said, “He had no form nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2), and at another time one so glorious and awe-inspiring and wonderful that those who beheld such great beauty, the three apostles who had gone up with Jesus, fell “on their faces” (Matthew 17:6).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moses and the prophets speak what Christ speaks, and the disciples' fall shows that we need his mediation to bear God's voice.
comments.comment: What they speak together shows that the prophets of old uttered the same things as Christ, even if in riddles. The disciples fall from extreme fear, and the Savior raises them, showing that unless he had become flesh, mediated between God and humans, and strengthened our nature, it could not have borne to hear God’s voice (Matthew 17:3–7).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter spoke without knowing, since heavenly dwelling had to wait until after Christ's resurrection and ascension.
comments.comment: He did not know what he was saying. Before the Savior’s passion and resurrection, and before the dissolution of death and the corruption of our bodies, it was impossible for Peter to dwell with Christ and to long for the tents in heaven. Those things must come after the Savior’s resurrection and ascent into heaven (Matthew 17:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Peter 'did not know what he was saying'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father commands us to hear Christ, not to give up Moses and the prophets, who stand beside him as servants speaking with him.
comments.comment: He has commanded that we hear him, because God the Father no longer wills us to obey legal writings, nor even the shadow-sketches in type, but rather to follow what has been enjoined on us through the Savior — without thrusting out Moses and the prophets. For they were standing beside him and speaking with him, so that their presence might signify servant-like service to us, while their conversing might signify intimacy with Christ and, as it were, speaking the same things (Matthew 17:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Father says 'Hear him' with Moses and Elijah beside Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's voice is not heard by the ear, just as no one has ever seen God.
comments.comment:
…the Father announcing the Son appears from the voice heard there, as if proclaiming and itself the testimony coming from above through all; for a voice of God is not to be considered heard by the ear, nor is the sensible from the incorporeal.

And just as 'no one has seen God ever' (John 1:18), neither has anyone heard God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The disciples fall in fear to show how necessary Christ's mediation is, since no one could bear God approaching in glory.
comments.comment: The voice of God the Father is good and worthy of wonder; yet the disciples fall (Matthew 17:6), already held by unmixed fear, so that through this too we may learn how necessary the Savior’s mediation has appeared for those on earth — understood according to the manner of the incarnation. For if he had not become as we are, who of us could have borne God approaching from above and displaying his ineffable glory, scarcely bearable for any generated being? For the blessed Paul also said that he “dwells in unapproachable light.” (1 Timothy 6:16) And before this such a voice was borne at the Jordan, and a crowd was present.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the disciples fall down at the Father's voice.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus' command to tell no one the vision fits his character, for he avoided speaking about himself and showed he was the Christ by deeds.
comments.comment: …it does not fit the one who said to his disciples about the vision on the mountain, “Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Matthew 17:9), to have told his disciples what John saw and heard at the Jordan. One may see this also in the character of Jesus, who everywhere avoided speaking about himself and for that reason said, “Even if I speak about myself, my testimony is not true” (John 5:31). And since he avoided speaking about himself, and wished to show that he was the Christ by his deeds rather than by his words…
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Not knowing John as Elijah, the Jews also failed to know and killed the Lord.
comments.comment: Christ shows that the Jews are greatly ignorant of the scriptures, from which they did not recognize John — that is, the first Elijah, “who prepared the way of the Lord.” (Matthew 17:11–12) Not knowing him and killing the forerunner of Christ, they also failed to recognize the Lord himself and killed him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ says Elijah has already come.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The father's unbelief deserved a refusal, yet Christ rebuked the spirit to show his own power and freed the child.
comments.comment:
Even if the father of the demon-possessed boy, grieving, ought to have gone away without obtaining the favor — because he did not make a blameless approach, but cried out against the apostolic band and said they could not rebuke the demon, rather accusing the Lord of the powers himself (for the one who says those who received authority from Christ to cast out unclean spirits were weak for the work rather accuses the grace, not those who received it) — therefore that unbelieving and so distorted father ought to have been sent away empty.

Yet so that no one might think Christ himself powerless to accomplish the marvel, “he rebuked the unclean spirit,” (Matthew 17:14–18) and at once the child was freed from illness, “and he gave him to his father.” For before he was healed he was not the father’s, but the spirit’s that held him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The moon cannot cause the demon's attack, since demons falsely blame elements that are good by nature.
comments.comment: If the moon could produce a passion in someone by its natural law, why does it not send this on all humans, just as it pours its light on all? Again it is clear that the moon was made for shining, not for begetting demons. And if this came from the moon’s natural working, then when the demon was crushed the moon too — the cause of the passion — ought to have been harmed. But that is not so. Demons, wanting to deceive humans, put the names of the elements around themselves so that the elements might be accused as wicked — which they are not. By nature the elements are good, serving only the laws given them and having no authority from choice (Matthew 17:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the boy's illness is not caused by the moon.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's weariness is aimed at unbelief, not at the man himself.
comments.comment: The unbeliever will somehow also be distorted and know no way to walk straight. Christ does not deem such people worthy of his company; if one may say something human, he grows weary and is distressed. Yet this is not aimed at this person’s face — and one must not think what is unfitting about them (Matthew 17:17).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ stayed among the not-good in gentleness during his time in the flesh, in order to correct them.
comments.comment: When he says, “How long shall I dwell with you who insult and are unbelieving?” (Matthew 17:17) he shows that the time of the incarnate presence required him to dwell with the not-good in God-befitting gentleness, so that through what he does he might correct them. “How long,” he says, “shall I dwell with you so insolent and unbelieving?” — showing that his presence with flesh compelled him to associate with the not-good in order to correct them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Christ's 'How long shall I be with you?'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Mustard-seed faith means either hot, boiling faith or a faith small in word.
comments.comment: “If you have faith as a mustard seed” (Matthew 17:20) — that is, hot and boiling, or faith likened to the tiny grain because of smallness in word. For “we have the treasure” (2 Corinthians 4:7) of faith “in earthen vessels.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ foretold the passion after showing his glory so the disciples would not think they were deceived when he was seized.
comments.comment: So he brought the chief disciples up the mountain and showed them the glory with which he will shine upon the world in due times; then, coming down from the mountain, he freed someone from a wicked and harsh spirit. Yet he had wholly to endure the saving passion for us and bear the Jews’ perversity. When that happened it would not be strange for the disciples to be in tumult and perhaps to think and say among themselves: He who raised so many dead by God-befitting authority, who rebukes seas and spirits, who crushes Satan by a word — how has he now been caught and fallen into murderers’ snares? Were we deceived in thinking him God? So that they may know what will wholly and altogether come, he foretells to them the mystery of the passion (Matthew 17:22–23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ foretells his passion right after showing his glory.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ joins the resurrection to the passion, and the disciples grieve out of love though it is announced to come soon.
comments.comment: Mixing in the word about the resurrection, he weaves power together with weakness, glory with ingloriousness, the height of divinity with the cheapness of humanity. For he died as man and lived again as God. The disciples are grieved from love toward Christ, even though the resurrection was announced to come soon — because humans grieve more hotly when they hear grievous things and feel those more than the sweetest (Matthew 17:22–23).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ says the passion is not yet near, to show his foreknowledge and that he suffers voluntarily, for the disciples' benefit.
comments.comment:
…he therefore says that what is going to happen in Jerusalem is not yet approaching, nor the time according to which it was necessary to suffer, so that he might reveal the divine foreknowledge being such, and that he was about to suffer voluntarily, not departing from where he was to be persuaded through ignorance.

And it happened for the disciples' benefit so that they would not be troubled as if men had prevailed against him.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The drachma was a legal ransom set by Moses, given equally by rich and poor.
comments.comment:
…this was a legal matter concerning the drachmas, having been determined by Moses saying: 'each will give a ransom for his own soul, the half of a drachma' (Exodus 30:13).

These things indeed the Jews were collecting from everyone, and the drachma was being given as a ransom for two souls according to the law; neither was it being added to the rich one, as the law has said, nor was it being diminished for the poor one 'from the half of a drachma'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the two-drachma tax was.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: They ask Peter craftily, expecting that Christ opposes Moses' law by not paying.
comments.comment: And they ask Peter craftily. Since, they say, he is accustomed to oppose Moses’ laws, he does not even pay the didrachma (Matthew 17:24) — knowing that Christ had also said, “I came not to destroy the law but to fulfill,” (Matthew 5:17) and that the manner of the economy [God's plan of salvation] requires this. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the collectors ask Peter about the tax.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By saying the sons are free, Christ shows that the Son is free by nature, since only created things are slaves of their maker.
comments.comment: Thus, the noble Son of God testifies by his own nature to being free from above and not to have the character of a sister to the creation—for everything produced is a slave to the one who brought it into being, and the created thing is a slave to the creator—and he says to Peter: 'From whom do the kings of the earth receive taxes or customs?' (Matt 17:25). 'From their sons or from strangers?' Answering, 'From strangers,' Jesus said to him; 'therefore the sons are free.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sign from the sea teaches that we are fish drawn from life's turmoil with Christ the royal stater in our mouths, as ransom for two.
comments.comment: Though able to bring forth the stater from the earth, he did not do that, but made the sign from the sea, to teach us a mystery full of contemplation. For we were fishes drawn up from life’s bitter turmoils as from a sea through the apostolic hooks, having in our mouths Christ the royal stater, given as ransom for two — for our soul and body, or for two peoples, Jews and gentiles — likewise ransoming poor and rich, since the old law also unreservedly demanded the drachma’s tax equally from rich and poor.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ sends Peter to the sea for the coin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ shows himself lord of the sea, and the fish is a type of the church hauled up by the apostles' hook.
comments.comment:
He presents himself as creator and lord of the sea and those in it and every element, as the proper Son of God and Father.

For this fish held a type of the church, which of old was seized by the salt and dread of unbelief and was deeply submerged in the depth, and was baptized and tossed by the storm and surge of worldly pleasures; but it was hauled up by the hook of the apostles, through teaching and fishing and the word that hunts, toward the knowledge of God, … 'who called us out of darkness into his marvelous light' (1 Pet 2:9).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The kingdom of the heavens is already present, as a calling to holiness or a measure of faith.
comments.comment: We especially reckon the kingdom of the heavens even in the present, and we say it is either the calling in sanctification or the measure in faith and holiness. For the Savior also hints at something of the sort when he says, “The kingdom of the heavens is within you.” (Luke 17:21)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the kingdom of the heavens means in the disciples' question.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The little ones have many angels, and each one who fears the Lord has one, so none is left out.
comments.comment: You have this in the Gospel: 'See that you do not cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble; for their angels always see the face of our Father in heaven' (Matt 18:10). They stand before God, we see His face, they see the invisible one invisibly. Behold, therefore, of the many little ones, many angels are spoken of, but of those fearing the Lord, one angel is said. It is said singularly, for not even one is excluded.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ brought the angels down to guard human life, so it is dreadful to treat as nothing those they watch over.
comments.comment:
Because a great and hard-to-count host of demons wanders this whole world, overturning our affairs by many kinds of deceit, Christ has set tutors over us from heaven — not as if human nature were inferior (far from it; they are far above what is ours, and the point is clear), but as ones who oppose demonic greed with their own strength and are able to contend for our life. With everything else, Christ has also set this right for our souls.

Long ago, when we were ruined, heaven was shut, and the angels took no account of any of us, as if sharing the Master of all’s indignation at the insult. But when God was pleased “to sum up all things in Christ,” he came to earth, brought the holy angels down, and appointed them guardians of our life (Matthew 18:10). That is why he also said, “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51) — “of Man,” that is, for the sake of the human. Heaven, shut in the times already past, he opened for us, so that running up and down for our sake they might be servants of the economy accomplished for us through Christ.

Paul too says this: “Are they not all ministering spirits,” (Hebrews 1:14) and what follows. Jacob our forefather’s dreams have the same force: he saw, as he said, “the ladder” (Genesis 28:12) reaching from earth “to heaven,” and the dream signifies nothing else, I think, than that in due times there will be ascent and descent for the holy angels because the Only-Begotten shines in the world with flesh for the human. It is most dreadful, then, that those deemed worthy of such care from God — allotted angels as overseers and tutors — should be ranked as of no account, and that by us, their fellow-servants and brothers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the little ones have angels and what it means to despise them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Two who decide in concord will have their decision confirmed, because Christ joins them and piety, not numbers, makes it effective.
comments.comment: Since Christ gives those appointed to teach authority to loose and to bind — once people have turned toward desire for virtue and do not wander off again — one must fear the holy ones’ voices, even if those who decide are not many. Christ has also assured us of this: he did not say a decision is firm only when it comes from many, but promised that if even two should decide in concord and with care, it will come to pass. “For I will be with them,” he says, “and join in the decision, if only two are gathered because of me.” (Matthew 18:18–20) It is not the number of those present, he says, but the power of piety and love of God that will be effective.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why two or three gathered are enough.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's promise to two or three depends on their agreement, not on their number.
comments.comment: Nor should certain people deceive themselves with a false interpretation of what the Lord said: "Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, I am with them." … For when the Lord was urging unanimity and peace upon his disciples, he said: "I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about anything you ask, it will be granted to you by my Father who is in heaven. For wherever two or three are gathered in my name, I am with them" (Matthew 18:19-20). He was showing that much is given not to the number of those praying but to their unanimity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the context of 'two or three gathered'.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Selling the wife and the rest means the complete falling away from God.
comments.comment: Through the sale of the wife and the rest is signified the total removal and complete falling away of the pleasant things from God. The sale shows alienation from God; for those to whom that bitter, unsmiling word comes are alien to God: “Depart from me, workers of lawlessness; for I never knew you.” (Matthew 7:23)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If we do not forgive small faults after God forgave great ones, the angels set over us accuse us and ask that we be disciplined.
comments.comment: When the God of all forgives us the hard faults — shown by the many talents — if we ourselves do not remit to fellow-servants the hundred denarii, that is, the few worldly slips, then from the hatred of evil in them the angels set over us, who share the same yoke of mastery with us, make accusation before God — not as informing one who does not know (for he knows all as God), but rather, as is fitting, asking that those who choose to despise and dishonor the laws of mutual love be usefully disciplined.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fellow-servants are angels and men in charge who accuse us, indignant at the breaking of love's laws.
comments.comment: The fellow-servants who also report the one who used the master's servant without restraint are both angels and men entrusted with the administration, such as Paul was, who delivered the most shameful wrongdoer to the devil. … For our fellow-servants, not bearing our wickedness, accuse us before God, not as if He were ignorant, but as those indignant against those who strike the laws of philanthropy.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Remembering our own debts to God should make us gentle with our debtors, or we will suffer what the unforgiving servant suffered.
comments.comment: When, then, some of our many debtors behave more weakly concerning the payment of what is due to us, we shall do more humanely if we bear it with forgetfulness of wrongs toward them, remembering our own debts — how many we often passed by, not only toward men but toward God himself. … But if we will not become gentler toward those indebted to us, we shall suffer what befell the one who forgave not his fellow-slave the 'hundred denarii' — who, forgiven according to the parable lying in the Gospel, was seized, and his master exacts the forgiven sums, saying to him: 'Wicked and slothful slave, oughtest thou not to have pitied thy fellow-slave, as I pitied thee? Cast him into prison, till he pay all that is owed.' (Matthew 18:32) And the Lord adds to this: 'So also shall my heavenly Father do to you, if you forgive not each one his brother from your hearts.' (Matthew 18:23–35)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being handed over to torturers means discipline now by trials and illness, or punishment in the age to come, and God disciplines to make us better.
comments.comment: And if we suffer the repayment for these things, either we are disciplined in the present life, as if handed over to torturers (Matthew 18:24–35) by trials and illnesses, or at least we are punished in the age to come. That God disciplines convertibly, transforming the disobedient and hard to lead toward what is better, is easy to see; for divine scripture is full of such things — as in the wise saying, “Whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son he accepts,” (Hebrews 12:6–7) and again, “Endure for discipline,” and what follows.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'torturers' in the parable.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The unforgiving are punished and not called sons; we must remember our sins and be kind to the fallen.
comments.comment:
And he speaks of angels appointed to the tortures.

But 'until he pays all that is owed'—that is, he continuously delivered him over to be tortured—for he was never able to pay; here, indeed, God turns the man toward trials, diseases, and other tortures, but in the future, to be tortured unceasingly for eternity (Matthew 18:34).

And he did not say 'thus your Father will do to you,' but 'my Father'; for such are unworthy to be named sons of God.

Therefore, the word traces in brief the unutterable philanthropy of God, which the one not imitating as much as possible will undergo punishment from the righteous judge. … Thus, the word requires two things of us: to remember a certain one of his own sins and to be unforgetful of kindness toward the one who falls.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'my Father' and the lesson of the parable.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ does not approve of leaving a wife, though the law allowed it as a concession for hardness of heart.
comments.comment: But those already bound by marriage he does not permit to leave the wife once joined to them, so that the message of salvation may not fill the world under heaven with turmoil. For Christ, the Savior of us all, does not approve of this practice, even though the law, by way of concession, allowed the people of old to do it “because of their hardness of heart” (Matthew 19:8), as the Savior himself says.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses allowed divorce and Christ does not.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Abandoning one's own wife is not living with her, so joining another is adultery against the second.
comments.comment:
He says that adultery is not living with one's own; but he who abandons his own is not living with his own.

Therefore, 'he commits adultery against her'—that is, against the second, whom he joins to the one who is naturally conjoined to him, if he abandons his own.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Gospel does not forbid marriage, and the Lord allowed putting away a wife only for fornication.
comments.comment: The divine preaching of the Gospel did not forbid marriage, since God, I think, measures the commandment to human nature. For when the Pharisees, testing him, asked the Lord “whether it is lawful to put away his wife” (Matthew 19:3) for a cause other than fornication, he told them that whoever puts away “his wife, except on the ground of fornication, causes her to commit adultery” (Matthew 5:32; compare Matthew 19:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some are suited by nature to rise above the world, and even those not suited are perfected by practice.
comments.comment:
Regarding the division of the Lord, it is possible for those who live in the lower realm to endure the sorrow of this world rather than think as the righteous do (Mt 19:10), but for those who can rise above the world, as if carried by swift wings toward higher righteousness, they experience no pain and are free from the world's sorrows.

Therefore, not imposing a yoke, he said: not all grasp the word, but those to whom it is given.

And that 'to whom it is given' is a manifestation of natural gifts, which anyone might call a natural aptitude and the intelligence from birth toward the achievement of temperance; for there are indeed some differences by nature toward each virtue, some being more, others less, disposed toward it.

Even if natural things are by no means perfect, nor are they unchangeable and entirely unachievable, but even the apt toward good is perfected by practice, and the unapt is healed by much struggle.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'to whom it is given'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ set celibacy before those who wish to achieve it but did not make it a law, since not all can master the impulses of the flesh.
comments.comment: At this the disciples said to him, “If this is how the case stands between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.” And he said to them, “There are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to accept this accept it” (Matthew 19:10, 12). For he set it before those who wish to achieve it, but he did not bring it under law, since he knew that not all are able to master the impulses of the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why celibacy is offered and not commanded.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God allows marriage because not all can be wholly pure, but requires children to be reared.
comments.comment: But God has also allowed us to marry, since not all can receive what is better, that is, complete purity (Matthew 19:11); and he has charged those who marry to rear without fail what is born to them, and not to destroy the children given by providence.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some things are commanded and others left free, and celibacy is of the second kind: Christ did not command it but left it to choice.
comments.comment: Of the commandments some are commanded, and some are not commanded but left free and entrusted to choice by God. For those without which one cannot be saved—these are the ones commanded; but the greater ones than the commanded, which even if we do not do we are saved, are not a command of God. Hear, he says, the gospel of Jesus Christ teaching in it and saying: when you have done all that is commanded you, you ought to say we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do (Luke 17:10). And if, when I do all that is commanded, I am an unprofitable servant, when will I flee being an unprofitable servant? If being more ambitious you ascend from what is commanded; for example: if I keep "you shall not commit adultery" and not looking at a woman to desire her, I have done what I ought. But if I remain a virgin, not ordered and not commanded, I no longer say over the achievement of virginity: we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought. So also on the remaining commandments: if I do not steal or overreach, we ought to say we are unprofitable servants. But if I sell all that I have and give to the poor, I no longer say I am unprofitable; I have done what I ought. Therefore the apostle says: Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy. For in the Lord's saying to the disciples not all receive the word but those to whom it has been given, and he adds: let the one who is able to receive it receive it (Matthew 19:11–12); he did not command, but left it free.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only evil, not lack of wisdom, hinders approach to the Creator, so Christ says the kingdom is of such as children, not of children.
comments.comment:
Only evil and corruption of the creation prevents approaching the Creator, but the deficiency of wisdom is not a hindrance to the approach; for he seeks fullness, and by this the approach is granted.

Therefore also the precise expression of such things is 'the kingdom of the heavens' (Mt 19:14); for he did not say of these, but of such as these, since there is also a deficiency of wisdom in children, which the apostle was turning away from saying: 'do not become children in mind, but in wickedness be babes' (1 Cor 14:20).

And Mark also went beyond the text stating the reason and as if interpreting: 'of such as these is the kingdom' of the heavens (Mk 10:14); 'Amen I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a child, will by no means enter into it' (Lk 18:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ says 'of such as these'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who wish to follow God without distraction must withdraw from earthly things and make him their portion.
comments.comment: So too the Savior: when someone once came to him and asked how he might have eternal life (Matthew 19:16), he said, ‘You know the commandments: You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal’ (Matthew 19:18; Mark 10:19), and the rest of that kind. The man declared openly that he had kept such commandments, and he asked further, adding, ‘What do I still lack?’ (Matthew 19:20). The Savior answered, ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’ (Matthew 19:21). Those, then, who wish to serve God without distraction, and who think they must follow him, have to withdraw from earthly things, make him alone their lot, and grow rich on their hope in him, as is sung in the Psalms: ‘Delight in the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act’ (Psalm 37:4–5). So he sets apart the tithes for the Levites, in return for the labor of their service (Numbers 18:21). For the toil of the saints is not unpaid: their honors are choice and their rewards splendid. For the Savior says, ‘Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will put on (Matthew 6:25); but seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you’ (Matthew 6:33).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Christ answered the man as one who took him for a mere human, since goodness belongs to God and not to human nature.
comments.comment: And when he [Christ] says, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God" (Matthew 19:17), God, having numbered himself with human beings, said this according to his flesh, and in response to the mind of the one who approached him. For that man considered him only a man and not God, and the answer has this sense: "If you consider me a man," he says, "and not God, do not call me good; for no one is good." For goodness does not belong to human nature, but to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ asks 'Why do you call me good?'
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: The law is a good beginning that Christ does not cancel, but perfection is with him.
comments.comment: The early stage of the law is good, and Christ does not annul it; rather, he says, 'if you wish, enter into life' (Mt 19:17), keeping the commandments, showing the beginning of this way, but not fulfilling it; and his law is not something else, testifying through this; but perfection is with him.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ leads the man to the law as an entrance to eternal life, since the law only begins conduct and Christ is perfection.
comments.comment:
When Christ said, “If you want to enter into life,” (Matthew 19:17–18) or “keep the commandments,” that man, expecting him to say nothing other than “mine,” asks, “Which?” But he was much mistaken in his hope. Christ did not answer him as he thought, but leads him up to the law — not because the law is perfection (“no one is justified in the law,” according to what is written), but because practice according to the law is a kind of entrance to eternal life, little by little habituating the mind of those being tutored toward what is higher. For “the law has become our tutor unto Christ.” (Galatians 3:24) So the law is the beginning of bodily conduct, and Christ is perfection; for the beginning of goods, he says, is to do what is just. The law shows the just; Christ shows the good.

The law taught us to ward off with equals those who want to wrong us (“tooth for tooth” and “eye for eye”); but Christ, releasing us from that balance, leads us to the greater … “To the one who strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also; and to the one who wants to go to law with you and take your tunic,” (Matthew 5:38–40) he says, “leave him the cloak as well.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ answers 'Which?' by pointing to the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If the young man had truly loved his neighbor as himself, he would not have possessions beyond his neighbor's.
comments.comment: For you are clearly far from that commandment, and you bore witness to yourself falsely, that you loved your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 19:19). For see, what the Lord set before you convicts you of falling far short of true love. For if what you asserted were true, that from youth you kept the commandment of love (Matthew 19:20), and you gave back to each as much as to yourself, where did this surplus of possessions come from? For the care of those in need is costly to wealth: each one receives little for his necessary care, but all together divide up what exists and spend it on themselves. So the one who loves his neighbor as himself possesses nothing more than his neighbor. But you clearly have many possessions. Where did these come from? It is clear that you make your own enjoyment more important than the relief of the many. So as much as you abound in wealth, so much you fall short in love.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ's command exposes his claim to love his neighbor.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The man was loved for keeping the law, but perfection was not completed in him.
comments.comment:
Having said, Mark says, that 'Jesus, looking at him, loved him' (Mk 10:21), he stirs up a question: how was he loved who was not going to follow into 'life'?

Regarding the former, he who kept the law and these things from youth was worthy of love, but regarding perfection, he did not allow the love upon the following things to become perfect through a lack of time, just as he also did not show perfection.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The command to sell and give is an easy road to eternal life, and grieving at it shows how little the man loved his neighbor.
comments.comment: What harsh, heavy, or excessive word did the teacher set before you? Sell your possessions and give to the poor (Matthew 19:21). If he had set before you agricultural labors, or the dangers of trade, or all the other toils that come to those who make money, you would have had reason to grieve, distressed at the command. But if by so easy a road, holding no labor or sweat, he promises to make you an heir of eternal life, do you not rejoice at the ease of salvation, but go away pained in soul and mourning, and make useless for yourself everything you labored at beforehand? For if you did not murder, as you say, nor commit adultery, nor steal, nor bear false witness against anyone, you make your zeal about these things unprofitable for yourself by not adding what is lacking, through which alone you will be able to enter the kingdom of God. If a physician promised to correct the mutilations of limbs that were yours by nature or from illness, you would not be disheartened to hear it. But when the great physician of souls wishes to make you complete, though you are lacking in the most critical things, you do not receive the grace, but mourn and are gloomy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the man should have rejoiced at the command.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Leaving all wealth fits the apostolic way, whose narrowness the comparison to the camel shows.
comments.comment: It is good for the apostolic way here to fit 'laying aside all wealth' (Mt 19:23); for the wealth was shown by the comparison to the camel; 'for narrow and afflicted is the way leading into life' (Matthew 7:14).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The camel is a thick ship's rope, and the near-impossible task shows that the rich need grace.
comments.comment: By “camel” (Matthew 19:24) here he does not mean the burden-bearing animal, but the thick rope with which sailors bind the anchors. He does not show this as wholly impossible, but by the extreme difficulty places the matter somehow near and next door to the impossible. From this it is clear that the one about to accomplish it is no ordinary person — he needs grace.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'camel' and why only grace saves the rich.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By human weakness no one is saved, but the Savior's gentleness leaves no room for despair.
comments.comment: No one would have a soul free of passions in every respect, even if he were among the most industrious. For “who is clean from filth,” according to what is written, or “who will boast of having a pure heart?” And if “the one who stumbles in one thing has become liable for all,” as far as the word of condemnation goes, who would not then be held for the remaining single transgression, not even having escaped? For even the very sober would not escape sinning in the mind. So as far as human weakness goes, no one is saved; but as far as the Savior’s gentleness goes, salvation is not to be despaired of (Matthew 19:26) — for not every sin is unto death (1 John 5:16–17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how salvation is impossible for people yet possible for God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Everything is possible to God' does not include what is shameful, since then God would not be God.
comments.comment:
We, then, do not say that the corrupted body returns “to its original nature,” any more than the corrupted grain of wheat returns to being a grain of wheat (1 Corinthians 15:37; John 12:24). For we say that, just as an ear rises from the grain of wheat, so a certain principle lies within the body; and from this principle, which is not corrupted, the body “is raised in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42).

The Stoics, however, say that the body “wholly corrupted” returns “to its original nature,” because of the doctrines they hold about things that recur without variation in each cycle; and they say that “that very first make-up from which it was dissolved” will be put together again, establishing these things, as they suppose, by the necessities of logic.

Nor do we retreat to “a most absurd refuge” when we say that “everything is possible to God” (Matthew 19:26; Mark 10:27). For we know how to understand that “everything”: it does not refer to things that have no existence, nor to things that cannot be conceived. We say, too, that God cannot do shameful things, since then God would be able not to be God; for if God does anything shameful, he is not God.

But since Celsus lays it down that God does not will “what is against nature” either, we draw a distinction in what is said. If someone calls wickedness against nature, we too say that God does not will what is against nature, neither what springs from wickedness nor what happens without reason. But if one means what happens in accordance with God’s reason and his will, then such things must at once be not against nature; for what God does is not against nature, even if it is extraordinary, or seems extraordinary to some.

And if we must use a forced term, we will say that, compared with nature as it is more commonly understood, there are some things above nature which God might at some time do: raising man above human nature, causing him to change into a better and more divine nature, and keeping him so, as long as the one so kept also shows by his deeds that he wills it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles chose all things over what they had.
comments.comment: [The apostles:] Not as if they were leaving great things, but they, from those which they had, stood up and showed the choice preferring all (Mt 19:27).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Regeneration' here means the resurrection of the dead.
comments.comment: And he [Christ] called the resurrection of the dead regeneration; for he says to the disciples: 'You also will sit in the regeneration on twelve thrones' (Matthew 19:28), instead of 'in the resurrection, in the age to come'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'in the regeneration'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A throne is where the mind sits in spiritual knowledge, and to judge means to teach.
comments.comment: Such a status was also promised to his disciples, that the Lord would give them to sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28). And a throne is that in which the mind sits, a spiritual knowledge gathering together those who have wandered from godliness. And to judge here means to teach, as also 'open your mouth with the word of God and judge all healthily,' instead of teaching.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A throne can mean a kingdom or a teaching office, as with the seat of Moses.
comments.comment: For a throne is often taken to mean a kingdom, even if it is used instead of a teaching office, as is clear from 'The Lord King is established forever' (Psalm 29:10), and again: 'Your throne, O God, is unto the ages of ages' (Ps 45:6), and even more: 'A throne of authority is prepared with righteousness' (Proverbs 16:12). But it is also said to the disciples: 'You also shall sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel' (Matt 19:28). When it is said, 'The scribes sat upon the seat of Moses' (Matthew 23:2), this seat is one of teaching.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Apostles judge by virtue.
comments.comment: According to Matthew 19:28-29, the apostles judge by virtue, reproving evil.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The promise widens to all who do likewise, who get God's intimacy, holy brothers, paradise and the Jerusalem above in place of kin, fields and houses.
comments.comment: So that no one may think what was said fits only the disciples, he widened the word to all who do the like. Even if the rest will not obtain the same things as the disciples, they will still have, instead of kin according to the flesh, intimacy with God and brotherhood with the holy — he means the elders and elder women of the church, whom they had through love as kin, beloved by disposition, loving far more than fleshly kin, from whom they also received money to manage as they wish, with the goods to come also stored up for them — and instead of fields, paradise, and instead of houses of stone, the Jerusalem above, mother of the firstborn.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what is received instead of what is left.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The reward is heavenly things that far surpass earthly ones, not more of the same kind.
comments.comment: He does not say they will receive many fathers instead of one, or many mothers instead of one, or many fields instead of few, but that the heavenly will surpass all earthly things with incomparable excellences, and what is being saved will be preferred to what is being lost (Matthew 19:29).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how to read the 'manifold' reward.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The multiplied kin are fellowship in the gospel, with love filling all with kinship, and leaving fleshly ties is good for the spiritual life.
comments.comment: And 'now' is the enjoyment of manyfold things according to fellowship, not according to possession; just as the Savior set forth all the things of the brothers for those fighting for the sake of the gospel—thus many houses, and brothers and sisters, and mothers and children, and farms—as an existence for those leaving their own, because love has filled all with kinship and all need. … Therefore, to leave behind according to the flesh is a good thing because of the spiritual life …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Leaving wife and marriage is not praised as evil but so it is no obstacle to the minister.
comments.comment: So, therefore, not even the separation from wife and marriage is to be counted as something evil to be praised, but so that even this is not an obstacle to the minister; and the preference of spiritual things altogether shows that the fleshly things are not foreign …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: For my sake, for the gospel and for the kingdom of God all mean the same, since Christ's name is the power of both.
comments.comment:
And it is no difference to say 'for my sake' or 'for the sake of the gospel' as Mark, or 'for the sake of the kingdom of God' as Luke.

For the very name of Christ is the power of the gospel and of the kingdom, and the gospel is hung upon the name of Christ, and the kingdom of God is granted through his name.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Gospels word the reason differently.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Luke adds a wife, who is given in the same spiritual way as other kin, and leaving kin is good only when they drag toward impiety.
comments.comment: Luke has also added concerning a wife (Luke 18:29) — according to Paul, who commands to honor “elder women as mothers, younger as sisters in all purity.” (1 Timothy 5:2) Just as he gives brothers who are not brothers, parents who are not parents, and children who are not children, so also a wife who is not a wife, fulfilling the intimacies in another, clearly spiritual manner, not bodily. Leaving the race according to the flesh is good for the spiritual life; for he says to separate from parents and from a wife when they drag toward impiety. Just as one must despise soul and body for piety, so one must also prefer this to all things.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The promise of many kin leaves out a wife, since in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage.
comments.comment: Together, keep the holy multiplication Scripture promises — of brothers and children and parents and fields and houses. But wife is not counted with these. For it is not said, 'Everyone who left brothers or sisters or parents or children or fields or houses or wife for my name's sake shall receive manifold.' 'For in the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels in the heavens.' (Matthew 19:29) (Matthew 22:30)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The day is the whole age, in which the Lord calls the righteous to work for a wage.
comments.comment: Fleeing love of glory, the Lord speaks as about another householder, though he himself is householder and distributor of the kingdom of the heavens. By “day” he means the whole age, in which at different times after Adam’s transgression he calls some righteous into God-reverent work, setting them a wage for the works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the day and the hiring mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hours are the ages of the world, with calls in the time of Adam, Noah, Abraham and Christ, the last called being idle nations with no one to preach to them.
comments.comment: Those about the first hour are those around Adam and Enoch; those about the third, around Noah and Shem and the righteous from them — for the time is second and the call second, when the ordinances also differ. The workers called about the sixth are those in Abraham’s times, when again came the legislation of circumcision; those of the eleventh, those at Christ’s presence, of whom alone it is said, “Why do you stand here idle all day?” (Matthew 20:6) — having no hope of the Lord, godless in the world, idle in every good work, like those standing in the marketplace handling nothing at all, but running through their life vainly and to no purpose. The Lord also exhorts them, saying, “Why do you stand idle?” They answer, “No one hired us” — for neither Moses nor any of the holy ones preached to the nations, but only to Israel. Still the Lord sends them too into the vineyard.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The five calls show that in every age some succeeded and some failed, and the Father pays through the Son at the end.
comments.comment: He says five calls happened, to show that in each time some succeeded and some missed — as the “five prudent virgins and the five foolish” (Matthew 25:1–13) show, being in the same times — and that some were found virtuous, while some despised the coming age through folly. At the end of life, which is evening (for the time from Christ’s advent until the consummation is the time after the eleventh hour, as John says, “It is the last hour”), the householder, he says, commands the wage to be given beginning from the last. The householder may be understood as the Father, using the Son as distributor not as a mere servant but as co-worker, because through him he administers and works whatever he wills.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The denarius is the Spirit's grace, leading the holy into life.
comments.comment: He gives each a denarius — the Spirit’s grace, conforming the holy to God, engraving the heavenly characters in their souls, and leading them up into life and incorruption.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the denarius stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The first workers' hope of more shows human nature, not the mind of holy men, yet more is owed them for living under death and the devil.
comments.comment:
What the first ones thought—that they would receive more—demonstrates a nature, rather than the intellect of holy men; for they do not reckon this at the time of the resurrection, nor will they accuse then (Mt 20:10).

More is owed to the former, because they were living under the rule of death and the devil; for this is the burden of the day and the scorching heat, when even the coolness of the Spirit was not present to assist men toward righteousness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The first workers seem owed more because they lived under death and the devil, when the Spirit's help was absent.
comments.comment: In this the first seem to have toiled more than the last, having endured the devil’s burning longer while sin, corruption, and death were not yet abolished. If the matter is weighed by equality, something more seems owed to the former, because they lived while death and the devil ruled — that is the burden of the day and the heat, when not even the Spirit’s dew was present helping humans toward righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the burden of the day and the heat.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel was called first but ranked after the Gentiles, so the last became first.
comments.comment:
Palladius: What does this mean, then?

Cyril: This, my friend, I would say: the law is burdensome, a load hard to bear. And a clear sign of this would be that the extra things are not carried on the shoulders, because those under the yoke are weak. That is why the inspired disciples said to those who, after coming to faith, were turning to the worship of the law: ‘Now therefore why are you putting God to the test, by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither you nor your fathers were able to bear?’ (Acts 15:10) But the Kohathites set on their own shoulders the things by which Christ is signified, and make of them a light load, easy to carry. Is this not plainly what Christ himself said: ‘My yoke is easy, and my burden is light’? (Matthew 11:30)

Palladius: So it seems.

Cyril: I would add this as well to what has been said, for it will help not a little toward full conviction. In the first census of the Levites, those of Gershon were placed at the head, then Kohath in the middle, and last Merari; these are the Levitical clans (Numbers 3:17). But in the second census, the one counted from twenty-five years of age, Kohath is set before the others and named first (Numbers 4:2–3). After him, and last, come Gershon and Merari, whose service is the extra things of the tent (Numbers 4:22–33). Each of these two clans has only two families, while Kohath extends to as many as four (Numbers 3:18–20). Do you grasp the riddle, then?

Palladius: Not in the least.

Cyril: Israel was called among the first; but when the flock of the Gentiles ran in between, Israel was ranked after it. And so the last have become first, as the Savior said, and the first last (Matthew 20:16).

Palladius: True.

Cyril: And it is plain that the Jewish people are few in number, while the countless multitude from the Gentiles far exceeds them.

Palladius: Of course.

Cyril: That is why God says to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: ‘Now let me alone, and in my anger I will consume this congregation, and I will make of you a great nation, and much greater than this one.’ (Exodus 32:10; Deuteronomy 9:14) With services such as these, then, the whole body of the Levites was honored; and the limit set to their sacred service was to be subject to the one who held first place and to act under the hand of Aaron. But to aim higher than this, and to seek something better than what had been allotted to it and fixed by God, was shown by the event itself to bring punishment and ruin. For it is written again in Numbers: ‘Korah the son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, spoke, with Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On the son of Peleth, son of Reuben; and they rose up before Moses, together with two hundred and fifty men of the sons of Israel, leaders of the congregation, members of the council, men of renown (Numbers 16:1–2). They gathered together against Moses and Aaron and said to them: “Enough from you! For… (Numbers 16:3)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Those after Christ's coming receive the Spirit first through baptism and are named sons of God, while the ancients had a spirit of slavery.
comments.comment: But the last, having the Master’s generosity instead of toils, receive the wage first, since all after the advent, through baptism and union with the Spirit, have become “sharers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4) and were named sons of God, while all before the advent were named born of women — though they too are to be called to this. For even if the prophets became partakers of the Spirit, it was not as the faithful: somehow the Holy Spirit becomes like leaven in the faithful’s souls and transforms the whole human into another state of life. That is why we become “sharers of the divine nature” and cry out boldly, “Abba, Father.” The more ancient did not obtain the same grace. So Paul says, “You did not receive a spirit of slavery again unto fear, but you received a spirit of adoption” (Romans 8:15) — meaning the ancients received a “spirit of slavery,” not having the dignity of adoption. Having received the intelligible denarius first, we are necessarily said to have been preferred above the others.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cup and baptism mean death: a cup of punishment drunk, and a descent into Hades with a rising again.
comments.comment:
Regarding the cup and baptism, he speaks of death (Mt 20:22); saying 'to drink a cup' as if of wine, just as it is said in Jeremiah that the punishment is to be a 'cup of wine' which one is able to drain and cast down; and 'baptism' signifies the descent into Hades, which had its ascent from there, just as the one being baptized dives into water and rises again;

and by saying 'water' he revealed the turbulence of those in Hades.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To take the cup means to suffer for piety and stand against sin even to death.
comments.comment: And for this reason, he says, “I will take the cup of salvation,” meaning the suffering in the contests for the sake of piety, the standing against sin even to death. And this would be what the Savior himself taught in the Gospels: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); and again to the disciples, “Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matthew 20:22). He was indicating the death he accepted for the salvation of the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the cup is.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: No one will sit, since sitting belongs to God alone, and the apostles sought it without knowing what glory means.
comments.comment: [Christ to James and John:] You ask whether some are still going to sit. Learn that no one will. Such a thing belongs to the first substance alone, not to what is human. For the apostles, not understanding what it is to sit “on twelve thrones” (Matthew 19:28) and what being glorified then means, were seeking that sort of seat (Matthew 20:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ refuses to grant the seats.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To be served would suit him as God, but to serve is human and fits the one who lowered himself to human things.
comments.comment: the Son says: “he did not come to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28) For to be served by creation would fit him very reasonably, as God and Master and having under his feet everything that is made; but to serve is human — yet, as far as it touches the accounts of the economy with flesh, not unfitting for the one who wholly lowered himself toward human things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Son of Man can come to serve.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Though the crowd said 'Jesus of Nazareth,' the blind man called him the Son of David.
comments.comment: What, he asks, does the crowd intend? They say to him, "Jesus the Nazarene is passing by" (Luke 18:37). Oh, the wonder! Other things are being taught, and other things are being preached; he hears Jesus the Nazarene, but he does not call him Jesus the Nazarene, but Jesus the Son of David (Matthew 20:30).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: Christ sends two disciples to bring the colt, fulfilling the prophets.
comments.comment: Five days before his saving passion, wanting also to fulfill the prophets’ voices spoken about him, he commands the two disciples to go away into the village opposite Bethphage and Bethany and bring him the unbroken colt.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The two disciples stand for apostles and evangelists, or angels, and the call is shown to be divine because even the devil cannot resist the Savior's words.
comments.comment: He says the disciples are two — that is, apostles and evangelists — who became Christ’s co-workers and servants for this. Or he also means angels who serve Christ for our ransom, “ascending and descending on the Son of Man.” (John 1:51) And if the one who bound them with the cords of sins asks, “What are you doing?” (Matthew 21:1–3) still, unable to withstand the Savior’s words, he will fall silent — not willingly, because of the excess of power. In this the call is shown to be divine.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The colt shows the new people called to the Lord, untamed by law and prophets and loosed from the vine of the first covenant.
comments.comment:
The event is a sign (Mt 21:2); for it is not a necessity for the one entering Jerusalem with the Lord to sit upon a donkey, who traversed all Judah and Galilee on foot, but to be seen on a colt at that specific time shows the heavenly leader and king sitting upon the new people of Jerusalem; for the colt made the newness of the calling manifest, but also the old,

which is not clean according to those now called; for a donkey is not clean according to the law, but is set apart by the various recognitions of uncleanness from clean animals, because the donkey is single-hoofed and does not chew the cud.

The people are the untamed colt, upon which neither law nor prophets had seated, awaiting their Lord; for this is also what the Savior said to the sent-off disciples: 'loosening, bring to me' (Mt 21:2).

To what, then, was the donkey tied?

To the vine, according to what was said: 'binding his colt to the vine and the donkey to the halter.'

Loosening, therefore, from the vine, from the first covenant, bring to me.

That it was done so that the said thing might be fulfilled: 'The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger' (Isa 1:3).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Matthew names a donkey and a colt while the others name one beast, but there is no conflict.
comments.comment: That Matthew says a donkey and a colt were brought to the Lord, while Luke and Mark recalled only one beast, is no conflict: when the colt was being led as the disciples were commanded, the donkey also sprang along, following her child as an affectionate mother (Matthew 21:1–7).
comments.selected_reason: Resolves the apparent conflict over one beast or two.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ rode the colt of the nations while the synagogue followed behind, so the first became last, and both peoples had sunk to the level of a donkey.
comments.comment:
Christ is said to be “coming” (Matthew 21:7–9) as one who came from above: being God by nature and Son of the Father, he became man and came in the Lord’s name, being called Lord. So as God by nature he is called blessed — that is, glorified. Christ was sitting on the colt, and the mother followed. What was done was a sign for us of a most necessary matter: Christ rested on the new people that once worshiped idols, and in due times the Jews’ synagogue will also follow — though in the time of the call it had the older place, having been called first through Moses and the prophets. But because it struck against the saving God, it justly comes behind the colt only with difficulty and has become a tail — that is, an attendant behind those from the nations — and the first has become last.

See how he who knows “kidneys and hearts” showed human nature carried into the last irrationality: both the Jews’ synagogue and the multitude of the nations are likened to a donkey, the most irrational of all. For some “served the creation rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25) God, and others, dishonoring the tutoring law, went outside good mind and understanding and turned toward every form of baseness; “they were compared to senseless cattle and made like them,” (Psalm 49:12) according to the psalmist’s voice. A donkey is also otherwise a symbol of uncleanness; for the animal is unholy and has condemnation from the law. Such are all who wander and love sin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The colt led by two disciples is the untaught nations brought by prophets and apostles, and the children are the new people.
comments.comment: The colt is led when two disciples have been sent from Christ; for two orders serve him for this — prophets and apostles — through whom the nations are netted into faith. And it is led from a village, so that from this too he may show the rustic mind of the nations, not raised in the law, but living rather carelessly and wildly — yet it changed toward the gentler, for it came under Christ teaching these things.
