And children, raising “palm branches,” (Matthew 21:7–9) were running before him and composing the doxology together with the disciples, so that through them too we may see the new people from the nations as if written on a tablet. For it is written: “And a people being created will praise the Lord.” (Psalm 102:18)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Casting out the animals foretells a change of worship, and the scourge shows the slavish state of those under the law.
comments.comment: He also foretells the change of worship by casting out the animals being slaughtered and the legal traditions. He raises the scourge to show that if they do the same again they will taste blows, and to show the slavish state of those under the law he brings a scourge fitting for household slaves (John 2:15).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's severity in the temple was a sign of rebuke, not an act of violence, for he struck no one.
comments.comment: It is a more severe work being done not in the gentleness of speech, since he also drove out those who were trading and overturned the tables; and even according to the prophetic word he did nothing by violence, according to 'he will not fight nor cry out' and 'his voice will not be heard in the streets.' And John said that he 'made a scourge of cords'; and this is a sign of rebuke and severity. Therefore, this too must be counted among the symbols; for he did not strike anyone with a scourge, but it was a sign of the lash being brought upon those who use worldly things for the sake of God's things.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The temple trade served the law's sacrifices, but with the truth now come Christ ends them and makes the temple a house of prayer.
comments.comment:
There was in the temple a crowd of merchants — money-changers, or small-coin dealers — and with them sellers of oxen and sheep, and people selling turtledoves and pigeons. These things were useful for the sacrifices of worship under the law. But it was already time for the shadow to cease and for the truth in Christ to shine. So Christ, the Truth, rightly honored with his own Father in the temple that is his, commanded the sacrifices and smoke under the law to be curtailed, and showed the temple to be a house of prayer. For to rebuke the merchants and drive from the sacred precincts those selling what is useful for sacrifice is exactly that and nothing else.

Another evangelist says Jesus also “made a whip of cords,” (Matthew 21:12–13) (John 2:15) threatened blows, and raised it against them. Those who honor legal worship needed to know, after the truth was shown, that having a “spirit of slavery” (Romans 8:15) and refusing to be freed, they will be under scourges and subject to slavish punishment. … He also sets Isaiah against them as accuser — for so the evangelist says.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ drove the sellers out of the temple.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The healing of the blind and lame as the Jews are cast out is a type of the nations, and those who sell holy things must stop.
comments.comment: What happened was a riddle: when the Jews were cast out of the temple with the typological sacrifices, the blind and lame are healed — a type of the nations. And let those who sell the Spirit’s gifts and the priesthood also learn that the Lord cast the sellers of pigeons out of the temple with a scourge, and let them stop gathering profits for themselves from ordinations (Matthew 21:12).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ accepts the children's praise and cites the Psalm, which ascribes such praise to the Lord, so the Son of David is God.
comments.comment: As our Savior Christ of all was going up to Jerusalem, children went before him, praising and saying: “Hosanna to the son of David.” The doxology is wholly God-befitting. The Pharisees were indignant and came saying: “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus said to them: “Yes; have you never read: From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise?” (Matthew 21:15–16) Here we must recall blessed David: “O Lord, our Lord, how wondrous is your name in all the earth, for your majesty is exalted above the heavens. From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise.” (Psalm 8:1–2) The children praised, saying “Hosanna to the son of David,” and he accepts the doxology as one praised. Blessed David did not ascribe this to a common human, but rather to the Lord, whose name has become wondrous in all the earth; for the majesty too was exalted above the heavens. How, then, is the son of David according to the flesh — Christ — not God?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ approves the children's praise.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: He withdraws from their lovelessness.
comments.comment: Because of the Jews’ lack of love for God, he withdraws (Matthew 21:17).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The rebuke of the fig tree is symbolic, aimed at fruitless Israel and not at the tree, which was not to blame for bearing no fruit.
comments.comment: To those using such a purpose, the Lord symbolically rebukes through the fig tree in the Gospels, having come to it and finding nothing but leaves, saying, 'No more shall fruit come from you for an age' (Matthew 21:19). And we do not say that the rebuke was spoken to the fig tree itself; for the sensible fig tree did not bear fruit not because of its own cause. But it is also said regarding Israel having fallen into impiety: 'There is no cluster in the vines, nor figs in the fig trees.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the cursing of the fig tree is a symbol, not a punishment of a tree.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fig tree is the synagogue's worship in types, now unfruitful, which can no longer benefit the Jews.
comments.comment:
But the fig tree is to be understood here as the synagogue of the Jews and the worship in types and shadows, not having fruit that is edible and pleasing to God, the worship in the Spirit.

Therefore, as one not producing sweet fruit, the Lord Jesus dried it up in a certain way, being hungry and seeking fruit from out of humanity.

Surely, from what he said, that 'fruit shall by no means come from you' (Mt 21:19), he teaches that the worships according to the law are no longer able to benefit the Jews.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Pharisee should know from David that Christ is a priest after Melchizedek, and that God may move the law to something better.
comments.comment:
If you knew the “God-breathed scriptures,” senseless Pharisee (2 Timothy 3:16), and the holy prophets’ voices, you would have remembered blessed David saying to Christ the Savior of all: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” (Psalm 110:4) Tell me, then: which of the scribes or Pharisees has served God “according to the order of Melchizedek”? None at all. Even Abraham our forefather, root of Israel’s line, was blessed under Melchizedek’s priesthood. Melchizedek and his priesthood were a type of Christ the Savior of all, who has become our high priest, bringing near to God the Father all who have believed in him and perfecting them into sanctification through worship beyond the law.

Why then are you vexed, Pharisee? Do you accuse the Lawgiver, tell me, of loosing the law, and of not following his own commands? But God is wholly beyond the law. For the one who set the laws not chiefly for himself but for us transfers what was arranged, in due time, to whatever he chooses, and raises it to what is better. So there was a time for the things in types to cease and for the better to be shown. That is why he said somewhere through Isaiah’s voice, “The people’s ordinances will be abolished”; for they grew idle once the new command was shown, which the Son has spoken to us through himself.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Deceitful people do not deserve deeper teaching.
comments.comment: It is untimely to unfold the deeper things to deceitful people who do not come to learn (Matthew 21:23).
comments.author: Theophilus of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ asks about John because the Pharisees feared to be asked why they did not believe.
comments.comment: Christ asked what opinion they held about the Baptist, because the Jews were accustomed to call the holy ones liars and to say they invent prophecy from their own judgment, not sent from God. The Pharisees fear to say the truth, lest they hear: “Why did you not believe?” (Matthew 21:25)
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ answers their question with a question about John.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The first son is the Gentiles, whom God called first and who, after turning to idols, repented and went into the vineyard.
comments.comment: A man had two sons, and the first son is the Gentiles, whom God the common Father called first. For he sowed the teachable and natural law in their minds and gave the visible creation as heralds, but the good order of their soul was poured out onto wood and stones. For they said to the wood, “You are my father.” Therefore they did not endure being hindered, for they said, “We do not know the Lord.” So these, having regretted it later, went away into the vineyard (Matthew 21:28–32).
comments.selected_reason: Identifies the first son in the parable.
comments.author: Theophilus of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In the vineyard parable the temple is the tower, the altar the threshing floor, the priests the farmers, and the prophets the servants.
comments.comment:
The temple is a tower, in which those approaching were required to offer the fruits of piety to God, all of them fulfilling everything according to the law.

Moreover, the altar is a threshing floor upon which the blood of the sacrifices was poured out; the priestly order are farmers, and all those handling this service, so as to prepare for the people the harvest from the teaching of the law to offer to God with a 'good' 'conscience'.

A prophet speaks of the servants sent at the appointed time, those sent to remind the people or the priests of what is owed to God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The vineyard is Israel, planted by God, who patiently kept sending prophets to admonish it while it dishonored them.
comments.comment: The vineyard is Israel (Matthew 21:33–41), as the psalmist says, “You brought a vine out of Egypt,” (Psalm 80:8) and Isaiah, “A vineyard was made for the beloved.” (Isaiah 5:1) God planted it and went abroad a long time — that is, he was long-suffering. Yet he is seen caring for the place and holding it in mind; for there was no intervening time when prophets and righteous men were not being sent from God to admonish. But they became disobedient, and having dishonored those sent, they sent them away empty — that is, with nothing good to say about them to the God who sent them.
comments.selected_reason: Says who the vineyard is and what the servants stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The householder is God and the vineyard Israel, which he guarded against the plots of enemies.
comments.comment: He calls the Householder the God who is the master of all, and the vineyard the people of Israel constructed through piety, saying that he was provided with the security of the help of God, by which, having been delivered from the plot of the strangers, he remained upon his own (Mt 21:33-41).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Son is sent after the servants, not as one of them but as true Son and Lord, so the Hebrews were wrong to think they could take the kingdom alone.
comments.comment: Are you too sons of God the Father? Does the lot descend to you by nature if you put the heir out of the way? How will you become lords of what you desire? And how is that not worth laughing at? For Christ, as Son and essential heir of God the Father’s dignities, became man and was calling those who believe in him into share of his own kingdom; but the Hebrews wanted to have the kingdom alone — which was both impossible and ignorant. Notice here that after the household servants the Son is sent, not as one counted among servants, but as true Son and therefore Lord. Even if he wore a slave’s form economically, he was still God and true Son of God the Father, and had lordship by nature (Matthew 21:37) (Philippians 2:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Son, not another servant, is sent last.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son comes, suffers, rises and destroys them.
comments.comment: Regarding the Son, he speaks of his arrival (παρουσίαν), having suffered by them and having risen and having destroyed them miserably (Matthew 21:41).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The other tenants are the apostles.
comments.comment: And who would these be? The choir of the holy apostles, through whom come the priests and teachers of the new covenant (Matthew 21:41).
comments.selected_reason: Says who the other tenants are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: David marvelled at the corner, the meeting of two peoples in one, which saves those inside it and crushes those outside.
comments.comment: Blessed David marveled at this corner (Matthew 21:42) — that is, the meeting of the two peoples into one — saying, “This was from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Psalm 118:22–23) So the stone is saving for the corner made by him, but crushing and ruin for those who remained outside this intelligible and spiritual concurrence. For some, Christ is “a rock of stumbling and a stone of scandal.” (1 Peter 2:8)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The stone is Christ, the corner joins Israel's remnant with the nations, and the kingdom taken is saving knowledge and the Spirit.
comments.comment: By “stone” here he means Christ, and by “corner” the joining and fellowship of these two peoples — the remnant saved from Israel and those from the nations. For this reason “the kingdom of the heavens will be taken from you” (Matthew 21:42–43) — that is, the knowledge of salvation, the way toward everything praiseworthy, and sharing in the Spirit, through which one acquires the kingdom of the heavens.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the stone, the corner and the kingdom taken away mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's words came true because the oracles of God were taken from the Jews and given to us, though they still hold the writings without seeing the mind in them.
comments.comment: God took these treasures from that people and through Christ, who said: 'The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits,' (Matthew 21:43) gave them to us. So 'I will give because of your sins your treasures into plunder.' And he gave that people's treasures to us; for 'first they were entrusted with the oracles of God,' then after them we were entrusted, the oracles of God having been taken from them and given to us. And we say that 'The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits' was spoken by the Savior and has been fulfilled—not that the writing was taken from them, but now they no longer have the law and the prophets by not seeing the mind in them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the kingdom was taken and given to others.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The marriage is the joining of the faithful to the Son.
comments.comment: By “marriage” (Matthew 22:2) he means the joining of the faithful to the Son, calling Jews into it — long ago through the prophets, later through the disciples before the passion and resurrection.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the marriage in the parable stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wedding is the Church joined to the Word, and those who are called are held back by neglect and life in the flesh.
comments.comment:
This is a wedding of a church being joined to the Word, and a preparation for the wedding through the giving of the gifts of the rich, which is likened to those being prepared for guests in a rich banquet.

For Paul says that we are 'in everything' 'made rich' in Christ, 'in word and in knowledge'.

The first and second servants are called: the first being those who ran toward the presence of the Lord as fellow-workers and successors of the apostles.

But neglect prevents those who are called; for those 'walking according to the flesh' do not follow the divine call toward Christ.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Jews refused the call through Moses and then through the apostles, preferring earthly possessions and money to intimacy with God.
comments.comment: Those called through the first household servants refused to come: thrusting aside the law through Moses, they turned to human teachings. Likewise those called second after them through second messengers — that is, the holy apostles — left what was beneficial and withdrew as far as possible to what seemed good to themselves. Some went to their own field, which signifies possession of earthly things and zeal about them; others to commerce, which again shows us love of money and the spasm around it. For love of flesh and worldly love of pleasure, empty distractions, and care for making money deprive us of eternal enjoyment and intimacy with God (Matthew 22:2–5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who refused the invitation and why.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The king's army is the Roman army, called God's.
comments.comment: Clearly the irresistible hand of the Roman army. We call the Roman campaign God’s, inasmuch as he is Master and Creator of all (Matthew 22:7).
comments.selected_reason: Says who the king's army is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The call of the Gentiles ends any distinction of race and goes to the evil and the good alike.
comments.comment:
Furthermore, there is the call of the Gentiles, and no longer is there a distinction of race, nor does Israel have the privilege; rather, grace is for those who are negligent and those who are rejected, for 'both the wise and the foolish' as Paul says, and both the evil and the good as the parable says.

For he calls those who have taken care of themselves, comparing them to the generally wicked.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the invitation goes to everyone, evil and good.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Nothing stops the willing from coming to the wedding, yet some who were called did not become chosen because they lacked the right garment.
comments.comment: To them we will say that the one who gave the wedding feast for his son sent his servants to gather those who had been called, but they would not come (Matthew 22:2–3). After them, those who were called according to their own purpose came in, and so the wedding hall was filled with guests (Matthew 22:10). So nothing is seen standing in the way of those who are willing to come. Foreknowledge does no wrong to anyone at all, nor does it give anyone an advantage. Otherwise, let them teach us whether those who in their disobedience outraged the God who called them were not foreknown as well. More than that, some were called and rushed into the wedding, yet they did not become chosen, nor were they justified or glorified. For what reason? Because they were not wearing a garment fit for the wedding (Matthew 22:11–12).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wicked who obey the call may change, but those who entered falsely are cast out by angels and left with no activity and no divine glory.
comments.comment:
And the evil may undergo a transition from wickedness, if they entirely obey the good-doing call and 'put on the new man'; but if not this, they were indeed called, but they were not chosen, and indeed their call is overturned; for they are rebuked even for having been convinced of a false entrance.

But the ministers who cast out such people are angels.

And the binding of feet and hands is … A cessation of all activity.

For no longer is any practice given to the wicked, the time of strangers having been fulfilled in which they have done nothing good.

But by saying 'darkness' more externally, he speaks further on of divine virtue and glory.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Binding means he can no longer do any good.
comments.comment: Otherwise he is said to have hands and feet bound as no longer able to do anything good there; for the working of the good extends only as far as the present (Matthew 22:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the binding of hands and feet means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Herodians are Herod's soldiers or tax collectors.
comments.comment: They say that the Herodians are the soldiers of Herod or those demanding the taxes imposed on the Jews by the Romans.
comments.selected_reason: Says who the Herodians were.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Those testing Christ wanted to look like his strongest opponents.
comments.comment: Regarding the question of those testing him, as it is recorded (Mt 22:16), witnesses who wished to be present wanted to appear as those most opposed to the true Christ, saying that Herod is the Christ, and as being in authority and able to accuse.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God wanted Israel free, but their sin put them under rulers who taxed them, then the Romans.
comments.comment: The God of all wanted Israel free of human domination. But because they trampled the divine laws, they came under the hand of those then in power, who laid tributes on them. And tax thereafter — when rule passed over to the Romans (Matthew 22:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Israel owed tribute at all.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who asked about tribute were exposed as cunning when Christ asked for the coin and told them to render to Caesar and to God.
comments.comment: Likewise, those proposing an unproven word concerning whether it is necessary to give tribute to Caesar or not are exposed, as they themselves were accused of being deceitful and speaking with much cunning from that very moment; for when being asked, the Savior said: 'Show me the coin' (Matt 22:19), meaning 'whose image and inscription it has.' And those saying: 'Caesar's,' were strongly rebated upon hearing: 'Therefore render to Caesar the things of Caesar, and to God the things of God' (Matt 22:21).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Sadducees' dispute was about bodies, not souls: the dead rise when the soul is reunited with its body.
comments.comment:
But the dispute with the Sadducees was not about souls, but about bodies, so that the answer was about these (Mt 22:23).

It is said then that the dead rise, when the soul is with a body, not as if the soul were dissolved in the interval, but as being inactive and lacking the proper things of life which are with a body; for man and life are one thing in common, and both must be reunited toward the life from death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Sadducees asked and what resurrection means in the answer.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Sadducees go wrong because they doubt that God can make things from nothing and change corruptible bodies.
comments.comment: This is what the Savior said in the Gospel: 'You wander, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God' (Matt 22:29). You wander, saying that he does not make things from non-being; for they say this: 'To do is later than to be; for there must exist something underlying. Those who are dead are without hope of resurrection.' Since, therefore, they do not receive these things through the power of God, because of this they stumble. God is able to bring from non-being into being and to transform corruptible bodies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what error Christ names when he mentions the power of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous, once made perfect, become equal to the angels, who neither marry nor are given in marriage.
comments.comment: We know also that the angels are so far above human beings that human beings, once made perfect, become equal to angels; for “in the resurrection of the dead” the righteous “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of heaven” (Matthew 22:30; compare Mark 12:25), and they become “equal to angels” (Luke 20:36).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be like the angels in the resurrection.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The envious Pharisees ask in hypocrisy, hoping Christ would add to the law, and Matthew's lawyer and Mark's scribe do not disagree.
comments.comment: From measureless shamelessness the Pharisees, envious because he was being praised by the crowds after the Sadducees were put to shame, ask again with hypocrisy, testing him — whether he will also add again to the first command as if correcting the law — so that they may find a handle against him. Matthew and Luke said the one who asked was a “lawyer,” (Matthew 22:34–40) Mark a “scribe.” That is no disagreement: some show him learned in the law, others a leading scribe, that is, an interpreter of the law to the people.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisee expected Christ either to set his own teaching beside Moses or to make himself God, and either way he would be caught.
comments.comment: Since the Lord was being praised after the Sadducees were shamed and withdrew, the Pharisees, envious at this, came forward, and someone thought very learned in the law among them asks which commandment is great in the law. He supposed Christ was about to cross out Moses’ teaching and set his own beside it, or to say, “You shall love the Lord your God — and me,” (Matthew 22:34–42) yoking his own glory to the Father’s glory, and so find a place to cast him into danger as making himself God — or, if he passed over that in silence, to say, “Then I do not accept you as God.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the trap in the question about the great commandment.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ exposes that they came from envy, and he teaches that God must be loved wholly, not in part.
comments.comment: The Lord exposes their wickedness: they did not come to ask so as to be helped, but from having nothing and being held by envy. He also teaches that one must not love God in part and cling to earthly things in part. Because the Lord said this command is more summary than all, the lawyer seemed to be thrusting him into danger as making himself God. Hence, though he had not said that, the lawyer praised him, as Mark says.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ said nothing new and then questioned them in turn.
comments.comment: But the Lord said nothing new, only what is of the law, and having muzzled the Pharisees by this, he himself asks them whose son they think the Christ is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The first commandment contains all piety, the second what is just toward people, and loving God completely brings loving the neighbor.
comments.comment: The first command teaches every form of piety; for loving God from the whole heart is the cause of every good. The second contains what is just toward humans. The first opens the way for the second, and the second is held together from it; for the one who has accomplished love toward God clearly also loves the neighbor in all things as himself. Such a person happens to be the fulfiller of all the commands.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the two great commandments relate.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: David called Christ Lord in the Spirit, which does not make the Father a slave, and his words about his own spirit are not about the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment:
He did not say 'Lord of the Spirit', but 'of David' (Mt 22:43); for not because he called Christ 'Lord' while speaking in spirit, must the Father be made a slave, as those impious toward the Spirit dare to do.

For David says, 'and a son' of the handmaid of God, and this does not yet fit with the Holy Spirit, but is said regarding his own spirit.

He spoke in spirit, for instance, when he said, 'do not take your Holy Spirit from me' (Psalm 51:11).

And 'do not take your spirit from me' did not yet fit with the Holy Spirit; for he was not about to take it from himself, nor even when he confessed his sin were those confessions of the Spirit.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: David is puzzling because fathers are lords of their sons, yet he calls his own descendant Lord.
comments.comment: How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord? For one ought, he says, to name fathers lords of their sons, because they have the sons under their authority; yet David, on the contrary, calls the one from his own seed his Lord (Matthew 22:43–46) (Psalm 110:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the puzzle Christ puts about David's Lord.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lawyers burden others with the law but never touch it.
comments.comment: Woe to you, then, lawyers: while the law is admittedly burdensome, on others who trample it you bring the penalty of death, but you yourselves do not even touch the law (Matthew 23:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the heavy burdens the scribes lay on others.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord cuts off love of glory in teachers by sending them to the order of servants and to humility.
comments.comment: Since one generally sees those who teach new doctrines arriving at the dignity of teaching from love of empty glory and boastfulness, the Lord removes this suspicion and cuts off the road as leading to ruin. So if, he says, you love glory and first places, seek the order of servants and of those later, and practice humility (Matthew 23:11–12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ sets humility before those who teach.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: There are no sons of Gehenna by nature.
comments.comment: Look, that there are not by nature any sons of Gehenna (Mt 23:15); rather, it should be sought whether the Gentiles, before they judaized, were not sons of Gehenna.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A son of Gehenna is one destroyed by unbelief and lawlessness.
comments.comment: By “son of Gehenna” (Matthew 23:15) he means the one being destroyed from unbelief — as having slid into this through impiety and reached such a measure of lawlessness as to have unmediated intimacy with the flame, and all but kinship toward bearing the torments without dispute.
comments.selected_reason: Says what 'son of Gehenna' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They valued the temple's gold above the temple, though the gold was precious only because of the temple's name.
comments.comment: Because they marveled at gold, they valued the gold in the temple above the temple, it being necessary not to value the matter, but the name, since the temple was called by the name of God, and the gold was shown to be precious because of the name of the temple (Mt 23:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why valuing the temple's gold above the temple is wrong.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Under the law the altar sanctified the gift, but now the gift on the spiritual altar is greater than what receives it.
comments.comment:
The gift of the altar was more glorified because what was previously placed on the altar as a sheep or a calf or something like that, through the placement upon the altar, was already a gift of God and was called so and was shown to be holy; for the altar was anointed with the oil that sanctifies, and the gift through that received sanctification.

Not however in the spiritual things is it thus; for gold in the present temple of God is the Spirit itself, and the body of Christ is the gift upon the spiritual altar.

Therefore, the things being put in are greater now than the things receiving; for these indeed sanctify, but those are sanctified.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Heaven is God's throne because the angels who do his will give him rest there, and earth is his footstool because he lived among humans in the flesh.
comments.comment: That is why the scriptures name heaven “God’s throne” (Isaiah 66:1): God rests upon the powers above. For in heaven are the angels who do his will and always glorify him; that is rest for him. “But the earth is the footstool of his feet” (Isaiah 66:1): for in it he associated with humans through flesh. And God’s “foot” is his holy flesh, and it is named in various ways.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why heaven is called God's throne and earth his footstool.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisees tithe small herbs while neglecting judgment, mercy and faith, which God values above tithes.
comments.comment: You exact tithes, he says, Pharisees — perhaps even of fine herbs — while leaving aside the commands whose transgression is greater. And what are those injunctions? Judgment — that is, judging what is right and blameless — and mercy — that is, genuineness toward God. For judgment and mercy and faith toward God are better than tithe and firstfruits. That is why through the prophet the God of all says: And now, Israel, “what does the Lord God seek from you but to do judgment and to love” (Deuteronomy 10:12) (Matthew 23:23) and to seek “mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God”? For in being very ready to follow, what is saved into genuine faith is seen. …
comments.selected_reason: Says which weightier matters the Pharisees neglected.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ urges a clean mind and heart, not only outward form.
comments.comment: Through these he describes the Pharisees’ life, advising not to be molded only by outward fashionings, but also to have the inside clean — what belongs to mind and heart (Matthew 23:25).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Cleansing the vessel by water was proper for the righteous, who were bodily clean, so as to satisfy both the law and the Lord.
comments.comment: For it is much better to cleanse the vessel of justice by the water, just as it was upon the men themselves (Mt 23:25). The righteous were bodily clean, those being cleansed by the waters, as David says, 'I will wash my hands in innocents' (Ps 26:6), so as to be in accordance with both the law and the Lord.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The law taught purity by symbols, but those who kept the cleansing customs while seizing gain became abominations, and cleansing by righteousness is better.
comments.comment:
Through symbols the law taught purity in life.

And the custom according to the Jews was such a thing, to cleanse the cups and the vessel of the dish from the ancient traditions, so that they might hold this clean from the touch of sinners and thus avoid the fellowship of sinners, as if they were not even touching the vessels they had touched.

But much more they prepared through such customs to flee from sin itself.

But those who carefully observed these customs, while themselves seizing and violently gaining profit, became abominations through their works. 'Therefore, flee from injustice, O blind Pharisee, not even seeing what you do' (Mt 23, 25-26), he says; 'and clean to you are the things in the cup and in the dish, if they are not taken through injustice.

Much better is the vessel cleansed by righteousness beside the water.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The hypocrites speak words of light while planning deeds of darkness, and the outside of the cup cannot be clean unless the inside is.
comments.comment: They devise deeds worthy of darkness within, yet through their outward parts they bring forth words that seem to be full of light. For they are truly wolves who have put on sheep's clothing (Matthew 7:15). They wash only the outside of the cup and dish (Matthew 23:25), not knowing that unless the inside is cleansed, the outside cannot become clean.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture of the cup washed only on the outside.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The sons of the prophets' killers honored the prophets with tombs and so condemned their own fathers.
comments.comment: Let us search carefully what the Savior says. The Jews’ fathers killed the holy prophets in their times, who were ferrying the divine word to them. Those born from them, confessing that the prophets were august and honorable, fitted crowns around them — that is, tombs (Matthew 23:29–36) — assigning the honor most fitting to the holy, and by believing them prophets and holy men they became judges of those who killed them. For by the very means they chose to honor the slain, through those means they accuse their fathers as having acted impiously.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how honoring the prophets' tombs condemns the fathers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who blamed their fathers' bloodshed were about to commit worse, killing the Author of life and his disciples.
comments.comment: But those who condemned their own fathers for such terrible bloodshed were about to be caught by equal evils — rather, by still worse. They “killed the Author of life,” (Acts 3:15) and added to the impieties against him other bloodsheds against his marvelous disciples. For as long as someone examines others’ injustices judging by natural reasoning, he sees what is base and blames it; but when he himself is led into the same passions, he is carried upon them as if blind.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The names are the same as the prophets, sages and scribes of old, but they are spiritual teachers sent by God, who alone can give the Spirit.
comments.comment:
Those having spiritual wisdom, which Paul says, and scribes who interpret the old things newly, so that the names are the same as with the prophets and sages and scribes of old, but the things themselves are not the same; for neither is the prophecy, nor the wisdom, nor the scribal art about the same things.

But he who said 'I will send' showed the divine; for it is God's to send prophets and sages and scribes, the one capable of giving the Spirit of prophecy and wisdom and knowledge.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The justice for all blood falls on the last generation because the judge's long patience ended on those who killed the Lord of all.
comments.comment:
In what manner will the justice for every blood come upon the last generation of the murderers (Matthew 23:35–36) — though God says through the prophet, “Fathers shall not die for children,” (Deuteronomy 24:16) and again the reverse, “each shall die by his own sin”? What then do we say? How will those to whom Christ spoke these things be made to give account for others’ bloodshed? Will Cain not be punished for Abel? And Lamech saying, “I have killed a man for my wound and a youth for my bruise” (Genesis 4:23)? So if each is weighed down by his own evils, how will the wretched undergo justice on behalf of all? For “God is not unjust,” but is a just and strong and long-suffering judge, according to what is written.

We say, then, that some such sense fits what was said. Suppose something like this: robbers arise in a certain country. They plunder the villages round about and kill those in them. The ruler of the province does not at once bare the ruling sword against them, but is eager rather to reform them by threats. They are no less cruel. So that the horror may at last be turned back, when some are caught he does not spare them, but subjecting them to most cruel tortures he sets the final danger upon them — not indignant only at those last crimes, but much more because the wildness of the first ones also deceived him while he was long-suffering. I think one of those last who were harshly punished will say that they themselves received everyone’s sins, because the judge’s anger ended upon them.

You will think something like this also about God. Having been long-suffering in the previous times, he was reasoning up to these that the measure of long-suffering must be defined; for the divine anger also had to strike upon these. The earlier ones were sinning against humans and fellow-slaves; but these have killed the Lord of all. He is not harsh because he punishes the last, but marvelous because he endured until the present.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the last generation answers for all the blood shed.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "This generation" means the whole race of murderers, since scripture names like manners a generation.
comments.comment: If someone wants, because the Lord said “this generation,” (Matthew 23:36) not only those to whom the word was addressed to be indicated, but as it were the whole race of the murderers, he leaves what is right. For we find holy scripture naming like manners and, as it were, same counsels as a “generation.” Blessed David said, “A generation of the upright will be blessed,” (Psalm 112:2) and “This is the generation of those seeking the Lord.” (Psalm 24:6) So “this,” even if said demonstratively, we say does not indicate only those then present and hearing, but every murderer and the whole race falling under the same impiety; for like will be ranked with like as brother and same-kin.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He charges Jerusalem as a murderer because she killed the prophets and stoned those sent, though many times she could have received mercy.
comments.comment:
On account of which he was about to bring wounds upon her because she is a murderer (Mt 23, 37).

Therefore he charges her as a murderer; for she, he says, is killing the prophets and stoning those sent to her, and because she, being able many times to receive mercy, was not willing; for it showed many times and many generations …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The picture of wings shows what is fitting for God, as Moses and David also say.
comments.comment: Having said this he shows what is God-befitting in himself even while in human form. For Moses also said about God, “Spreading his wings he received them” (Deuteronomy 32:11) (Matthew 23:37); and again David, “But the sons of humans will hope in the shelter of your wings.” (Psalm 36:7)
comments.selected_reason: Shows that the hen's wings echo how Moses and David speak of God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God gathers his people under his wings like a motherly bird, but they scattered themselves by sin.
comments.comment:
After He brought the people back from captivity, they were scattering themselves through sins.

He teaches the God-befitting thing by speaking of wings and shelter, as it was said by Moses concerning God: 'He received them under His wings' (Deut 32:11); and by David: 'the children of men hope in the shelter of Your wings' (Ps 36:7).

For since Satan was scattering them, partly into idolatry and partly into loves of pleasure, He sent prophets, and then came through Himself so as to 'gather' them 'into one.'

But they did not endure to be under His shelter; for He says, 'As a devoted bird, I always had you, drawing you back toward myself, but you did not want to, but were scattering yourself through sinning, casting yourself away from God.'

But the bird is motherly and warm in love, caring for the children and giving herself up for them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God wishes to gather all, but he does not force the good, since forced good is not good.
comments.comment: For he says that he wished to gather all men into the knowledge of truth, as a bird gathers its young under its wings, but you did not wish to (Matt 23:37). For necessity does not force the good to become so, nor is it possible; for such a thing is no longer good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'you were not willing' shows about God and human choice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The house was left when the people added the killing of the Christ of God to their fathers' sins.
comments.comment: Before his sojourn many sins had indeed come to the people, but not of such a kind that they should be abandoned altogether and handed over to a long captivity. But when they filled up 'the measure of their fathers' … and added to killing the prophets and pursuing the righteous the killing of 'the Christ of God,' then what was spoken came to be: 'Your house is left to you.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the house is left desolate.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: After the nations come in, believing Jews will see Christ's divinity and say he is the redeemer foretold, who came in the Lord's name as no other prophet did.
comments.comment: What was said has an intelligible sight through faith. For when “the fullness of the nations enters” (Romans 11:25) and they believe in Christ, then the Jews who believe after that see the beauty of Christ’s divinity, beholding the Father to be in the Son, and saying that he is the redeemer proclaimed through the prophets, of whom the prophet foretold as coming in the Lord’s name. For the other prophets did not come in the Lord’s name; they were saying, “Thus says the Lord,” and “I am a slave of the Lord, and I worship the God of heaven.” (Matthew 23:39)
comments.selected_reason: Explains when and how the Jews will say 'Blessed is he who comes'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By going out from the temple Christ shows divine grace leaving the Jews for others, as the ruined sanctuary later proved.
comments.comment: Having said, “Your house is left to you,” (Matthew 23:38–24:1) he does the matching act: he goes out from the temple and walks on, and by this shows the departure of divine grace from the Jewish race as it transfers to others. He used strong language; yet it also came about in deed when the sanctuary was utterly ruined.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ leaves the temple.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ turns aside from admiring the temple to foretell its fall to the Roman army, as a penalty for killing the Lord.
comments.comment: Some were showing Christ the great works in the temple and the adornment of the offerings; for they supposed he would marvel with them at what was seen — though he is God and has heaven as his throne. He sets aside talk about those things, but has foretold that it will fall from its foundations in due times, when the Roman army brings it to that end and all Jerusalem exacts from Israel the penalties for killing the Lord. For after the Savior’s cross these things happened to them to suffer, yet they did not understand the force of what was said. They supposed he was weaving words about the completion of the age. So they asked when these things would be, and what the sign would be when it was about to happen (Luke 21:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what prompts the prediction of the temple's fall.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: False christs and false prophets will appear before his descent, and the disciples must not follow them.
comments.comment: The Lord follows the aim of those who bring the question, and for now speaks about the completion of the present age. For before his descent from the heavens takes place, some forerunners will appear — false christs and false prophets molding his face around themselves — but do not follow them, he says (Matthew 24:4–5).
comments.selected_reason: Says who the many coming in his name are and what to do.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We should pray not to leave the body idle of good work, which the sabbath hints, or unfruitful, which winter shows.
comments.comment: Perhaps the word also has a riddle, so that we should pray not to depart from the body either while idle of good work — which the sabbath hints — or in unfruitfulness — which winter makes clear. For it should be noted that God did not make a winter of evils; yet we are in winter whenever the passions of the flesh dominate in us. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus warned the disciples against those who proclaim themselves the Christ and try to turn them with illusions.
comments.comment: Jesus, then, was turning his disciples away, not from heeding sorcerers in general and those who promise to work wonders by any means whatever (for his disciples had no need of that), but from those who proclaim themselves to be the Christ of God and try, by certain illusions, to turn the disciples of Jesus to themselves, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains whom the warning about false christs targets.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wilderness recalls John and the treasuries Christ's birth in a cave.
comments.comment:
He speaks of the wilderness because John lived in the wilderness so much (Matthew 24:26); and of the treasuries because Christ was born in a cave and a small hut at the first appearance (Mt 24:26).

He says he contrasts the inhabited world with the desolate wilderness through the treasuries (Mt 24:26).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ's first appearance moved from place to place, but his second will be manifest to all like lightning, and the saints will be gathered as eagles to a corpse.
comments.comment:
For just as eagles tear at a dead animal to be fed, so when Christ appears, the saints will be drawn to Him (Mt 24:27-28).

For it will not be as at the first appearance, moving from place to place through the flesh during the transition, but at the second, His appearance will be manifest to all 'in the twinkling of an eye' (Mt 24:27), like a lightning bolt that does not need to be signaled.

And immediately all the saints, having grown wings like eagles, are gathered to Him; for where Jesus fell as a corpse according to the economy of suffering, in order that He might raise those who fell, all will be gathered together …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The eagles are a likeness for the angels and saints who suddenly appear from the unseen at his glorious coming, being high and heavenly in mind.
comments.comment: … a certain likeness and a parable and an example has been spoken; for just as, when a carcass and a dead body is found lying, eagles and other flesh-eating birds are suddenly lifted up from the unseen to be fed, being carried from those high places through the air, so also, he says, the presence of the Son of Man shall be. For his appearing again upon the earth according to the second and glorious presence to judge the inhabited world, and angels in host, wielding spears, shall be manifest, and all the saints, being moved, 'in an instant, in the blink of an eye' (1 Cor 15:52) according to the last trumpet, as the apostle says, just as certain birds, eagles, being swift in movement, shall appear from the unseen; most fittingly being likened to eagles because of thinking the high and heavenly things and being worthy to live the citizenship of the kingdom of heaven.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The eagles are those lifted above earthly things who will run together to the Son of Man when he arrives.
comments.comment: Just as when a dead body lies there the flesh-eating birds run together upon it, so, when the Son of Man arrives, then all the eagles — that is, those who fly into the heights and highest places and have been lifted above earthly and worldly things — will run together to him (Matthew 24:28).
comments.selected_reason: Says who the eagles are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Heaven and earth will be re-elemented at God's will, so the sun and moon darken and stars fall, as the creation is renewed with humanity.
comments.comment: How will they not shudder? For as heaven and earth are re-elemented toward what seems good to God (it is not possible to say something precise in such matters), the sun and the moon will be darkened, and the stars will fall like flowers, while the one who created them re-elements them again as he wills; the elements themselves will also be disturbed. For as humanity is renewed, the creation made because of the human is also recapitulated and co-created (Matthew 24:29).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the darkening of sun and moon as the renewal of creation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son of Man comes in glory and power, and the saints and angels shine with him as his army.
comments.comment: The present voice [Zechariah's prophecy] is able to signify a second and glorious appearance of the Savior, concerning which John in Revelation spoke highly and God-appropriately thus: 'Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, and those who pierced him' (Rev 1:7). This understanding is based on what the Savior said concerning himself: 'Clouds shall see the Son of Man coming upon the clouds of heaven with much power and glory' (Matt 24:30). For how could he who comes royally not shine with much glory? And he comes also with much power, with the saints coming with him, not of men alone but also of angels. For it follows that 'those having become his attendants and servants' and 'the ministering spirits sent for service' shall shine with him, so that he himself may be known as their king and they as his powers, that is, an army.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the coming on the clouds with power and glory means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sending angels shows divinity.
comments.comment: … for angels are of God, and to send them is God's own.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ checks the disciples' curiosity by saying that as a man he does not know.
comments.comment: Since the disciples wanted to learn things beyond themselves, he finds an opening to check them from such inquiries in not knowing insofar as he is human, and he says that not even the holy angels in heaven can know these things (Matthew 24:36).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ declines idle curiosity by saying that even angels and the Son as man do not know, because he wants the disciples busy with what is fitting.
comments.comment: It was the Savior Christ’s custom to do something like this with his holy disciples especially: if they inquired into things that had a reputation for love of learning yet were free of higher searching, he would grant the account and try to make it exact with fine care. But if they wanted to learn over-again things beyond the measure that fits them, he would wrap the matter quietly and strongly persuade them to choose busying themselves with what is more fitting. So since the disciples wanted to learn things beyond them, he usefully pretends not to know insofar as he is human, and says that not even the holy angels in heaven know, so that they may not be grieved as if not trusted with what is moderate. And see how he persuades them to be quiet with his own reasonings and puts them to shame: that the Father has not revealed it even to angels, nor was it made known to the Son himself (Matthew 24:36).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ says he does not know the day.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Not knowing does not divide the Son from the Father, because ignorance is a passion the Son does not have, and what the Father knows the Son knows.
comments.comment: Even if the completion was clear, what would they not have done? If the Son is the wisdom of the Father, and if what he himself knows wisdom does not know, he is found again not knowing — or else his nature is better than his wisdom, and the simple God is found composite and unlike himself. Yet not-knowing and knowing do not make a difference of essence, any more than they do among humans; ignorance is a passion, which the Son does not have, but he is God by nature and, even on the heretics’ terms, unreceptive of passions. But if all that is the Son’s is the Father’s and all that is the Father’s is the Son’s, either both do not know, or the Father knows and the Son knows as having by nature all that is the Father’s. For he does not say this about lordship over creatures; yet whenever scripture names “Father,” (Matthew 24:36) it signifies the whole of the divinity thought and worshipped in the holy Trinity.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son's not knowing is a human way of speaking, since the Father's wisdom cannot be ignorant of what is hidden in it.
comments.comment: You have learned to confess one Christ, the Word of God made flesh — that is, become human. How then did he not know the day of the consummation? We say that for the creation not to know the mysteries in God is neither unusual nor otherwise unfitting: “For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11:34) according to what is written. And if the Son is said to have been made a little lower than angels (Hebrews 2:9) — clearly insofar as he became human, though he is beyond all creation in a divine way — what wonder if he is also said, together with the angels, not to know the mystery in God, though he is the Father’s wisdom and power (1 Corinthians 1:24)? Then how would the Father’s wisdom not know what is hidden in him? And if the Spirit is said to “search all things, even the depths of God,” (1 Corinthians 2:10) and the Spirit is Christ’s, how would he himself not know what his Spirit knows exactly? So even if he is said not to know in a human way, yet he knows in a divine way. And so, asking “Where have you laid Lazarus?” (John 11:34) as if it were possible for him not to know according to the human, he worked in a divine way, raising him from the dead.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: As the flood destroyed the world, the ungodly will be destroyed when the elements dissolve into fire.
comments.comment: Just as the world then was destroyed, being overwhelmed by the flood, so the ungodly and sinners will be utterly destroyed when the elements of the heavens and the earth are dissolved into fire; that is, the similarity is that they will perish just as those who perished in the flood. For the Lord says, 'As it was in the days of Noah, they were eating, drinking, marrying, being given in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark and the flood came and swept them all away, so will the coming of the Son of Man be' (Matt 24:37-39). Adding more to explain that it will be so, He says that the day of judgment will come stealing like a thief, in which the heavens will pass away swiftly and unexpectedly, the elements being removed by the approaching fire; after which the heavens having passed away in a rushing manner, there will be new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness and the promises of God hold dominion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the days of Noah are compared to.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saved are taken and the destroyed left, and the women grinding are teachers who make scripture easy to take in.
comments.comment: See that the word divides humans into two ranks — the saved and the destroyed. He says the saved are taken along, and the destroyed are left, that is, rejected. By “field” (Matthew 24:40–41) here understand the world, where “the one sowing to the Spirit harvests eternal life, and the one sowing to the flesh, corruption.” (Galatians 6:8) He likens teachers to the women grinding, who in a way thin out the scriptural thoughts and set the divine oracles before humans as easily accepted and easily understood. For the law also, commanding that a millstone or upper millstone not be taken in pledge so that someone who takes the tools of food may not hinder those fed through them, indicates teachers in a riddle. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is taken, who is left, and the grinding women.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The faithful, prudent steward who shares the master's kingdom is the right teacher, who is rare and precious.
comments.comment: Faithful in teachings, prudent in work, and a most reasonable steward of fellow-slaves: for such a one will share in the master’s whole kingdom. That is what “he will set him over all his belongings” (Matthew 24:45–47) makes clear. He does not say who this is, but speaks indefinitely, to show how scarce and precious right teachers are. He rightly requires both; if either is missing, the other limps.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the faithful and wise servant is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Careless teachers who live in luxury will be cut off from the Spirit received in their ministry and handed over to punishment.
comments.comment: The word is against leaders who spend their time in luxuries. For he named the careless teacher a bad and wicked slave, who, because the judge is absent and not seen through long-suffering, strikes those under his hand bitterly and mixes with flesh-lovers. For those who sin as if the judge were not present and as if they were not reckoning on judgment. By some of them being struck he shows those harmed in soul by the leaders’ luxury, as the apostle says: “Thus sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience.” (1 Corinthians 8:12) So he threatens those living in luxury with undergoing the last things. For he splits him and divides him from himself with pains by his living word — from the Spirit united to him in the age, that is, the divine gift. Those who pretend to think right things but do not think as they ought, wearing virtue only by outward shape, will be cut in two on the fearful day of judgment, which is lasting alienation from the Spirit. For now, even if it has not been mixed into the unworthy, it somehow seems present to those once sealed, awaiting the salvation that comes from their turning. Then it will be cut off from the whole soul that profaned its gift, and his portion will be set with the hypocrites. By “hypocrites” (Matthew 24:48–51) he means those who try to teach what is right, yet through what they do harm the disciples more. So, he says, for those who will not use in the present life as they ought the ministry entrusted to them by the Lord, he will not only add nothing further, but taking away the participation in the Spirit already come to be in them — which they obtained when appointed to church ministry — he will thus hand them over to punishment. For it is not possible for someone to be handed over to punishment together with the Spirit; he does not hint a bodily cut, but the stripping of the Spirit’s adoption. So they are punished for what they were laughing at, and they will “gnash their teeth,” …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To be cut in two is to lose the Spirit given back to us in Christ, since no one can be punished together with the Spirit.
comments.comment: Let us examine what it is to be cut in two (Matthew 24:51). When Adam came to be in the beginnings of punishment — God, giving nature its most complete beauty, makes him sharer of his own Spirit. For “he breathed into his face a breath of life” (Genesis 2:7); for what truly gives life is the Spirit of life, that is, of Christ. But since he slipped from deceit into sin, the Spirit was removed. When God and Father was pleased “to recapitulate all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10) and to bring human nature back up into its ancient beauty, we received back through grace what the intrusion of sin had damaged in us. For Christ breathed into us after the resurrection, renewing us into the ancient beauty: “Receive,” (John 20:22) he says, “holy Spirit.” So the Spirit is united to us; for “the one cleaving to the Lord is one spirit.” (1 Corinthians 6:17) Therefore, if we are found at the end in efforts according to piety, we receive back the fullness — now having the Spirit as in the order of a pledge — but if we are accused in sins we are damaged even of the Spirit’s pledge itself; for it is cut off and departs, as it were, at the time of judgment. And this, we say, is the cutting in two of which he speaks here; for it is not possible for someone to be given over to punishment together with the Spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being cut in two means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one is punished together with the Spirit.
comments.comment: In the time of the completion the Holy Spirit is taken away; for it is not possible for someone to be given over to punishment together with the Spirit (Matthew 24:51).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ten virgins stand for the souls of every age, wise and foolish, all lit by God's natural and written law.
comments.comment: He likens the leaders of the peoples to virgins. … Since scripture customarily divides all of life into five, he assigns to each time both holy and foolish souls, as each time has wise and simple, just and unjust. In that they all went out with the lamps, he shows that all souls were illumined by God with natural and innate laws, and also with the written laws through Moses. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All go out to meet God, but only those who add the oil of good works keep their light burning.
comments.comment: … And all went out to meet the bridegroom — that is, all set themselves to please God and to be joined spiritually to the bridegroom who sows in the hearts of the faithful every form of virtue, which is why he is also called bridegroom. Yet some, though having the illumination from God, did not endure to live reasonably — which the prudent souls did, through good works making the illuminating grace given them from within by God shine out still more, … By oil understand good love of work, which the idle do not have; when it is absent, the divine illumination in us passes over toward what is less beautiful. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the lamps and the oil mean in the parable.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sleep is the death of the flesh, which comes on everyone until the trumpet.
comments.comment: … He likens to sleep, and calls drowsiness, the death of the flesh, which of necessity comes upon both the prudent and the senseless, whom the angels’ trumpet raises at the time of Christ’s presence. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why all ten virgins fall asleep.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: At the resurrection each must account for his own life, and no one can be saved on another's virtue.
comments.comment: … For all are raised when death is abolished, good and bad, and all are prepared for defense before the judge — that is, to arrange the lamps as each reckons his own life. When the base bring nothing along, the soul begins to be gloomy and as if quenched and to go into madness, so that they think they will be mercied through others’ virtue. That is why they are rejected when those say, “Perhaps it will not suffice for us and for you.” (Matthew 25:1–13) For each person’s virtue will scarcely suffice for the soul’s salvation, …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The foolish virgins are refused because no one can be saved through another's virtue, or without working at his own.
comments.comment: Souls that neglect virtue wither and are as if quenched, and they go into madness, having thought that at the Savior’s second presence they can be saved without the working of the virtues. That is why they are also rejected by the prudent who say to them, “Perhaps it will not suffice for us and for you.” (Matthew 25:8–9) For this indicates here that someone can scarcely ever be saved through his own virtue, and certainly not through that of others; for it is foolish that someone who does not work should have received the wage of the working.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the wise virgins will not share their oil.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sellers are the prophets, apostles and teachers who teach virtue, but no time remained.
comments.comment: … “But go to those who sell” — who are prophets, apostles, evangelists, through whom one learns to work virtue, and right teachers of right doctrines. When they went away readily, the time did not allow it, making examination of what had been lived and not giving a beginning of working. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The bridegroom does not open or know them because they cared for themselves too late and lived by faith without works, or works without faith.
comments.comment: So because of the frankness that belongs to virginity they ask that it be opened to them. And he does not open, because in due time they did not care for themselves. And this is “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:11–12): for he knows those who not only show faith but also have works; but those who have lived by only one of the two have never even come into knowledge of the bridegroom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the door stays shut and what 'I do not know you' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The householder is God, his journey is Christ's ascent, and the talents are spiritual gifts given to his servants according to their understanding.
comments.comment: The “man” (Matthew 25:14–30) who is a householder is the creator and Lord of this whole world. The word of the parable likens his journey either to Christ’s ascent into the heavens or to the unseen and out-of-sight character of the divine nature. By God’s “belongings” understand those in each country and city who have believed in him. He calls “his slaves” those whom Christ in due times crowns with the boast of priesthood; for the inspired Paul writes, “No one takes the honor for himself, but the one called by God.” (Hebrews 5:4) To these he hands over those who have come under him, giving a spiritual gift to each according to the mind and fitness he has. We say this is the distribution of the talents, not supplied to the household servants in equal measure because of the difference of understanding. …
comments.selected_reason: Says who the man, the slaves and the talents stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The time from the ascension to Christ's return is the going abroad, and the talents are differing ministries given according to ability.
comments.comment: He calls the period from the ascension into the heavens until his own presence an 'abroad-going' (Mt 25:14–18), in which it seems for us to remain. The 'immediately' signifies the urgency, as it is necessary to work the things of God. The difference between five talents and two talents and one is that of ministry, so to speak—bishop, presbyter, deacon; for the amount of the talent shows more or less of the ministry. Therefore he rightly said to each according to his own power, so that it might happen that each is able to fulfill the ministry in proportion to what was entrusted to him; for he wishes to show that he also requires readiness from all, and he is rewarded similarly.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: God's gifts are shared out in proportion to each person's capacity, as a trainer feeds athletes unequally, and so the talents were given.
comments.comment: … If, for example, a trainer provides food to athletes and to those around the contest—for he also has others like bodyguards—he gives to each according to a proportion: to one athlete seven pounds of meat—and this is his portion—to another four; and to the one not competing, he gives two. Thus, a portion is given to each according to his power and his capacity. In this way also the parable of the talents in the Gospel occurred. He gave to each of his slaves his own silver, 'to each according to his own ability, to the one five, to the other two, and to the other one' (Matthew 25:15). …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain picture of why the talents are unequal.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Each received according to an ability he had prepared by choice, not by nature, and the one who buried his talent neither worked nor earned interest.
comments.comment: … And take for me the parable of the Gospel concerning the talents: 'to each according to his own ability' Matt 25:15 he gave the rational things belonging to him, not to each according to his nature, but according to the ability which he himself had prepared by choice. 'And to the one he gave five, to the other two, to the other one' Matt 25:15. 'The one having received five talents worked with them' Matt 25:16 and doubled them. Having borrowed, he paid back. The one with two likewise. The one having received the one and having buried it in the earth, neither worked with it nor gave interest, he hid it in the earth Matt 25:18. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Work for God should start at once, and burying the talent means keeping the gift idle and useless to others.
comments.comment: … “Straightway” they went and worked, he says — the “straightway” here signifying to us that it would be fitting to work the things of God without any delay. Those held by hesitation and idleness will be in the worst evils. For he buried, he says, the talent given to him in the earth — that is, he kept the gift idle in himself and useless to others. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'straightway' and the buried talent.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The faithful servant is rewarded for benefiting others; the other is condemned for not displaying what he owed.
comments.comment: To show the doubling of what was given, he calls the displaying of what is proper with haste to be the cause of becoming a benefit to others (Mt 25:20–25), instead of which he says he will make him ruler over many as a fitting reward: 'for this is that I will make you ruler over many' (Mt 25:21). To condemn, he said it is the not displaying of what is due, but working the given grace as if it were vanished.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The slave blames the master's demanding command for his failure to act.
comments.comment: Regarding Matthew 25:24, 'Hard,' he says, 'is your command, to seek obedience from men, to whom you did not make the hearing easy through the word. Therefore, fearing that I might become ineffective, I kept only what was for myself, and did not strive concerning others.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the servant's excuse in the parable of the talents.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The gift goes to the one who worked, since the Spirit leaves the idle.
comments.comment: … So the talent is taken from him and will be given to the one who is rich; for the Spirit and the giving of the divine gifts will depart from such people, while for those who have worked lovingly there will be a richer increase of gifts. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the talent goes to the one who has most.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: John places the last supper before the Passover feast, and Matthew's 'first of the unleavened' is read the same way.
comments.comment: It was the custom of those eating the Passover, and they were dining. And John has said nothing of a remembrance of the Passover, having made it by saying: 'Before the feast of the Passover, Jesus knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end' (John 13:1) and the following. 'Before the feast of the Passover' he says, not in the feast of the Passover, so that we also received 'the first of the unleavened' (Matthew 26:17) naturally, having understood it as before the unleavened. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus named neither house nor man so Judas could not betray him early.
comments.comment: So that the betrayer might not hand him over to his killers “before the feast of the Passover,” (Matthew 26:18) the Savior disclosed neither the house nor the man with whom he fulfilled the Passover (John 13:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus gives no name or address for the Passover room.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'So-and-so' hides a name on purpose and fits every holy person who first receives the disciples and then Christ.
comments.comment: By saying “so-and-so” (Matthew 26:18) he does not make a name clear specifically, but obliquely indicates one of the holy. For the word also fits every holy person, who first receives the Lord’s disciples — evangelists and apostles leveling his soul beforehand — and then Christ himself, who will come not as one called but of his own accord, dwelling with the Holy Spirit beside the one with whom he sees the holy baptism. For that is what “the man carrying the jar of water” (Mark 14:13) makes clear, as Mark and Luke say (Luke 22:10).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Foretelling that Judas would betray him did not make Jesus the cause, since he foresaw what Judas's own wicked character would dare.
comments.comment:
… Celsus thinks that what is prophesied by some kind of foreknowledge comes to pass because it was prophesied. We do not grant this. We say that the one who prophesied is not the cause of what will be on the ground that he foretold it would happen; rather, what will be, which would have been even if it had not been prophesied, gave the one who foreknew it the cause for foretelling it. And all of this lies within the foreknowledge of the one who prophesies it: when it is possible for a given thing to happen and possible also for it not to happen, one particular one of the two will come about. …

For it did not follow from Jesus’ having truly foretold what concerned the traitor, or what concerned the one who denied him, that he himself became the cause of their impiety and unholy deed. He who, as we hold, knew “what was in man” (John 2:25) saw the traitor’s wicked character, and saw what he would dare because he loved money and did not hold firmly to what he ought to think about his teacher; and so, among many other things, he said this too: “He who has dipped his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me” (Matthew 26:23).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Dipping the hand in the bowl does not single Judas out from the others but names the betrayer as a close table-mate, as David foretold.
