comments.comment: We will not surely understand from this that none of the other disciples, but only Judas, dipped the morsel in the bowl with him. I think what was said has some such sense: he wants to say, as is likely, that the betrayer will be the one who dipped his hand with me in the bowl (Matthew 26:23) — that is, the fellow diner and table-mate, sharer and participant of table and of salt. For thus he also was accusing him through the voice of blessed David, saying, “But you, man of equal soul, who sweetened foods for me at the same table.” (Psalm 55:13) And again, “He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me.” (Psalm 41:9) John made this very point more clearly; for he said the Lord had said, “It is that one to whom I will give the morsel when I have dipped it.” (John 13:26)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'dipped his hand with me in the bowl' points to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Not born' does not mean the unborn feel anything, but that non-existence is better than misery.
comments.comment: Not as if some good or base thing somehow belonged to those not yet born, who are outside sensation (it is still utterly silly to think thus), but that for those about to fall into all misery, if they should be brought into being by God, non-existence is surely much and incomparably better (Matthew 26:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the saying 'it would have been better for that man not to have been born'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Never to have existed is better than a bad existence, and Judas, the Christ-killer's servant, could not share the saving communion.
comments.comment: … It has been said that the good thing is not to have come to execution (Mt 26:24); for non-existence is a preferable state from a bad existence. When Judas went out, John made it manifest; for the servant of the Christ-killer would not have accepted the saving communion; even though the Lord brought him through all other things, but this no longer was permitted. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The church should likewise exclude the wicked from holy communion, as Judas went out after the morsel.
comments.comment: … And for us the type is to expose the wicked regarding the holy communion, even if we bear them through all other things by forbearance; for it is clear that he would kill the Savior, 'he went out' (John 13:27) after being delivered to the devil; for 'after the morsel he entered,' he says, 'into him the Satan' (John 13:27), so as having taken him, he led him away as a traitor. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ gave his body and blood before going up to the Father so that we would still have his presence and life in us.
comments.comment: After Judas went out, the Savior handed over to the eleven the saving mystery. For a little later Christ was about, having risen with his own flesh, to go up to the Father, so that we might have the presence of his body — for without Christ’s presence it is impossible for a human to be saved and freed from death and sin if the Life is not with us. So he gave us his own body and blood, so that through them the power of corruption might also be destroyed, and that it might dwell in our souls through the Holy Spirit, and we might become sharers of sanctification and be called heavenly and spiritual humans. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ gave his body and blood at this supper.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's 'This is my body' and 'This is my blood' mean that the bread and wine are truly changed into his life-giving body and blood, to be received by faith.
comments.comment:
The Lord gives thanks when he takes the cup — that is, in the form of prayer he converses with God the Father, declaring him as it were sharer and co-approver of the life-giving blessing that will be given to us, and at the same time giving us a pattern first to give thanks and thus to break the bread and distribute it. That is why we too, setting what was said before God’s face, beg intently that it be remolded for us into the spiritual blessing, so that by partaking of them we may be sanctified bodily and spiritually.

He said demonstratively, “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26–28) and “This is my blood,” so that you may not think what appears is a mere type, but that through some ineffable energy of the God who can do all things what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ — of which, when we partake, we take in Christ’s life-giving and sanctifying power. For it was necessary that he be mingled in us in a God-befitting way through the Holy Spirit, as it were with our bodies through his holy flesh and precious blood. And these we have also received as a life-giving blessing in bread and wine, so that we may not shrink when we see flesh and blood lying before us on the holy tables of the churches. For God, adjusting himself to our weaknesses, sends into what lies before us a power of life and transfers them toward the energy of his own life. And do not doubt that this is true when he says clearly, “This is my body” and “This is my blood”; rather receive the Savior’s word by faith, for being truth he does not lie.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'This is my body' and 'This is my blood' mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ calls the types by the names of the truth so that we marvel at the power, and by eating and drinking we share through his body in God.
comments.comment: … He clearly distinguished the type by the name of the truth, saying: 'this is my body'; and for this reason he named the types with the names of the truth, so that they would not be trivialized by what is seen, but would marvel at the power. Thus, eating and drinking showed the participation which would not have occurred without a body; for if the divine power had not been joined to a body and unified by blood, we would not have had communion through it to God. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Many' stands for all, and through the one righteous man many are made righteous.
comments.comment: … And speaking of many, he says that the blood is being poured out, concerning all, he says that through the one righteous many shall be established (Mt 26:28). This indeed also here shows that one suffers on behalf of many. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The new drink is not new wine but a new gladness that Christ will give after the resurrection to each according to his measure.
comments.comment: “Until I drink it new in the kingdom” (Matthew 26:29): drinking wine does not fulfill need only, but also brings all-various pleasure to the sense. After the resurrection from the dead, when corruption has been shaken off from human bodies, the nature of things itself will also be transferred toward newness, so that our gladness itself may also be new. The mixture from wine is a symbol of temperance, which he also says will become new; and he does not at all say the drink itself will be new, but what results from it — that is, the gladness. For after the resurrection human nature will withdraw from its customary and earthly enjoyment, and will transfer toward a newness of delight that is clearly that of Christ our Savior of all, who sends his innate and own gladness into the souls of those who worship him and distributes it in proportion to each one’s measures. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'drink it new in the kingdom' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Kingdom of the Father is the resurrection.
comments.comment: He named the resurrection the Kingdom of the Father (Mt 26:29), from which both the kingdom approached him and this fellowship approached the rest of mankind.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: The disciples were troubled because it was hard to grasp why the one who raised the dead was handed over, and the Father struck him by allowing him to suffer.
comments.comment:
The disciples were troubled not as light people, but because the matter was full of much perplexity and the knowledge of this mystery was hard to grasp — how the one who raised the dead and did countless signs beyond human measure was handed over to so dishonorable a death. This was the one who had said through the prophet, “I will strike the shepherd.” (Zechariah 13:7) (Matthew 26:31) That is why David also says to the Father, “For the one whom you struck, they themselves pursued.” (Psalm 69:26)

Yet this did not happen entirely and wholly by the Father’s will; he wanted him not to suffer, if the Jews had accepted him. But since they did not receive him, the Father consented to the Son who chose to suffer this. That is why it is also said that the Father struck “the shepherd,” since he allowed him to suffer though able to prevent his suffering. The word said to Pilate by Christ is also to be understood thus: “You would have no authority at all against me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11) — instead of “the Father did not consent to me who chose to suffer.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Father is said to 'strike the shepherd'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By promising to go before them into Galilee, Christ announces the resurrection and his move from the Jews to the nations.
comments.comment: He did not leave the disciples to remain only as far as the gloomy things; he foretells the resurrection, loosing their grief, and promises to go before them into Galilee, by which he signifies that he is about to depart from the Jews and transfer to the nations. He does not appear from heaven immediately — which is also why he appeared there (Matthew 26:32).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ promises to go ahead into Galilee.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's agony in his human nature was real, so that the disciples would not think his passion unreal.
comments.comment: Even that must not be wondered at, how the Lord appears to be in agony according to the human nature (Mt 26:37), even though the disciples were rejoicing over those things which he had often suffered. Just as, being able to overcome death himself, he withdrew for the sake of the salvation of the world, so also, to struggle according to human nature, he continued struggling, persuading them not to think any passion to be something else, but truth, and especially being able to easily lead their understanding into that imminent resurrection.
comments.author: Theodore of Heraclea

comments.capsule: Christ's grief is that of the impassible Word who made the soul's and body's suffering his own, and it confirms the incarnation.
comments.comment: He is grieved as a human, and the impassible one makes his own what belongs to the soul and what belongs to the body. Since what belongs to humanity is common to him, just as what befits divinity alone has somehow also become common to the flesh through the ineffable and inexpressible union, let what happened scandalize no one; for the Word’s coming together with flesh, having suffered what is its own, will confirm well in us the mystery of the incarnation (Matthew 26:37–38).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Son of God can be grieved.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cup is death, and Christ's declining it exposes the lie that he chose to suffer so the crucifiers were only helping.
comments.comment: By “cup” in these things he calls the stupefaction through death and the drunkenness that as it were puts one to sleep toward sleep. Declining to drink it — that is, not making suffering very much according to pleasure — accuses the impiety of those who crucified him. For they may not surely say, “Since he chose to suffer, we are rather helpers of the will” (Matthew 26:39); for the declining will convict them of choosing to speak falsely.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus may be praying out of love for the Jews, that they not be abandoned for what they did to him.
comments.comment: … I know also an explanation of the passage along these lines. The Saviour saw what the people and Jerusalem would suffer in punishment for what the Jews had dared to do against him. For no other reason than his love for them, wishing the people not to suffer what they were about to suffer, he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” It is as if he were saying: Since, through my drinking this cup of punishment, a whole nation will be abandoned by you, I pray, if it is possible, that “this cup pass from me,” so that your portion, which has dared to act against me, may not be wholly abandoned by you. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prayer does not make the Savior a coward, since the same Lord says in the Psalms that he fears no one.
comments.comment: But likely someone, through the 'Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me,' (Matthew 26:39) will deem the Savior cowardly concerning death. To whom we must say that, if all Scripture is one instrument of one God, the same Lord who says 'let this cup pass' also says in the Psalms, 'The Lord is my light and my savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers drew near to eat my flesh, my tormentors and enemies fainted and fell. Though a camp stand against me, my heart shall not fear; though war rise against me, in this I hope.' (Psalm 27:1-3) And Matthew, Mark, Luke record the Gethsemane words diversely: 'let this pass from me' / 'bear away' / 'Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee; bear away this cup from me' (Mark 14:36) — and all add 'but not as I will.' …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ shows the weakness of the flesh in asking that the cup pass, and the willingness of the spirit in 'not as I will'.
comments.comment: We said earlier too that some sayings belong to the “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15) who was in Jesus, such as “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6) and others like it, while others belong to the man understood to be in him, such as “But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from the Father” (John 8:40). So here too, in his human nature, he portrays both the weakness of human flesh and the willingness of the spirit (Matthew 26:41): the weakness in “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” and the willingness of the spirit in “Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two halves of Christ's prayer in Gethsemane.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The single plea of the flesh comes first, the several sayings of the spirit follow, and the whole is said with reserve.
comments.comment: … And if we must also keep to the order of what was said, notice that what belongs, so to speak, to the weakness of the flesh comes first and is a single saying, while what belongs to the willingness of the spirit comes afterward and runs to several. The single saying is “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); the several are both “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39) and “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matthew 26:42). We should also observe that he did not say, “Let this cup go away from me,” but that the whole was said reverently and with humble reserve: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ repeats the same prayer as a pattern, since we should ask again and again, and the third prayer confirms he was truly human.
comments.comment: He intensifies the prayer and weaves through the same words, setting what concerns himself beside us as outline and pattern. For I think we must not offer a prayer only once according to eagerness, but rather approach frequently and not blush at repeating the same until our requests depart to an end for us. For this reason Christ also made a third prayer about the same things, though he knew the will of God the Father very clearly; rather, through the third he was confirming that he had become human (Matthew 26:42–44).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ prays the same words three times.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judas was not wholly against Jesus, and the pretence of a kiss shows some reverence still remained in him.
comments.comment: Next, that he was “betrayed by those he called his disciples,” the Jew in Celsus learned from the Gospels, though he turned the one man Judas into many disciples, so as to seem to make the charge greater. But he did not go on to examine all that is recorded about Judas: that Judas fell into conflicting and opposed judgements about his teacher, and was neither against him with his whole soul, nor kept with his whole soul a pupil’s reverence for his teacher. For “he who betrayed him gave a sign” to the crowd that had come to seize Jesus, “saying, ‘The one I kiss is the man; seize him’” (Matthew 26:48). In this he kept something of his reverence for him; for had he not kept it, he would have betrayed him openly, without the pretence of a kiss. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judas used a kiss, the sign of love, as a tool of deceit, and the 'Rejoice' was a lie from the liar within him.
comments.comment: Perhaps Judas thought he could escape notice, holding forth a kiss as a type of love while having a heart full of unholy plans. So he approaches Christ as from drunkenness, expecting to declare the exceptional virtue an instrument of deceit and of love, and he was also adding, “Rejoice, Rabbi.” (Matthew 26:47–50) Do you say “rejoice” to the one ensnared toward death through you? Are you not even ashamed of the shape of the betrayal? But from here one could see that, having the liar in himself — that is, Satan — he was also lying when he said “rejoice.” …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the deceit behind Judas's kiss and greeting.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus was not caught, because he gave himself up willingly as the Lamb of God, and he refused his disciple's sword.
comments.comment: … And since he says that he was also “caught,” I would reply that if being caught means being taken against one’s will, Jesus was not caught. For at the fitting time he did not prevent himself from coming into the hands of men, as “the Lamb of God,” so that he might take away “the sin of the world” (John 1:29). … Moreover, to the one who wanted to help him, who struck “the servant of the high priest” and cut off “his ear” (Matthew 26:51), he said: “Put your sword back into its place; for all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot now call on my Father, and he will set beside me here more than twelve legions of angels? How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen this way?” (Matthew 26:52–54). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Twelve legions' stands for 'you twelve disciples': Christ needs no help, but gives himself up as the scriptures foretold.
comments.comment: He said “twelve legions,” saying it instead of “you twelve disciples,” so that “I do not need your help; for I have not used the authority, but I give myself over to the Jews, since the scriptures foretold that this would be, that the Jews are about to do these things.” (Matthew 26:53)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is not blaming the leaders for being slow but showing that the arrest happened by his permission, since he accepted suffering to restore human nature.
comments.comment:
Does Christ then blame the Jewish leaders because they were not already laying an early snare of death for him? That is not what he means. Rather: though you could seize me day by day while I taught in the temple, you did not — for I was saving the need to suffer for the fitting time. So Christ did not say this as accusing Jewish madness, nor as rebuking their slowness toward bloodshed because they did not seize him at the outset when he was present and seen.

He convicts them rather that the arrest was not the work of power in them, but of his will, who economically accepted the unwanted suffering and made it willed — not because suffering was good in itself, but because what would follow from it was about to restore human nature to what it was from the beginning, showing that taking him was the work of his permission (Matthew 26:55).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Jesus means by 'Day after day I sat teaching and you did not seize me'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Caiaphas adjured Jesus so that silence would count as breaking the law and speech would be called false, and 'You have said it' is Christ's own confession.
comments.comment: God of all said somewhere through Moses: “If a soul sins and hears a voice of adjuration, and he is a witness or has seen or known, if he does not report it, he will receive the sin.” (Leviticus 5:1) So a charge of lawlessness was written against people if they answered nothing when they heard an adjuring voice. That is why Caiaphas craftily adjures the Lord: so that if he still wished to be silent after this, Caiaphas might condemn him as a transgressor — knowing that one adjured who stays silent becomes liable to the law’s penalty — but if he spoke the truth, they might kill him as a false christ for calling himself God while, in the flesh and what is seen, having nothing more than other humans. That is why Christ said, “You have said it” — instead of “your own mouth has now confessed it.” (Matthew 26:63–65) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the high priest puts Jesus under oath.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ sets his glory before them to make their judgment heavier, and Caiaphas tears his garments to make the charge fiercer.
comments.comment: … And so that he might make the judgment against them heavier — I mean the judgment on their unwillingness to believe in him — he again sets his glory plainly before them, saying, “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God.” “Me, who have become in the form that is yours, the Son by nature and truly of God the Father, you have made of no account; and since you have sunk to such ignorance that you do not know his mystery and mine, though you are learned in the law, I necessarily say this: that only a short and bounded time was given you for impiety against me, as far as the precious cross; for after this I will at once run back into my own honor, ascend to the glory that was in the beginning, and sit with God the Father even with the flesh.” While Christ said this, Caiaphas tore his garments, saying, “He has blasphemed.” He did this to make the accusation fiercer and to raise what was said by the act. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The King of kings is struck and mocked as one of us, as a pattern of extreme forbearance.
comments.comment: One might fittingly say what one of the holy prophets said: “Heaven was amazed at this and shuddered still more exceedingly, says the Lord,” (Jeremiah 2:12) the God of all, the King of those who reign and Lord of those who lord it. He is dishonored as one of us, endures being struck (Matthew 26:67–68), and undergoes the laugh of the impious, setting beside us a pattern of his extreme forbearance. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ endures being struck and mocked.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Jews mocked him as a prophet in a child's game.
comments.comment: … The Jews, playing at the Lord as if regarding the name of the prophet, were performing a child's game (Matthew 26:68), hence they were saying, 'Prophesy to us, Christ, who is he who struck you' …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who handed Jesus to Pilate were themselves handed over to Roman armies, as the prophets foretold.
comments.comment: They brought Jesus to Pilate — and they themselves were handed over to the Roman armies. And what was foretold about them through the holy prophets has been fulfilled. One says, “Woe to the lawless; evils will come upon him according to his works.” (Isaiah 3:11) Another: “As you did, so it will be to you; your recompense will be repaid on your head.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judas's repentance and confession show that Jesus's teaching had left some goodness in him, even as he betrayed him.
comments.comment:
… Will this not, then, persuade everyone concerning Judas’s purpose, that together with his love of money and his wicked purpose to betray his teacher, he had something mixed into his soul, planted in him by the words of Jesus, which bore the look of a remnant, so to speak, of goodness? For it is written: “When Judas, who betrayed him, saw that he was condemned, he repented and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying, ‘I have sinned in betraying righteous blood.’ But they said, ‘What is that to us? See to it yourself.’ And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he withdrew, and went away and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:3–5).

If Judas, the lover of money, who also stole what was put into “the money box” for the poor (John 12:6), “repented and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,” it is clear that the teachings of Jesus were able to produce some repentance in him, and had not been utterly despised and spat out by the traitor. Moreover, the words “I have sinned in betraying righteous blood” were those of a man confessing his sin. See how burning and violent a grief arose in him from repentance for his sins, so that he could no longer bear even to live, but threw the money “into the temple,” withdrew, went away and hanged himself. For he passed sentence on himself, and so showed how much the teaching of Jesus could do even in Judas, the sinner, the thief and the traitor, who could not utterly despise what he had learned from Jesus. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows what Judas's repentance in Matthew says about him.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judas did not die by strangling but lived on after it, as Acts says.
comments.comment: … Observe that Judas did not die from strangulation, but lived on after being driven to it before being suffocated. And the deeds of the apostles declare this, that 'having become rash he struck' (Acts 1:18) and the following. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus helped himself in the sense of virtue by his silence, as Isaiah foretold.
comments.comment: … We ask him: what does “helped himself” mean? If it refers to virtue, we shall say that he helped himself very much indeed. For he neither said nor did anything improper; but truly “he was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent” (Isaiah 53:7), and the Gospel testifies that “so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7; Matthew 27:12–14). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Choosing a robber and murderer over Christ proves how little justice mattered to them, and it made their punishment heavier.
comments.comment: These things are a great proof against the Jews, who chose a robber and murderer rather than Christ. So little did justice matter to them, and thus, for “piety,” they were accusing Christ. And though the one appointed to judge was freeing him, they urge a death verdict against the leader and teacher of all piety, and, so that they might undergo a still heavier punishment, they cried out, “Take this one; release Barabbas to us.” (Matthew 27:21–26) See clearly: they “denied the Holy and Righteous One,” as blessed Peter says, “and asked that a murderer be granted them,” (Acts 3:14) so that they would be sharers of that man’s portion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the choice of Barabbas shows.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Pilate gave over an innocent man and foolishly thought washing his hands would free him of the sin.
comments.comment: Pilate, neglecting right and just judgment, did not even reason that he was giving an innocent man over to death, though he was master of delivering him. And he washes his hands, having supposed that through this he was free of the sin — which is foolish to think. Perhaps, as a gentile, he imagined that the water itself sufficed for cleansing of sins (Matthew 27:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Pilate's hand-washing does not clear him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord blamed this outcry through Jeremiah, saying he had left his house to its enemies.
comments.comment: The Lord was blaming this unholy outcry of theirs (Matthew 27:25) through Jeremiah’s voice: “I have abandoned my house; I have left my inheritance; I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in a thicket; she raised her voice against me; therefore I hated her.” (Jeremiah 12:7–8) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Robe, crown of thorns and reed unknowingly pictured Christ's lifting up for the world's salvation, and the thorns he removes with his own head.
comments.comment: Because of this, those killing him, not understanding what they were doing, instead performed a symbol: this robe, which is the red garment of Joshua in Jesus, and the one who 'stretched out his hand' being one of the sons of Judah from Tamar, signifies the lifting up of the Savior for the salvation of all, against the blood of the world and the people in it. But those being suffocated by 'cares, wealth, and pleasures,' having taken the word of God and not bringing it to completion, crown Jesus with thorns, insulting him; but he, having taken up our thorns, dissipates them with his own head. And they put a reed in his right hand, supposing it to be his kingship. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The soldiers mocked him as a king with a red robe, thorn crown, reed and bowing, in a foolish game.
comments.comment: … but the soldiers play at the name of the king; for this is why there is a red robe instead of purple, a crown of thorns instead of gold, a reed instead of a scepter, and the bowing as to a king and saying, 'Hail, King of the Jews.' Upon which was also the spitting and the striking with the reed, which was a practice for training soldiers and a folly of a foolish people playing a game, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the soldiers give him robe, crown and reed.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Both Gospels are true: Christ bore the cross and Simon carried it later, and his rule upon his shoulder is the cross.
comments.comment: The Savior is led to the saving suffering. They laid his cross on Simon of Cyrene. Another of the holy evangelists also said that Jesus himself “bore” (John 19:17) the wood. Both are wholly true: the Savior bore the cross, and somewhere in the middle of the road they met the Cyrenean, seized him, and transferred the cross onto him. For it was said about him through Isaiah’s voice: “A child was born to us, a son also was given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder.” (Isaiah 9:6) For his rule became the cross, through which he has reigned over what is under heaven — if it is true that he “became obedient unto death, even death of a cross; therefore God also highly exalted him.” (Philippians 2:8–9)
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Simon carrying the cross fits John saying Jesus bore it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Adam was buried at the Place of the Skull, so Christ's death there brings life.
comments.comment: About the Place of the Skull it has come down to us that the Hebrews hand on that Adam’s body was buried there; and since “in Adam all die,” (1 Corinthians 15:22) Adam also rose, and “in Christ all will be made alive.” (1 Corinthians 15:22)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the link between the Place of the Skull and Adam.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gall and vinegar are the wickedness and baseness of plotters, which Christ tastes and will not drink.
comments.comment: … For those who plot against the word of truth always bring to the Christ of God the gall that comes from their own wickedness and the vinegar that comes from their own turning toward what is base; and he, “when he has tasted it, will not drink” (Matthew 27:34).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ crucified between robbers fulfills that God would be counted with the lawless in the judgment of lawless men.
comments.comment: … Second, we say that even these things were in some way foretold in the Gospels, since God “was numbered with the lawless” (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12) in the judgment of lawless men, who wanted rather a robber released, the one who had been thrown into prison “for sedition” “and murder” (Luke 23:18–19; John 18:40), and Jesus crucified, and who crucified him between two robbers (Matthew 27:38). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's suffering heals us and, among two robbers, shows him reckoned with the lawless, who stand for the two peoples.
comments.comment:
You saw how the Creator and Lord of all corrects his nature: bringing it back to what was in the beginning by becoming as we are, he underwent our sufferings for us, through us. Two robbers were hung with him when he hung on the cross — an insult, admittedly, as far as the Jews’ aim went, yet also a reminder of the prophecy that says, “And he was reckoned with the lawless.” (Isaiah 53:12) …

These two robbers were outlining the two peoples. One displayed senselessness to the end and would not even confess that the last captivity he underwent under the Romans was being borne as requital for the outrages against Christ. The other, at the very end, did not despair of forgiveness, but corrected the rawness of evils by theology. And the Lord’s undergoing the cross in the middle of the robbers revealed his voluntary death as his presence toward the two peoples — toward whom he was coming willingly, having willed to renew both by his own incarnation — even if the former people refused like the one robber, saying, “We have no king except Caesar,” (John 19:15) demanding the guiltless blood on their own head and exulting in the murder as just, from which both they and that robber alike fell out of the kingdom (John 19:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ is crucified between two robbers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One robber joined the mockers, but the other believed, rebuked them, confessed his sin and called the dying Christ king, and so won heaven.
comments.comment: One of the robbers, sharing the Jews’ lovelessness toward God, belched out the same words as they: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” (Luke 23:39) But the other, walking the opposite road, is fittingly marvelled at. He has believed in him though hung in so bitter a punishment; he rebukes the Jews’ loose-mouthedness and the co-hung man’s voices; he confessed the sin so that he might appear more just. For he bore witness that Christ was wholly without blame and was an accuser of the crucifiers’ madness; and so he seized the lot of the holy — the enrollment above and in the heavens. Seeing him crucified, he was calling him king; he expected the one in dishonor and suffering to come in God-befitting glory; he seized the faith though not raised in nobility — and he also benefits us, opening the heavens to us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two robbers' opposite responses.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The darkness was a sign that the one hung on the wood is the Lord of creation, and it fell on a country that rejected the true light.
comments.comment: Darkness came upon the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth, the sun failing, so that they might know that the one hung on the wood is that very one who took creation as ally for them when he warred against the Egyptians for their sake. The sun’s light failed, and darkness was scattered over their whole country, the sun drawing in its ray and as if no longer enduring to send it to those who had become killers of the Lord. And in another way we say the Jews’ country — or those who inhabit it — was darkened, because it did not receive the sun of righteousness and “the true light.” (John 1:9)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the darkness at noon.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A darkness at full moon cannot be an eclipse, so it shows creation mourning and the Jews' minds darkened.
comments.comment: … And Phlegon, a philosopher among the Greeks, remembers this darkness as having happened paradoxically on the fourteenth of the moon (Mt 27:45), when no eclipse usually occurs, when the interval from the sun is far, as from the beginning of the heaven to the end; for eclipses happen when these two luminaries approach one another; for a solar eclipse happens by the moon running to meet it, not at the full moon, when it is at the diameter of the moon. This happened as the creation was mourning over what occurred, and therefore making it manifest, that because this opposition was done by the Jews, their mind was darkened and the intelligible sun departed from them. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ cries 'my God' as a human, restoring our freedom to speak boldly to God, with no loss to his divinity.
comments.comment: The Lord spoke this cry as a human, so that he might set right for our human nature the freedom to say boldly to God, “Why have you abandoned me?” (Matthew 27:46) — for only the pure and those outside sin may say this without fear. And when he says “my God” to the Father, he undergoes no harm regarding his own divinity and glory, being God by nature, whenever as a human he says what befits humanity — since we too, if we call God Father, do not thereby cast off being humans by nature and creatures of God, even if by grace God calls us into sonship through faith in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Christ can say 'My God, why have you abandoned me?'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ speaks from our person, since he suffers for us, and it is we who were forsaken, not he.
comments.comment: … And when he says, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46), he speaks from our own person, because having taken the form of a servant and having become in the likeness of human beings, and having been found in appearance as a human being, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:7-8), and so on. And as Isaiah says, "He bears our weaknesses and suffers pain for us" (Isaiah 53:4), so that he does not suffer pain for himself but for us. And he was not forsaken by God, but we were; and for us who had been forsaken he came into the world. …
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: Jesus laid down his soul by his own authority, crying out and giving up the spirit before the executioners could break his legs.
comments.comment: … Now my Jesus said of his own soul, which was parted from the body not by the necessity common to men but by the extraordinary authority given to him over this also: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again” (John 10:18). For since he had “authority to lay it down,” he laid it down when he said, “Father, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34) and, “crying out with a loud voice, he gave up the spirit” (Matthew 27:50). In this he forestalled the executioners in charge of the crucified, who cut the legs of those crucified, and cut them for this reason, that they may not suffer punishment any longer (compare John 19:31–33). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Through Christ, souls released from bodies are no longer sent to Hades but into the hands of the living God.
comments.comment: Something great and exceptional was accomplished for our souls through Christ. Since we have been justified through faith in God, and in him human nature was found enriched with faultlessness, he has opened something new for us: that souls released from bodies no longer run into Hades as before, but are rather sent into the hands of the living God. Knowing this, holy Stephen said, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” (Acts 7:59) And another of the apostles writes, “So that those who suffer according to God’s will should also entrust their souls to a faithful Creator.” (1 Peter 4:19)
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Stephen and others can entrust their spirits to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The torn veil shows the temple mourning and the end of the law's shadow, and opens the holy of holies to all justified by faith.
comments.comment:
The tearing of the veil was no unclear sign that the temple itself all but mourned, and those brought down into ruin and destruction who crucified the Master of that very temple — perhaps also convicting them …

But what happened also seems to hint something else needful for our benefit: the veil that hid the holies of holies within, when the time arrived in which the law’s shadow had to be drawn together and the worship in types to cease, and the holies of holies to be opened to those justified through faith in Christ, is torn around, God as it were showing them to the worthy, so that henceforth, with nothing restraining, those who go in Christ’s track may run into the inner tent (Matthew 27:51).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the torn veil means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The quake, split rocks and risen saints signify a change for the better, the opening of the nations' hearts, and the abolition of death.
comments.comment: The earth was also shaken, signifying the transfer toward what is better — or also showing indignation against those who had outraged him. The splitting of the rocks is a sign that the nations’ “stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26) was opened to receive the gospel seed. The holy who rose and appeared to many did not alone receive the gift of resurrection ahead of time; it became a sign that death was abolished through Christ’s death. I think the law was also looking toward this when it commanded that one who killed unwillingly and fled should run back again to the homeland after the high priest’s death; for Christ’s death gave us who were liable the ascent into the Jerusalem above. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the signs at Christ's death.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The saints appeared only after Christ rose, to show that his death gives life; they rose as a sign, not to eternal life.
comments.comment:
… The rising of the bodies of the saints made manifest the death of Christ, being the cause of life (Mt 27:52).

Not indeed were they shown before the Lord's rising, because first the resurrection of the Savior had to be known, and then those rising through him were to be seen; and it is clear that they rose again for the sake of a sign; for the firstborn of the dead were not being raised to some eternal life, but just like the rest. …

So that it might not be thought that what happened was a fantasy, they were shown to many. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the saints appear after the resurrection.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ's power drew the centurion and some Jews who struck their breasts, as he said he would when lifted up.
comments.comment: And the crowds who had come to the spectacle were returning, striking their breasts — freeing themselves, perhaps, from impiety against Christ by crying out against the crucifiers, even if not openly, because of the leaders’ unholiness. So great was the power of the one being crucified — this centurion afterward proving steadfast in the faith (Matthew 27:54). The Lord was speaking truly when he said, “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself.” (John 12:32) For look: lifted on the precious cross, he began to net many into knowledge of the truth. He drew the centurion, and he also drew some of the Jews, who were striking their breasts, pricked in mind and looking up toward the Lord with the eyes of understanding (Luke 23:48).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the crowd and the centurion's response.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even the Jews noticed the divine power, but forgetfulness and misleading teachers weighed on them, while the mockers were struck.
comments.comment:
… Luke says that the crowds who came were 'beating their breasts and turning back'; thus the divine transcendence did not escape the notice even of the Jews, even in this very passion and dishonor of the Savior, but the usual forgetfulness of men weighed them down and the deception of the teachers led many astray. …

And the centurion believed, and those playing and mocking in this way were struck by what happened. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus was laid in a new tomb hewn in one rock because his burial, like his birth, had to be pure.
comments.comment: … For he was not like the rest of the dead: even in death he showed signs of life, the water and the blood (John 19:34), and was, if I may call him so, a new kind of corpse. It was right, then, that he should be placed in a new and clean tomb, so that, just as his birth was purer than every birth, because he was born not from intercourse but from a virgin, so his burial too might have purity. This purity is shown through the symbol of his body being laid in a new tomb, one not built of gathered stones with no natural unity, but standing in a single rock, united throughout, quarried and hewn. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus was laid in a new tomb cut from one rock.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The women brought spices because they expected the body to stay dead, as even the apostles did not yet grasp Scripture.
comments.comment: Since the Lord endured the suffering on the cross for us and gave his own flesh as the exchange for the life of all, and was in the tomb like one “helpless among the dead, free,” (Psalm 88:5) as the psalm sings, the women ran bringing what was needed for the care of the body, full of spices. For they thought he would lie with the others and remain dead in the tomb. And do not marvel if women did not know that, being God and life, he would dissolve corruption’s power and run back to life — when even to the apostles themselves the word about his resurrection seemed mere nonsense and a fabricated thing, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the women came to the tomb with spices.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Matthew and Mark mention the one angel who rolled the stone away, while Luke and John mention the two seen by the women, so the accounts agree.
comments.comment: … He did not notice, I think, that Matthew and Mark reported one (Matthew 28:2–5; Mark 16:5), and Luke and John two (Luke 24:4; John 20:12). These accounts were not contradictory. For those who recorded one say that this was the one who rolled away “the stone” from the tomb (Matthew 28:2); while the others say that the two are those who, “in dazzling clothing” (Luke 24:4), stood by the women who had come to the tomb, or those who were seen inside “sitting in white” (John 20:12). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: An angel rolled the stone away so that those who thought the Word dead would learn that he lives and goes before his followers.
comments.comment: … I do not want to labour over the details of the passage, nor to seem to philosophize out of season by setting out a figurative interpretation at this point. So I will speak of the narrative itself. On its face it appears more dignified that the lesser one, the servant, should have rolled away “the stone” than that he who was rising for the benefit of human beings should have done it himself. Not to mention that those who plotted against the Word, who wanted to kill him and to show everyone that he was dead and nothing at all, wanted his tomb never to be opened, so that no one might see the Word alive after their plot. But the angel of God, who comes for the salvation of human beings as fellow worker of the Angel, is stronger than the plotters and rolls away the heavy stone. He does this so that those who think the Word is dead may be persuaded that he “is not among the dead” (Luke 24:5–6) but lives and “goes before” (Matthew 28:7) those who wish to follow him. And he goes before them in order to show them what follows on from what he showed them earlier, when, in the first stage of their instruction, they could not yet take in things greater than those. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The angel tells them not to seek the living Lord among the dead, since he was raised to open the way for us into incorruption.
comments.comment: … So the women came to the tomb; and though they did not find Christ’s body, for love of him they see a holy angel (Matthew 28:5). He became for them an evangelist and herald of the resurrection: “Do not seek,” (Matthew 28:1–7) he says, “the one who is always living, who is life by nature, among the dead; for he is not here” — that is, in death and the tomb — “but he has been raised,” becoming for us rather than for himself the way of the run back into incorruption. For that is why he let himself down into emptying and underwent likeness toward us: so that “by the grace of God,” as blessed Paul says, “he might taste death for everyone,” (Hebrews 2:9) and this might become death’s death and the dissolution of the curse once brought upon the first-formed. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the angel's message means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Angels announced Christ's birth to the shepherds and now announce his resurrection, as the heavenly armies attend the Son.
comments.comment: … Know that angels evangelized the birth to the shepherds in Bethlehem, and now rational powers proclaim the resurrection. Heaven has therefore ministered to the proclamations about him, and the armies of the spirits above surround the Son as Master and Lord of all — even when he became flesh, that is, a human.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus did not appear to one woman alone, since Matthew has the two Marys meeting and worshiping him.
comments.comment: … But it is not even true that he appeared to one little woman alone. For it is written in the Gospel according to Matthew: “After the sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. And behold, there was a great earthquake; for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, approached and rolled away the stone” (Matthew 28:1–2). And a little later Matthew says: “And behold, Jesus met them” (clearly, the Marys mentioned before), “saying, ‘Greetings.’ And they came up, took hold of his feet and worshiped him” (Matthew 28:9). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He forbade touch, not worship, since only the new may touch the new.
comments.comment: … The Savior does not forbid worship, but he forbade touch, as John writes; for to be similarly mixed with him was no longer possible before the renewal of men; for it is proper for the new to touch the new. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus allows worship but not touch.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: His 'Rejoice' to the women lifts the reproach and curse laid on them in Genesis and leads them to good hope.
comments.comment: The female race has gained both the loosing of reproach and the overturning of the curse. For the one who once said to them, “In pains you will bear children,” (Genesis 3:16) gave them a pause when he met them in the garden and said, “Rejoice.” (Matthew 28:9) With exceeding gladness the women came to him — and he was healing what had suffered, and leading them into good hopes.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the risen Lord greets the women with 'Rejoice'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soldiers, like Judas, took silver and hid the marvels they had seen.
comments.comment: … And Judas indeed betrays Jesus for silver, overlooking the signs he saw, but the soldiers, having received sufficient silver—what they had seen they reported to the chief priests in advance, but the marvels they kept silent—and they spoke of things that did not happen. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the paid soldiers did.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Thieving disciples would not have died for his teaching.
comments.comment: … For the disciples, having stolen the body—as they themselves spread it abroad—would not have contended so genuinely for his teaching as to be dishonored and die for it. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the theft story is false.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Matthew's 'they doubted' is spelled out in John by Thomas, since each evangelist runs past some things.
comments.comment: You see how some of the evangelists run past certain things. For “they doubted” (Matthew 28:16–17) is clearly unfolded in John, where the one who doubted is shown — and he was Thomas. So mentioning the appearance in Judea that happened second also shows how the matter stood. But he said that he appeared to them in Galilee — which alone John seems to me to omit, since it lay before him to say the rest: how often he appeared, and where, and indeed how, narrating clearly (John 20:24–29).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Words spoken on Galilee's mountain, whose name means 'overturned', rolled like a wheel over the world, and the nations were baptized.
comments.comment:
… And it does not seem to me to be without purpose that these words were spoken on the mountain of Galilee and not elsewhere; for Galilee is interpreted as the 'overturned' by the Greek language.

Therefore also the wheel is called Gelgel.

So then, just as these words, having been brought forth from the mouth of the high mountain of salvation, rolled like a wheel against the inhabited world and ran over all, all the nations and cities were baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Mt 28:16-19).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Matthew's vision was seen by the eleven and many more.
comments.comment: John speaks of other visions; the one Matthew speaks of here the eleven saw, and not only they, but also the many, as is likely (Matthew 28:17).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'It was given to me' is said humanly, since the Son always had authority over all as God.
comments.comment: Still economically, and in a more human way, he said “it was given to me.” (Matthew 28:18) Yet he wants it understood that he has authority over all as God, and that, leaving the measure of the emptying, he ran back into the glory innate and always present to him, and is confessed God and Lord of all even with the flesh. So when he says “it was given to me,” it is not as if he first received it when he became human, but as receiving, in the rank of a human, what he always had because he exists from the Father and is God by nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Son can say authority was 'given' to him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Having authority in heaven, Christ received authority on earth too, so that earth may be brought to imitate heaven.
comments.comment: … after the resurrection, by the Lord to the eleven disciples: 'All authority has been given me, as in heaven, also on earth.' (Matthew 28:18) For having authority over those 'in heaven' — he says he has received in addition that 'on earth': those 'in heaven' having been enlightened even before by the Word, and at the 'consummation of the age' those 'on earth' too, through the authority given to the Son of God, imitating the things accomplished 'in heaven,' over which the Savior received authority. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is with his disciples always, not by place but by providence, and they bear fruit only by remaining in him.
comments.comment: God, then, in his kindness comes down to men, not in a spatial sense but by his providence. And the Child of God is with his own disciples not only at that time but always, fulfilling the words, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). And if “a branch cannot bear fruit unless it abides in the vine” (John 15:4), it is clear that the disciples of the Word as well, the spiritual “branches” (John 15:5) of the true vine, the Word (John 15:1), cannot bear the fruits of virtue unless they remain in the true vine, the Christ of God. He is with us too, whose place is here below on earth; and being with those everywhere who have grown into him, and indeed with those who do not know him, he is everywhere. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense Christ is 'with you always'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
